julienne.name: Julienne
julienne.short: Cut food into thin, even matchstick strips of 3 mm × 3 mm × 5-6 cm (1/8 in × 1/8 in × 2-2.5 in), usually from firm vegetables.
julienne.long:
Julienne is a classic cut that turns firm vegetables into thin, even sticks. The standard size is 3 mm × 3 mm × 5-6 cm (1/8 in × 1/8 in × 2-2.5 in). A very thin version, called fine julienne, is 1.5 mm (1/16 in) square. Strips of equal size cook at the same speed, look neat, and are easy to eat in salads, stir-fries, and garnishes.

Start by trimming a thin slice from a side so the vegetable lies flat and cannot roll. Cut it into even planks, stack a few planks, and cut them lengthwise into sticks. Work on a stable board with a sharp knife, and curl the fingertips of your guide hand into a claw grip so the knuckles guide the blade.

Julienne works best on firm foods such as carrot, celery, zucchini, bell pepper, and daikon. The most common mistake is planks of uneven thickness, which give sticks that cook unevenly, so take time to cut the planks evenly.
steps: Trim a thin slice from a side of the vegetable so it lies flat on the board.
Cut the vegetable into planks 3 mm (1/8 in) thick and 5-6 cm (2-2.5 in) long.
Stack a few planks, keeping the edges lined up.
Cut the stack lengthwise into sticks 3 mm (1/8 in) wide.
tips: Place a damp cloth under the board so it cannot slide while you cut.
Use a claw grip, with the fingertips curled in and the knuckles facing the blade, so your fingers stay out of the cutting path.
Keep the trimmings for stock or soup so nothing is wasted.
julienne.diagramAlt: Four numbered drawings show a carrot trimmed flat on a side, then cut into even planks, then the planks stacked, and finally cut lengthwise into thin matchstick strips.

brunoise.name: Brunoise
brunoise.short: Cut food into very small, even cubes of 3 mm (1/8 in) by first making julienne sticks and then slicing across them.
brunoise.long:
Brunoise is a very small, even cube, made by cutting a vegetable into julienne sticks and then slicing across them. The standard size is 3 mm (1/8 in) on each side. A fine brunoise is 1.5 mm (1/16 in). Cubes this small cook quickly, blend into sauces, and add color and flavor without large pieces.

Cut thin planks, cut the planks into square sticks, gather the sticks into a tidy bundle, and slice across the bundle at even intervals. Use a sharp knife and a stable board, and hold the bundle with a claw grip: fingertips curled in, with the knuckles guiding the side of the blade.

Brunoise is used for soup bases, sauce garnishes, and cold dishes with raw vegetables. The most common mistake is cutting sticks of uneven width, which gives cubes of different sizes, so check that the sticks are square before you cut across them.
steps: Trim a thin slice from a side of the vegetable so it lies flat, then cut it into planks 3 mm (1/8 in) thick.
Cut the planks into square sticks 3 mm (1/8 in) wide, which are julienne.
Gather the sticks into a tidy bundle and turn it 90 degrees.
Slice across the bundle at 3 mm (1/8 in) intervals to make small cubes.
tips: Cut the planks as evenly as you can, because every later cut depends on them.
Keep the fingertips of your guide hand curled in and the knife tip close to the board for control.
Move the finished cubes with the blunt back of the blade, never with the sharp edge.
brunoise.diagramAlt: Four numbered drawings show a vegetable cut into thin planks, the planks cut into square sticks, the sticks gathered into a bundle and turned, and the bundle sliced across into tiny cubes.

chiffonade.name: Chiffonade
chiffonade.short: Slice leafy herbs or greens into fine ribbons, usually 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in) wide, by stacking, rolling, and cutting across the leaves.
chiffonade.long:
Chiffonade is a way of cutting leafy herbs and greens into fine ribbons, usually 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in) wide. Stacking and rolling the leaves lets a single pass of the knife cut many leaves at the same time, and a clean cut bruises the leaves less than rough chopping does.

Remove any tough stems, stack 5-8 dry leaves, and roll them tightly into a cigar shape. Hold the roll with a claw grip and slice across it with a sharp knife, using a smooth motion. Then fluff the ribbons with your fingertips so they separate.

Use it for basil, mint, sage, spinach, kale, lettuce, and cabbage leaves, as a garnish or a fresh topping. The most common mistakes are a dull knife, which crushes the leaves and turns them dark, and wet leaves, which slip out of the roll. Cut basil just before serving because it darkens quickly.
steps: Remove tough stems and stack 5-8 dry leaves with the largest leaf at the bottom.
Roll the stack tightly into a cigar shape.
Hold the roll with a claw grip and slice across it at 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in) intervals.
Fluff the ribbons with your fingertips to separate them.
tips: Dry washed leaves completely, because wet leaves slip and stick together.
Use a very sharp knife so the leaves are cut cleanly rather than crushed.
Keep your fingertips curled back from the blade, because the rolled leaves can roll away as you cut.
chiffonade.diagramAlt: Four numbered drawings show leaves stacked, the stack rolled tightly into a cigar shape, the roll sliced across into thin ribbons, and the ribbons fluffed apart.

dice.name: Dice
dice.short: Cut food into even cubes, commonly small 6 mm (1/4 in), medium 12 mm (1/2 in), or large 20 mm (3/4 in), so the pieces cook evenly.
dice.long:
Dicing means cutting food into cubes of an even size. Classic sizes are small dice 6 mm (1/4 in), medium dice 12 mm (1/2 in), and large dice 20 mm (3/4 in). Pieces of the same size cook in the same time, so the food finishes evenly and looks tidy.

Trim a thin slice from a side so the food lies flat, then cut slabs as thick as the dice you want. Cut the slabs into sticks of the same width, turn the sticks, and cut across them into cubes. Keep the board stable on a damp cloth, use a sharp knife, and guide the blade with the knuckles of a claw grip.

Use small dice for quick-cooking vegetables and garnishes, medium dice for soups and sautés, and large dice for stews and roasting. The most common mistake is leaving the rounded edges untrimmed, which makes irregular cubes, so square off the block first and keep the trimmings for stock.
steps: Trim the food into a block with flat sides.
Cut the block into slabs as thick as the size of dice you want.
Stack the slabs and cut them into sticks of the same width.
Turn the sticks and cut across them into cubes.
tips: Choose the size by cooking time: small dice for fast cooking, large dice for long cooking.
Use a claw grip and keep the knife tip on the board so your fingers are never in front of the blade.
Halve onions and trim a flat side on potatoes and other round foods first so they cannot roll.
dice.diagramAlt: Four numbered drawings show a vegetable trimmed into a block, the block cut into slabs, the slabs cut into sticks, and the sticks turned and cut across into cubes.

mince.name: Mince
mince.short: Cut food into extremely small pieces, about 3 mm (1/8 in) or smaller, so the flavor of garlic, shallot, ginger, or herbs spreads evenly.
mince.long:
To mince is to cut food into extremely small pieces, about 3 mm (1/8 in) or smaller, which is the size of a brunoise or finer. It is used for aromatics such as garlic, shallot, ginger, and fresh herbs, so their flavor spreads evenly through a dish. The smaller the pieces, the more flavor is released.

With a sharp knife, slice the food thinly, then cut the slices into thin strips. Gather the strips and cut across them. Then rock the blade over the pile, keeping the tip on the board and pulling the pieces back together with the flat of the blade, until they are very fine.

Add minced garlic late in cooking and keep the heat moderate, because small pieces burn quickly and turn bitter. The most common mistake is chopping wet herbs, which turns them into a paste, so dry them first.
steps: Trim the food and cut it into thin slices.
Stack the slices and cut them into thin strips.
Gather the strips and cut across them into tiny pieces.
Rock the blade over the pile, pulling the pieces back together, until they are as fine as you need.
tips: Keep the fingertips of your guide hand away from the edge, and when rocking the blade, rest that hand flat on the top of the blade near the tip.
Sprinkle a little salt on garlic while mincing to stop it sticking to the knife.
Do not store minced garlic or herbs in oil at room temperature, because this can allow botulism bacteria to grow; keep them refrigerated and use them within 4 days.

batonnet.name: Bâtonnet
batonnet.short: Cut vegetables into square sticks of 6 mm × 6 mm × 5-6 cm (1/4 in × 1/4 in × 2-2.5 in), thicker than julienne.
batonnet.long:
Bâtonnet means little stick. It is a thicker cut than julienne: sticks measuring 6 mm × 6 mm × 5-6 cm (1/4 in × 1/4 in × 2-2.5 in). It is also the starting shape for a small dice, and it suits vegetable platters and roasted or sautéed side dishes.

Trim the vegetable into a rectangular block, slice it into planks 6 mm (1/4 in) thick, stack the planks, and cut them lengthwise into sticks of the same width. Use a stable board and a sharp knife, and keep the fingertips of your guide hand curled in a claw grip as you work.

Bâtonnets suit carrot, potato, celery, cucumber, and zucchini. Thicker sticks of 12 mm (1/2 in) are cut the same way for oven fries. The most common mistake is planks of uneven thickness, which give sticks that cook unevenly.
steps: Trim the vegetable into a block with flat sides about 5-6 cm (2-2.5 in) long.
Cut the block into planks 6 mm (1/4 in) thick.
Stack the planks and cut them lengthwise into sticks 6 mm (1/4 in) wide.
Check that the sticks are square and the same length.
tips: Trim a flat side on round vegetables such as carrots and potatoes before cutting so they cannot roll.
Use a claw grip and a sharp knife, because a dull blade slips and can cut your hand.
Soak cut potato sticks in cold water to remove surface starch, and dry them well before frying, because water makes hot oil spatter.

paysanne.name: Paysanne
paysanne.short: Cut vegetables into thin, flat pieces of about 12 mm × 12 mm × 3 mm (1/2 in × 1/2 in × 1/8 in) for rustic soups and stews.
paysanne.long:
Paysanne is a flat, thin cut from classic French cooking. The pieces are about 12 mm × 12 mm × 3 mm (1/2 in × 1/2 in × 1/8 in) and can be square, round, triangular, or rectangular, depending on the shape of the vegetable. The word means country style, and the cut is used for rustic soups and stews.

Cut the vegetable into long sticks about 12 mm (1/2 in) wide, or use a small round vegetable as it is, then slice across into thin pieces 3 mm (1/8 in) thick. Use a stable board, a sharp knife, and a claw grip. The thin shape gives a large surface, so the pieces cook fast and release their flavor into the broth.

Use paysanne for carrot, turnip, leek, potato, and celery root. The most common mistake is slices of uneven thickness, which leaves some pieces firm while others fall apart.
steps: Trim the vegetable into sticks about 12 mm (1/2 in) wide.
Line up the sticks with the ends together.
Slice across them into pieces 3 mm (1/8 in) thick.
tips: Cut the slices as thin as you can keep them consistent, because the thin shape is the point of this cut.
Keep a claw grip and slice with a smooth, controlled motion rather than pressing down hard.
Add paysanne vegetables to soup in order of cooking time, with the firmest vegetables first.

tourne.name: Tourné
tourne.short: Shape a vegetable by hand into a small 7-sided barrel about 5 cm (2 in) long, with blunt ends, for even cooking and an elegant look.
tourne.long:
Tourné is a decorative cut in which a vegetable is shaped by hand into a small barrel with 7 even sides, about 5 cm (2 in) long, and blunt ends. The name means turned. Because all the pieces have the same shape and size, they cook evenly and look elegant on a plate.

Cut the vegetable into pieces about 5 cm (2 in) long and trim each to a rough barrel. Hold the piece in one hand and the blade of a small paring knife against it in the other. Pull the blade down in a short curved stroke while you turn the piece against the blade. Keep the fingers of the holding hand out of the path of the blade and work slowly.

Tourné is used for potato, carrot, turnip, zucchini, and mushroom, usually cooked by steaming, boiling, or glazing. The most common mistake is cutting too deep in a stroke, which leaves flat patches instead of smooth curved sides, so take thin strokes.
steps: Cut the vegetable into pieces about 5 cm (2 in) long.
Peel each piece and trim it to a rough barrel with narrower ends.
Hold the piece between your thumb and fingers and place the blade of a small paring knife near the top.
Pull the blade down in a short curved stroke while turning the piece against the blade.
Repeat until the piece has 7 even sides and blunt ends.
tips: Use a small, sharp paring knife, because a dull blade slips and is more likely to cut your hand.
Practice on potatoes, which are firm and inexpensive.
Keep cut potatoes in cold water until cooking so they do not turn brown, and use the trimmings for stock or soup.
tourne.diagramAlt: Five numbered drawings show a vegetable cut into short pieces, a piece peeled and trimmed to a rough barrel, the piece held with a small knife near the top, a curved stroke turning the piece against the blade, and the finished 7-sided barrel.

supreme.name: Supreme
supreme.short: Cut citrus segments free of peel, white pith, and membrane to get clean, juicy pieces of fruit.
supreme.long:
A supreme is a citrus segment removed from the fruit with no peel, white pith, or membrane. The result is a clean, juicy piece of fruit that can be used in salads, desserts, and sauces. Orange, grapefruit, lemon, and lime can all be cut this way.

Cut off the top and bottom so the fruit sits flat, then slice away the peel and pith in strips, following the curve of the fruit and working over a bowl to catch the juice. Hold the fruit in your palm, cut along the membrane on each side of a segment with a thin, sharp knife, and lift the segment out. Squeeze the leftover membrane to release the rest of the juice.

The most common mistakes are leaving white pith, which tastes bitter, and cutting too far into the flesh, which wastes fruit. Keep the juice for dressings or drinks.
steps: Cut off the top and bottom of the fruit so it sits flat on the board.
Slice away the peel and white pith in strips from top to bottom, following the curve of the fruit.
Hold the fruit in your palm over a bowl to catch the juice.
Cut along the membrane on each side of a segment and lift the segment out.
Repeat for every segment, then squeeze the leftover membrane over the bowl.
tips: Use a thin, very sharp knife and always cut away from your fingers, because the fruit is slippery.
Choose firm fruit with thick skin, which is easier to peel cleanly.
Wash and dry the fruit before cutting so no dirt or germs from the skin are carried into the flesh.
supreme.diagramAlt: Five numbered drawings show a citrus fruit with the top and bottom cut off, the peel and pith sliced away in strips, the fruit held over a bowl, a knife cutting along the membrane beside a segment, and the loose segments collected in the bowl.

butterfly.name: Butterfly
butterfly.short: Cut a thick piece of meat, poultry, or shellfish almost through horizontally and open it flat like a book so it cooks faster and more evenly.
butterfly.long:
To butterfly is to cut a thick piece of food almost through horizontally and open it flat like a book. This makes the piece thinner and wider, so it cooks faster and more evenly, and it gives a larger surface for browning, stuffing, or marinade. It is used for chicken breast, pork chops, leg of lamb, and shrimp.

Place the food on a stable board with a hand flat on top and the fingers out of the path of the blade. Slice through the thickest side, parallel to the board, and stop about 1 cm (3/8 in) from the opposite edge to leave a hinge. Open the piece and press it flat. For shrimp, cut along the back and spread it open.

Cook poultry to a core temperature of 74 °C (165 °F), and pork and lamb to 63 °C (145 °F) followed by a rest of 3 minutes. The most common mistake is cutting all the way through, which leaves separate pieces that cook unevenly.
steps: Place the food on a stable board with a hand flat on top.
Slice through the thickest side, parallel to the board, stopping about 1 cm (3/8 in) from the opposite edge.
Open the piece like a book.
Press it flat, or cover it with plastic wrap and pound it gently to an even thickness.
tips: Wash the knife, board, and hands with hot soapy water after cutting raw meat or poultry.
Slice slowly with a long, sharp knife and keep your hand flat on top, away from the blade.
Check the core temperature with a thermometer, because thin pieces can overcook very fast.
butterfly.diagramAlt: Four numbered drawings show a thick chicken breast on a board with a hand flat on top, a knife slicing through the thick side and stopping short of the edge, the piece opened like a book, and the opened piece pressed flat.

score.name: Score
score.short: Make shallow cuts, usually about 3 mm (1/8 in) deep or less, in the surface of food to help it cook, absorb flavor, or hold its shape.
score.long:
To score is to make shallow cuts in the surface of food without cutting through it. Scoring lets heat, salt, and marinade enter, helps fat melt out, stops skin from curling, and creates a pattern. A typical depth is 3 mm (1/8 in) or less, with cuts 1-2 cm (1/2-3/4 in) apart, often in a diamond pattern.

Use a very sharp knife and cut with light, even pressure. For duck breast or pork skin, cut through the skin and into the fat layer only, not into the meat. For fish, cut shallow slashes across the skin so it does not curl in the pan. Scoring bread dough follows the same idea but cuts deeper.

It is also used for ham, squid, and thick vegetables such as eggplant. The most common mistake is cutting too deep, which lets juices escape and dries the food.
steps: Pat the surface dry so the knife does not slip.
Hold the food steady on a stable board.
Cut shallow parallel lines about 1-2 cm (1/2-3/4 in) apart, usually no deeper than 3 mm (1/8 in).
Turn the food and cut a set of lines across the first set to make a diamond pattern, if you want.
tips: Use a very sharp knife, because a dull blade drags and slips.
Cut away from your hand and keep your fingers well clear of the line of the cut.
Wash the knife and board with hot soapy water after scoring raw meat or poultry.

bias-cut.name: Bias cut
bias-cut.short: Slice food at a slant of about 45 degrees instead of straight across, which gives longer oval pieces with more surface for faster cooking.
bias-cut.long:
A bias cut slices food at a slant, usually about 45 degrees to its length, instead of straight across. This exposes more surface, so the pieces cook faster and brown better, and the long oval shapes look attractive. It is also called a diagonal cut.

Hold the knife at about 45 degrees to the food and slice at even intervals of about 5 mm (1/4 in), or thicker if the dish needs it. Keep the angle the same for every slice and hold the food with a claw grip, so the knuckles guide the blade. Use a stable board and a sharp knife.

It suits long, narrow foods such as carrot, celery, green onion, asparagus, zucchini, and baguette. It is common in stir-fries. The most common mistake is changing the angle or thickness as you go, which gives uneven cooking, so check your first few slices.
steps: Place the food on a stable board.
Angle the knife blade to about 45 degrees against the food.
Slice at even intervals, keeping the same angle each time.
tips: Use a claw grip and let your knuckles guide the side of the blade.
Slice firm vegetables with a smooth forward push rather than pressing down.
Keep each slice the same thickness so all the pieces finish cooking together.

rondelle.name: Rondelle
rondelle.short: Slice a round or cylindrical food straight across into even discs, commonly 3-12 mm (1/8-1/2 in) thick.
rondelle.long:
A rondelle is a round slice cut straight across a cylindrical or round food, such as a carrot, cucumber, or sausage. The word means little disc. Thickness can vary with the dish, from 3 mm (1/8 in) for thin slices up to 12 mm (1/2 in) for thick slices.

Trim the end so the food is flat, then slice straight down at even intervals. Hold the food with a claw grip, with the fingertips curled in so the knuckles guide the side of the blade. Use a stable board and a sharp knife. For a very thick vegetable, split it lengthwise and lay the flat side down so it cannot roll. The slices will then be half-rounds.

Use rondelles for soups, stir-fries, salads, and roasting. The most common mistake is slices of different thickness, which cook at different speeds. Keep the knife vertical, because a tilted blade makes wedge-shaped slices.
steps: Trim the end off the vegetable so it has a flat face.
If the vegetable is thick, split it lengthwise and lay the flat side down so it cannot roll.
Slice straight across at even intervals using a claw grip.
tips: Cut the slices the same thickness so they cook at the same speed.
Never hold a round vegetable with your fingers in front of the blade; stabilize it on a flat side first.
Use a sharp knife, because a dull knife slips on the skin of vegetables such as carrots and cucumbers.

macedoine.name: Macédoine
macedoine.short: A mix of vegetables or fruit cut into small, even cubes of about 6 mm (1/4 in), served as a garnish, side dish, or salad.
macedoine.long:
Macédoine is a mixture of vegetables or fruits cut into small, even cubes of about 6 mm (1/4 in), often with several colors. The word is used in French cooking for a mixed vegetable garnish, and it also names a salad or a fruit dessert made from the same mixed dice.

Cut each ingredient into planks, then sticks, then cubes of the same size. Firm vegetables such as carrot, turnip, and potato are boiled separately in salted water until just tender, then drained and cooled. Soft ingredients such as peas or cooked beans are added at the end. Use a stable board, a sharp knife, and a claw grip.

Serve it hot as a side dish, or cold with mayonnaise as a salad. The most common mistake is cooking all the vegetables together, which leaves some soft and others firm, so cook each vegetable separately.
steps: Cut each ingredient into planks 6 mm (1/4 in) thick.
Cut the planks into sticks 6 mm (1/4 in) wide.
Cut across the sticks into cubes of the same size.
Cook each firm vegetable separately until just tender, drain, cool, and then combine them.
tips: Keep every ingredient the same size so the mixture looks even and eats well.
Drain cooked vegetables well before mixing with mayonnaise so the salad is not watery.
Keep a salad with mayonnaise at 4 °C (40 °F) or below, and do not leave it out for more than 2 hours.

saute.name: Sauté
saute.short: Sautéing cooks small pieces of food quickly in a little fat in a wide pan over medium-high heat, with frequent stirring or tossing.
saute.long:
Sauté comes from a French word meaning to jump, which describes how food moves in the pan. Small, evenly cut pieces cook fast in a thin layer of oil or butter over medium-high heat. The exposed surfaces brown through the Maillard reaction, a browning process that speeds up above about 140 °C (284 °F) and builds savory flavor.

Use a wide pan so the pieces sit in a loose layer and moisture can escape as steam. Heat the pan first, add the fat, and add the food when the fat shimmers. Stir or toss often so every side browns evenly. Sauté suits vegetables, mushrooms, thin cuts of meat, and shrimp. Cook poultry pieces until they reach 74 °C (165 °F).

The most common mistake is crowding the pan. Too much food cools the pan and releases water, so the food steams and turns gray instead of browning. Cook in batches when needed.
steps: Cut the food into pieces of similar size so they cook evenly.
Heat a wide pan over medium-high heat, then add a thin layer of oil or butter.
Add the food in a loose layer when the fat shimmers.
Stir or toss often until the pieces are browned and just tender.
Remove the food from the pan right away so it does not overcook.
tips: Pat wet food dry with a towel before it goes into the pan so it browns instead of steaming.
Mix a little oil with butter, or use clarified butter, so the butter does not burn at higher heat.
Keep water droplets away from hot fat, because they make it spatter.

sear.name: Sear
sear.short: Searing cooks the surface of food over very high heat to form a deep brown crust, usually before or after another cooking method.
sear.long:
Searing browns the outside of meat, fish, or vegetables quickly over very high heat. The dry, hot surface triggers the Maillard reaction, which speeds up above about 140 °C (284 °F) and creates the brown crust and rich roasted flavor. Searing does not seal in juices, as is sometimes claimed; its purpose is flavor and texture.

Pat the food very dry and season it. Heat a heavy pan, such as cast iron or stainless steel, until it is very hot, then add a thin layer of oil with a high smoke point. Lay the food in the pan away from you and leave it untouched until the underside is deep brown and the food lifts easily, usually 2-3 minutes. Then turn it and brown the other side.

The most common mistake is moving the food too early or searing wet food, which gives a gray, steamed surface. Searing alone does not cook thick cuts through, so finish them in the oven or over lower heat.
steps: Pat the food dry with a towel and season it.
Heat a heavy pan over high heat until it is very hot.
Add a thin layer of oil with a high smoke point, then lay the food in the pan away from you.
Leave the food untouched until a deep brown crust forms and it lifts easily.
Turn the food and brown the other side.
Finish thicker pieces in the oven or over lower heat until they reach a safe core temperature.
tips: Check the core temperature with a thermometer: 74 °C (165 °F) for poultry, 71 °C (160 °F) for ground meat, and 63 °C (145 °F) for fish and for whole cuts of beef, pork, and lamb, which then need a rest of 3 minutes.
Sear in batches so the pan stays hot and the food browns instead of steaming.
If the oil smokes heavily, lower the heat and turn on the exhaust fan, because burnt oil tastes bitter.

roast.name: Roast
roast.short: Roasting cooks food uncovered in the hot, dry air of an oven so the outside browns and the inside cooks through.
roast.long:
Roasting surrounds food with hot, dry oven air. Heat reaches the food from all sides, so the surface dries and browns while the inside cooks more gently. Browning through the Maillard reaction speeds up above about 140 °C (284 °F). Fat on meat and oil on vegetables help the surface brown and keep it from drying out.

Choose a pan with low sides so hot air can circulate, and heat the oven fully before the food goes in. Vegetables roast well at 200 °C (400 °F), while large cuts of meat often cook more evenly at 160-180 °C (320-350 °F). Use a thermometer to judge doneness instead of time alone.

Rest meat after roasting so the juices settle. The most common mistake is crowding the pan, which traps steam and stops browning.
steps: Heat the oven fully before cooking.
Dry the food, then coat it lightly with oil and season it.
Place the food in a pan with low sides, spaced so hot air reaches each piece.
Roast until the surface is browned and the inside is tender or has reached a safe core temperature.
Rest large cuts of meat under loose foil for at least 10 minutes before cutting.
tips: Roast poultry until the thickest part reaches 74 °C (165 °F), and whole cuts of beef, pork, and lamb to 63 °C (145 °F) followed by a rest of at least 3 minutes.
Stir or turn vegetables partway through so they brown evenly.
Set meat on a rack in the pan so hot air reaches the underside.

bake.name: Bake
bake.short: Baking cooks food in the enclosed, steady dry heat of an oven, most often batters, doughs, and casseroles that need gentle, even heat.
bake.long:
Baking uses the steady, dry heat of an oven to set and brown foods such as bread, cakes, cookies, casseroles, and fish. The food is usually a soft mixture or dough that needs structure. Heat makes steam and gas expand, proteins set, and starches firm up, which gives the food its crumb and shape. The surface browns through the Maillard reaction above about 140 °C (284 °F) and, when sugar is present, through caramelization.

Most baking uses 160-200 °C (320-400 °F). Heat the oven fully before the food goes in, and place the pan in the middle for even heat. Treat the recipe time as a guide and judge doneness by cues: a golden color, a firm edge, and, for cakes, a skewer that comes out clean.

The most common mistake is opening the oven door too early, which drops the temperature and can make cakes and breads sink. Oven thermostats are often inaccurate, so an oven thermometer helps.
steps: Heat the oven fully to the temperature in the recipe.
Grease or line the pan, then fill it with the batter, dough, or food.
Place the pan in the middle of the oven.
Bake until the surface is golden and, for cakes, a skewer inserted in the center comes out clean.
Cool baked goods on a wire rack so steam can escape and the base stays crisp.
tips: Measure baking ingredients by weight when possible, because baking depends on exact ratios.
Avoid opening the oven door early in the baking time, because the temperature drops.
Bake casseroles and dishes that contain poultry or leftovers until the center reaches 74 °C (165 °F).

broil.name: Broil
broil.short: Broiling cooks food with intense heat from an element or flame above it, browning the top surface quickly.
broil.long:
Broiling uses very strong radiant heat from above, from an electric element or gas flame at the top of the oven. It is similar to grilling, but the heat is above the food instead of below. The top surface browns and chars quickly while the inside cooks. It works for thin cuts of meat, fish fillets, sliced vegetables, and for melting and browning cheese or sugar toppings.

Place the food on a pan or rack so the surface sits about 10 cm (4 in) below the heat, and preheat the broiler for 5 minutes. Stay close, because food goes from browned to burnt in less than a minute. Turn thicker pieces partway through.

The most common mistakes are walking away and placing thick cuts too close to the heat, which burns the outside before the inside is cooked. Place thick pieces lower, or start them in the oven.
steps: Set the oven rack so the food will sit about 10 cm (4 in) from the heat.
Preheat the broiler for 5 minutes.
Put the food on a pan or rack, lightly oiled and seasoned.
Broil while watching closely, until the top is browned.
Turn thicker pieces, or move them lower, to finish cooking through to a safe core temperature.
tips: Never leave the broiler unattended, because dripping fat can flare and catch fire.
Use a metal or broiler-safe pan, because glass can shatter under intense heat.
If fat catches fire, switch off the heat and keep the oven door closed, and never use water.

pan-fry.name: Pan-fry
pan-fry.short: Pan-frying cooks food in a shallow layer of hot fat that reaches partway up the food, giving a crisp, golden crust.
pan-fry.long:
Pan-frying sits between sautéing and deep-frying. The pan holds more fat than a sauté, often about 6 mm (1/4 in) deep, so more of the food touches hot oil. Fat carries heat better than air, so the surface dries and browns fast and forms a crisp crust while the inside cooks.

Heat the fat over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay the food away from you, cook until golden, turn it, and cook the other side. Coated foods such as breaded cutlets and fish fillets do well here. Drain the food on a rack or paper towel and season it while hot.

Common mistakes are starting with cold fat, which makes the food greasy, and crowding the pan, which lowers the temperature. Adjust the heat so the fat bubbles gently around the food without smoking.
steps: Pat the food dry and coat it if the recipe asks for it.
Heat a layer of oil about 6 mm (1/4 in) deep in a heavy pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Lay the food in the pan away from you, leaving space between the pieces.
Cook until the underside is golden, then turn the food carefully with tongs or a spatula.
Cook the other side, then drain the food on a rack or paper towel.
tips: Dry the food well, because water makes hot fat spatter.
Lower the heat if the fat smokes, and keep a lid nearby to smother a fire, never using water.
Cut into the thickest piece of chicken to check that it is cooked through, or confirm 74 °C (165 °F) with a thermometer.

deep-fry.name: Deep-fry
deep-fry.short: Deep-frying cooks food fully submerged in oil heated to 175-190 °C (350-375 °F), producing a crisp, golden outside.
deep-fry.long:
In deep-frying, the food is completely covered by hot oil. The oil heats the food's surface above the boiling point of water, so the moisture there turns to steam and escapes as bubbles, and the surface dries into a crisp crust. This outward steam also keeps most oil out and the inside moist.

Use oil with a high smoke point in a deep, heavy pot filled no more than 1/2 full. Hold the oil at 175-190 °C (350-375 °F), measured with a thermometer. Fry in small batches, because cold food lowers the oil temperature. Drain the food on a rack and season it right away.

The most common mistake is oil that is too cool, which gives greasy food, or too hot, which burns the outside before the inside is cooked. Never leave hot oil unattended.
steps: Fill a deep, heavy pot no more than 1/2 full with oil that has a high smoke point.
Heat the oil to 175-190 °C (350-375 °F), checking with a thermometer.
Dry the food well, then lower it gently into the oil, away from you, a few pieces at a time.
Fry until golden and cooked through, adjusting the heat to hold the temperature.
Lift the food out, drain it on a rack, and season it while hot.
tips: Dry the food thoroughly, because water makes hot oil spatter and boil over.
If oil catches fire, switch off the heat and cover the pot with a lid, and never use water.
Let used oil cool completely before straining it, discard it when it is dark, foamy, or smells off, and never pour it down the drain.

stir-fry.name: Stir-fry
stir-fry.short: Stir-frying cooks small pieces of food very fast over high heat in a wok or wide pan, with constant stirring and tossing.
stir-fry.long:
Stir-frying comes from Chinese cooking. Food is cut small and evenly, then cooked in a little oil over the highest heat the pan can hold while being moved constantly. The high heat browns the food quickly and keeps vegetables crisp and meat tender. The smoky flavor from fast, intense heat is called wok hei in Chinese cooking.

Prepare everything before you start, because cooking takes only a few minutes. Heat the wok until it is very hot, add oil, and cook in order: meat first, then firm vegetables, then soft vegetables, with garlic and ginger for a few seconds. Add the sauce last. Cook meat in small batches so the pan stays hot.

The most common mistakes are too much food in the pan, which steams it, and pieces of different sizes. Stir-fried food should stay tender-crisp, so stop cooking as soon as it is done.
steps: Cut all ingredients into small, even pieces and measure the sauce before heating the pan.
Heat a wok or wide pan over the highest heat until very hot, then add a thin layer of oil with a high smoke point.
Cook the meat in small batches, stirring and tossing, then remove it.
Cook firm vegetables, then soft vegetables, and add garlic and ginger for only a few seconds.
Return the meat, add the sauce, and toss until everything is coated and hot.
tips: Add garlic and ginger last, because they burn in seconds and turn bitter.
Cut into the thickest piece of chicken to confirm it is white all the way through, with clear juices and no pink.
Dry the food and keep a lid nearby, because splashes and flare-ups are common over high heat.

toast.name: Toast
toast.short: Toasting browns the surface of bread, nuts, seeds, spices, or grains with dry heat, adding crunch and a deeper, roasted flavor.
toast.long:
Toasting uses dry heat, with no added liquid, to brown food and dry it slightly. Heat drives off surface moisture and starts the Maillard reaction, which speeds up above about 140 °C (284 °F). This creates new flavor compounds and a crisper texture. In nuts, seeds, and whole spices, heat also releases aromatic oils.

Toast nuts, seeds, and spices in a dry pan over medium heat, or on a tray in an oven at 160 °C (320 °F), and stir or shake them often. Bread can be toasted in a toaster, under a broiler, or in a dry pan. Watch for a golden color and a nutty smell, then move the food to a cool plate immediately, because it keeps cooking from stored heat.

The most common mistake is looking away. Small pieces go from golden to burnt in seconds, and burnt nuts and spices taste bitter and are best discarded.
steps: Spread nuts, seeds, or whole spices in an even layer in a dry pan or on a baking tray.
Heat them over medium heat, or in an oven at 160 °C (320 °F), stirring or shaking often.
Watch for a light golden color and a nutty or spicy smell.
Tip the food onto a cool plate right away to stop the cooking.
Let it cool completely before grinding or storing.
tips: Toast in small amounts so everything browns evenly.
Cool toasted nuts and seeds fully before storing them, because trapped warmth makes them soft and can spoil them.
Never leave a toaster, broiler, or hot pan unattended, because small pieces and crumbs can ignite.

caramelize.name: Caramelize
caramelize.short: Caramelizing heats sugar, or the natural sugars in foods such as onions, until they brown and develop a sweet, deep, slightly bitter flavor.
caramelize.long:
Caramelization is the browning of sugar by heat alone. Table sugar starts to caramelize at about 160 °C (320 °F) and then breaks down into many new flavor compounds as it darkens from pale gold to deep amber. It is different from the Maillard reaction, which needs protein, but both often happen together in cooking.

Sugar can be caramelized dry, by melting it in a heavy pan, or wet, with a little water, which cooks more evenly and is easier to control. Watch the color, not the clock. Onions, carrots, and other vegetables caramelize slowly over medium-low heat as water evaporates and their sugars brown; onions need about 30-60 minutes.

The most common mistakes are stirring sugar too early, which makes it crystallize, and cooking it too far, because past deep amber it burns and turns bitter. Remove it from the heat slightly early, because the pan stays hot.
steps: Spread sugar in a heavy, light-colored pan, or add a little water to wet it.
Heat over medium heat without stirring, and swirl the pan gently so the sugar colors evenly.
Cook until the sugar reaches the amber color you want.
Remove the pan from the heat right away.
Carefully add warm cream or butter, or pour the caramel out, as the recipe directs.
tips: Hot caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin, so never touch it, and cool any burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
Add liquid to hot caramel carefully, using a long spoon and standing back, because it bubbles and spits violently.
For onions, use a wide pan and medium-low heat, and add a splash of water when the pan looks dry.

flambe.name: Flambé
flambe.short: Flambé means igniting alcohol in a hot pan so it briefly flames, which burns off some alcohol and adds a light, caramelized flavor.
flambe.long:
Flambé comes from a French word meaning flamed. A spirit such as brandy, rum, or whiskey is added to a hot pan of food and set alight. The flame burns the alcohol vapor and lightly caramelizes sugars on the food's surface. It adds a sweet, rounded flavor and a dramatic display, but it removes only part of the alcohol, so the dish is not alcohol-free.

Use a spirit of about 40% alcohol by volume, because weaker drinks will not ignite and much stronger ones burn too fiercely. Measure a small amount, no more than 60 ml (1/4 cup), into a cup first. Take the pan off the heat, add the spirit, and light the vapor at the edge of the pan with a long lighter, leaning back. Let the flames die down, or cover the pan with a lid to put them out.

The most common mistake is using too much alcohol, which makes a tall, dangerous flame.
steps: Measure a small amount of spirit into a cup, away from the stove and any open flame.
Place a lid that fits the pan within reach, and clear away cloths and anything hanging overhead.
Take the pan off the heat before adding the spirit, because vapors can ignite from a gas flame.
Light the vapor at the edge of the pan with a long lighter, holding your arm and face back.
Let the flames die down on their own, or cover the pan with the lid to put them out.
tips: Never pour spirit straight from the bottle into the pan, because the flame can travel back into the bottle.
Keep a lid ready to cover the pan, because cutting off the air puts out the flame, and never use water.
Tie back long hair, roll up loose sleeves, and keep the pan away from overhead cabinets and the exhaust hood.

smoke.name: Smoke
smoke.short: Smoking flavors or cooks food with smoke from smoldering wood, adding aroma and color; hot smoking cooks the food, cold smoking does not.
smoke.long:
Smoking exposes food to smoke from slowly burning hardwood or wood chips. Smoke carries aromatic compounds that settle on the surface and give a distinctive flavor, a darker color, and some preservation. In hot smoking, the food cooks in the smoky chamber, usually at 107-121 °C (225-250 °F), which also moves the food quickly through the temperature range where bacteria grow. Cold smoking keeps the temperature low, does not cook the food, and needs proper curing first, so it is a separate technique.

Use hardwoods such as oak, hickory, apple, or cherry. Avoid softwoods such as pine and any treated wood. Good smoke is thin and pale blue; thick white smoke leaves a bitter taste. Season or cure the food first, dry the surface so smoke sticks, and keep the temperature steady. Cook to safe core temperatures, such as 74 °C (165 °F) for poultry.

The most common mistake is too much smoke, which makes food bitter. Heavily smoked and charred food is best eaten in moderation.
steps: Season or cure the food, then let the surface dry so smoke sticks.
Light the fuel and bring the smoker to a steady temperature with thin, pale smoke.
Place the food on the rack away from direct heat and close the lid.
Hold the temperature steady and add wood only as needed.
Cook until a thermometer shows a safe core temperature, then rest the food.
tips: Use only untreated hardwood or purpose-made wood chips, never painted, treated, or resinous wood.
Smoke only outdoors, away from buildings, because burning wood and charcoal produce carbon monoxide.
Keep the lid closed as much as possible, because each opening lets out heat and smoke.

grill.name: Grill
grill.short: Grilling cooks food on a rack over direct heat from charcoal, wood, or gas, giving a smoky flavor and browned grill marks.
grill.long:
In grilling, food sits on a metal grate above a heat source such as burning charcoal, wood, or gas flames. Heat reaches the food by radiation and by contact with the hot grate, which leaves browned marks. Fat dripping onto the heat creates smoke that adds flavor. The Maillard reaction, which browns the surface, speeds up above about 140 °C (284 °F).

Set up 2 zones: a hot zone with fire below for browning, and a cooler zone with no fire below for gentle finishing. Clean and lightly oil the grate, preheat for 10-15 minutes, and pat the food dry. Brown the food over the hot zone, then move thicker pieces to the cooler zone with the lid closed until they reach a safe core temperature.

The most common mistake is cooking only over very high heat, which chars the outside while the inside stays raw. Pressing on meat squeezes out juices, so turn food only when it releases from the grate.
steps: Light the charcoal or gas and let the grill preheat with the lid closed.
Set up a hot zone over the fire and a cooler zone with no fire below.
Clean the grate, then oil it lightly or oil the dry food.
Brown the food over the hot zone until it has marks and releases easily from the grate.
Move thicker pieces to the cooler zone and close the lid until they are cooked through.
Rest meat for a few minutes before serving.
tips: Check the core temperature with a thermometer: 74 °C (165 °F) for poultry, 71 °C (160 °F) for ground meat, and 63 °C (145 °F) for fish and for whole cuts of beef, pork, and lamb, which then need a rest of 3 minutes.
Use separate plates and tongs for raw and cooked food to avoid spreading bacteria.
Grill only outdoors, because charcoal produces carbon monoxide; open the lid before lighting a gas grill, and trim excess fat to limit flare-ups.

griddle.name: Griddle
griddle.short: Griddling cooks food on a flat, heavy metal surface heated from below, giving even browning across the whole contact area.
griddle.long:
A griddle is a flat, heavy metal plate or pan, often cast iron or steel, heated from below. Because the whole underside of the food touches the hot metal, heat passes by direct contact and the food browns evenly. Fat and juices stay on the plate instead of falling away, so the food cooks partly in its own fat. This suits eggs, pancakes, burgers, sliced vegetables, flatbreads, and sandwiches.

Preheat the griddle for 5-10 minutes until the surface is evenly hot. Brush on a thin layer of oil or butter. Place the food in an even layer with space between the pieces. A heavy plate holds heat well, so the food browns steadily.

Common mistakes are putting food on before the surface is hot, which makes it stick, and using too much oil, which fries the food instead of browning it. Scrape residue off while the surface is warm, not hot.
steps: Place the griddle over the heat and preheat it for 5-10 minutes.
Brush a thin layer of oil or butter over the surface.
Add the food with space between the pieces.
Cook until the underside is browned, then turn the food.
Scrape the surface clean while it is warm, not hot.
tips: Cook burgers and other ground meat until the center reaches 71 °C (160 °F).
Treat the surface as hot for a long time after the heat is off, because heavy metal stays hot.
Use a flat metal spatula, and wipe cast iron with a thin film of oil to protect it from rust.

air-fry.name: Air-fry
air-fry.short: Air-frying cooks food by blowing very hot air at high speed around it in a small chamber, giving a crisp surface with little or no oil.
air-fry.long:
An air fryer is a small countertop convection oven with a powerful fan. Hot air moves quickly around the food and removes surface moisture, so the outside dries and browns in a way similar to frying. It is not true frying, because the food is not in oil. A small amount of oil, or none, helps the surface brown and crisp.

Typical settings are about 180-200 °C (350-400 °F). Cut food into evenly sized pieces, pat it dry, and toss it with a small amount of oil. Spread the food in a loose layer in the basket so air reaches every side, and shake or turn the basket partway through. Frozen breaded foods, vegetables, chicken pieces, and reheated leftovers do well.

The most common mistake is overfilling the basket, which blocks airflow and leaves food pale and soft. Cook in batches instead.
steps: Preheat the air fryer if the maker recommends it.
Pat the food dry and toss it with a small amount of oil.
Spread the food in a loose layer in the basket.
Cook at about 200 °C (400 °F), shaking or turning the food partway through.
Check the browning and the core temperature before serving.
tips: Check that poultry reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part, because a browned surface can hide an undercooked center.
Use dry coatings such as breadcrumbs, because wet batter drips through the basket and burns, and weigh down any parchment paper with food so the fan cannot blow it onto the heating element.
Leave space around the air fryer for its vents, and clean the basket and tray often so built-up grease does not smoke.

char.name: Char
char.short: Charring blackens the surface of food over very high direct heat, adding a smoky, slightly bitter flavor and softening the flesh inside.
char.long:
Charring cooks the surface of food until it is dark brown to black in places. Very high direct heat, from an open flame, a grill, a broiler, or a hot dry pan, burns the outer layer. This adds a smoky, slightly bitter flavor that balances sweet and rich foods. It is used for peppers, eggplant, onions, corn, tomatoes, and cuts of meat.

Dry the food and coat it lightly with oil. Place it close to the heat and turn it as each side darkens in spots. Peppers and eggplant can be charred until the skin blisters and blackens all over; then cover them in a bowl for 10 minutes to steam, and the skin slides off easily.

The most common mistake is charring so far that the food turns to ash, which tastes acrid. Heavily burnt areas contain compounds that may raise health risks when eaten often, so char lightly and cut away any parts that are fully black and brittle.
steps: Dry the food and coat it lightly with oil.
Place it over very high direct heat, such as a flame, grill, or broiler.
Turn the food as each side darkens in spots, until the surface is blistered and dark.
For peppers and eggplant, cover them in a bowl for 10 minutes to steam, then peel off the skin.
Trim away any parts that are fully burnt.
tips: Hold the food with long tongs and stay clear of flare-ups, because dripping fat can ignite quickly.
Char lightly rather than heavily, and cook meat to a safe core temperature before judging its color.
Open a window or use the exhaust fan, because charring makes a lot of smoke.

boil.name: Boil
boil.short: Cook food in water heated until it bubbles hard, at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level.
boil.long:
Boiling cooks food in water heated until it bubbles hard. Water boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level and cannot get hotter in an open pot, so higher heat only makes more bubbles and more evaporation. At altitude water boils at a lower temperature, about 1 °C (1.8 °F) less for every 300 m (1000 ft), so food takes longer to cook.

Use a large pot with plenty of water so the temperature does not drop much when food is added. A rolling boil, with large bubbles that keep breaking the surface, suits pasta, potatoes, and green vegetables. Salt the water for flavor. Delicate foods such as dumplings and eggs do better in gentler bubbling, because hard boiling knocks them about and toughens proteins.

The most common mistake is crowding the pot, which stops the water boiling and leaves food unevenly cooked or mushy. Cook in batches if needed and cover the pot to bring the water to a boil faster.
steps: Fill a large pot with water and add salt if the recipe calls for it.
Cover the pot and heat until the water bubbles hard.
Add the food carefully and wait for the water to return to a boil.
Cook until the food is done, then drain it in a colander.
tips: Lower food into the water with a spoon or basket to avoid splashes and scalds.
At high altitude, expect longer cooking times for beans, pasta, and eggs.
Tip the colander away from your face when draining, because rising steam can cause burns.

simmer.name: Simmer
simmer.short: Cook food in liquid kept just below a boil, with small bubbles rising gently to the surface.
simmer.long:
Simmering holds liquid at about 85-95 °C (185-203 °F), hotter than poaching but gentler than boiling. Small bubbles rise slowly and break the surface now and then, rather than churning it. This steady, moderate heat cooks food through without tearing it apart or toughening it, and it slowly draws flavor into the liquid.

To simmer, bring the liquid to a boil, then lower the heat until only a few small bubbles appear. Partly cover the pot if the liquid is still bubbling too hard. Check the bubbles from time to time and adjust the heat, because the same setting gives stronger bubbling as the liquid thickens.

Simmering suits soups, stocks, sauces, beans, grains, and tough cuts of meat. The most common mistake is letting the pot boil hard, which makes stock cloudy, toughens meat, and breaks delicate food apart.
steps: Bring the liquid to a boil over high heat.
Lower the heat until only small bubbles rise to the surface.
Partly cover the pot if the liquid starts to boil again.
Check the bubbles often and adjust the heat to keep them gentle.
tips: Skim any foam from the surface of stocks and soups with a spoon for a clearer result.
Stir sauces that contain starch, milk, or cream often so they do not stick or scorch on the base of the pan.
Cool leftover soups and stocks quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate them within 2 hours.

poach.name: Poach
poach.short: Cook delicate food gently in liquid held at 70-80 °C (158-176 °F), with almost no bubbles.
poach.long:
Poaching cooks food in liquid that is hot but not bubbling, at 70-80 °C (158-176 °F). At this temperature proteins set slowly, so eggs, fish, chicken, and fruit stay tender and moist instead of tightening and drying out. The liquid can be water, stock, milk, wine, or syrup, and it often adds flavor to the food.

Heat the liquid in a wide pan until tiny bubbles cling to the base, then lower the heat so the surface only trembles. Lower the food in gently and keep the liquid steady; a thermometer helps. Fish and chicken are done when the thickest part reaches a safe temperature, and fruit is done when a knife slides in easily.

Poaching suits foods that are fragile or lean. The most common mistake is letting the liquid reach a simmer, which toughens the food and tears the white of a poached egg into ragged strands.
steps: Heat the liquid in a wide pan until tiny bubbles form on the bottom.
Lower the heat so the surface barely moves, keeping the liquid at 70-80 °C (158-176 °F).
Lower the food gently into the liquid.
Cook without letting the liquid simmer until the food is done.
Lift the food out with a slotted spoon and drain it.
tips: Cook poached chicken until the thickest part reaches 74 °C (165 °F) and fish until it reaches 63 °C (145 °F).
A poached egg with a runny yolk is not fully cooked, so serve eggs cooked until firm to anyone who is pregnant, elderly, very young, or ill.
Use very fresh eggs and a little vinegar in the water to help the white set neatly around the yolk.
poach.diagramAlt: A wide pan of liquid is shown in numbered stages: heating until tiny bubbles form on the bottom, lowering the heat so the surface barely moves, lowering the food in, cooking gently, and lifting the food out with a slotted spoon.

steam.name: Steam
steam.short: Cook food in the hot vapor rising from boiling water, without letting the food touch the water.
steam.long:
Steaming cooks food with the vapor from boiling water, which is at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level. Steam carries a lot of heat and releases it as it condenses on the cooler food, so cooking is fast and even. Because the food never sits in water, flavor, color, and nutrients that dissolve in water stay in the food.

Put water in a pot, set a rack, basket, or perforated tray above the water level, and bring the water to a boil. Add the food, cover tightly, and keep the water at a steady boil so steam keeps rising. Vegetables, fish, dumplings, and buns suit steaming. Cooking time depends on the size of the pieces, so test vegetables with the tip of a knife and check fish and poultry with a thermometer.

The most common mistakes are letting the water boil dry, which can scorch the pot, and lifting the lid too often, which lets steam escape and slows cooking.
steps: Pour water into a pot, keeping the water level below the rack or basket.
Bring the water to a boil.
Place the food on the rack or in the basket and cover with a tight lid.
Cook until the food is tender, adding hot water if the pot runs low.
tips: Lift the lid away from your face, because escaping steam can cause serious burns.
Cook fish until it reaches 63 °C (145 °F) and poultry until it reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part.
Do not overcrowd the basket, so steam can circulate around every piece.

blanch.name: Blanch
blanch.short: Briefly cook food in boiling water, then cool it quickly, to set color, loosen skins or prepare it for freezing.
blanch.long:
Blanching is a short dip in boiling water followed by fast cooling. The brief heat sets the bright color of green vegetables, softens the surface, loosens the skins of tomatoes and peaches, and stops the enzymes that make frozen vegetables lose flavor and color. The cooling stops the cooking so the inside stays crisp.

Use a large pot of well-salted boiling water so the temperature barely drops when the food goes in. Cook small pieces for about 30 seconds for thin leaves, up to 3 minutes for thicker vegetables, until the color brightens and the food is just tender. Then move it straight into a bowl of ice water until it is fully cold, and drain it well.

The most common mistake is leaving the food in the water too long, or cooling it too slowly, so it turns dull and soft.
steps: Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil.
Add the food and cook it briefly until the color brightens.
Move the food straight into a bowl of ice water.
Drain the food and pat it dry.
tips: Before freezing, follow a tested blanching time for each vegetable, because too short a time can leave the enzymes active, and dry the food well so ice crystals do not build up.
Work in small batches so the water keeps boiling when the food goes in.
To peel tomatoes or peaches, cut a shallow cross in the skin first and lift them out as soon as the skin starts to split.
blanch.diagramAlt: A pot of boiling water is shown in numbered stages: the water at a rolling boil, food lowered into it, the food moved into a bowl of ice water, and the food drained and patted dry.

braise.name: Braise
braise.short: Brown food, then cook it slowly in a covered pot with a small amount of liquid until it is very tender.
braise.long:
Braising combines browning with slow, moist cooking. The surface of the food is first browned in hot fat, which builds deep flavor. The food then cooks in a covered pot with liquid that reaches only part of the way up its sides, at low heat. The lid traps steam, and the slow heat turns the tough connective tissue in meat into gelatin, making it soft and juicy.

The liquid should stay at a gentle simmer, on the stove or in an oven set to about 150 °C (300 °F). Large cuts take several hours, and the food is done when a fork slides in with almost no resistance. Braising suits tough cuts such as beef shank, pork shoulder, and lamb shanks, as well as firm vegetables such as cabbage and fennel.

The most common mistake is adding too much liquid, which boils the food and dilutes the sauce. Cooking at too high a heat also dries and toughens the meat.
steps: Brown the food well on all sides in hot fat, then set it aside.
Cook onion and other aromatics in the same pot, then add liquid and scrape up the browned bits.
Return the food to the pot so the liquid comes about halfway up its sides.
Cover and cook at low heat, on the stove or in the oven, until a fork slides in easily.
Remove the food and reduce the cooking liquid to a sauce.
tips: Pat meat dry before browning so it browns instead of steaming.
Keep the lid on and avoid opening the oven often, so the temperature stays steady.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and reheat them to 74 °C (165 °F) before serving.
braise.diagramAlt: A heavy pot is shown in numbered stages: food browning in hot fat, onion and liquid added to the pot, the food returned with the liquid halfway up its sides, the covered pot cooking in an oven, and the sauce reducing beside the removed food.

stew.name: Stew
stew.short: Cook small pieces of food slowly in enough liquid to cover them, so the liquid becomes a thick, flavorful sauce.
stew.long:
Stewing cooks small, evenly cut pieces of meat, fish, beans, or vegetables in liquid that covers or nearly covers them. It is similar to braising but uses smaller pieces and more liquid, and the liquid is served with the food as part of the dish. The gentle heat softens tough pieces, and the juices of the food blend with the liquid into a rich sauce.

Brown the meat first if you want deeper flavor, add vegetables and liquid, then keep the pot at a gentle simmer, about 85-95 °C (185-203 °F), with the lid partly or fully on. Add quick-cooking vegetables later so they do not turn to mush. The stew is ready when the meat is tender and the sauce has thickened as much as you like.

The most common mistake is boiling the stew hard, which toughens the meat and breaks the vegetables apart. Cut the pieces to the same size so they finish together.
steps: Cut the food into pieces of similar size.
Brown the meat in hot fat, then add onion and other aromatics.
Add enough liquid to cover the food and bring it to a simmer.
Cover and cook at low heat, adding quick-cooking vegetables near the end.
Cook until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick enough.
tips: Skim excess fat from the surface before serving if the stew looks greasy.
If the sauce is too thin, remove the lid and simmer until it thickens.
Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate them within 2 hours, and reheat them to 74 °C (165 °F) before serving.

shock.name: Shock
shock.short: Plunge hot food into ice water right after cooking to stop the cooking and keep its color and texture.
shock.long:
Shocking means moving food from boiling water straight into very cold water, usually water with plenty of ice. Food keeps cooking from its own stored heat after it leaves the pot, and cooling it fast stops that process. This keeps green vegetables bright, pasta and noodles firm, and boiled eggs free of a gray ring around the yolk.

Prepare a large bowl of ice and cold water before you start cooking, with more ice than you think you need. Lift the food from the boiling water with a slotted spoon or a strainer and put it into the ice water at once. Leave it until it feels cold to the touch, then drain it well, because wet food dilutes sauces and dressings.

The most common mistake is using too little ice, which warms up quickly and cools the food too slowly.
steps: Fill a large bowl with ice and cold water.
Lift the cooked food out of the boiling water with a slotted spoon.
Put the food into the ice water at once.
Leave it until it feels cold to the touch, then drain and dry it.
tips: Use roughly equal amounts of ice and water so the bath stays very cold.
Shocked vegetables can be reheated briefly in butter or hot water just before serving.
Refrigerate cooled food within 2 hours if it is not served right away.

parboil.name: Parboil
parboil.short: Partly cook food in boiling water, then finish it by roasting, frying, stir-frying, or another method.
parboil.long:
Parboiling means boiling food only until it is partly cooked, not all the way through. It is the first stage of a cook that ends with another method. The boiling softens the inside of dense foods such as potatoes, carrots, and thick vegetables, so the final step can focus on browning, crisping, or adding flavor without the outside burning before the inside is done.

Cook the food in salted boiling water until the outside is tender but the center is still firm when pierced with a knife, which usually takes a few minutes depending on the size. Drain well and let the food steam dry for a few minutes, then finish it. Parboiled potatoes, for example, form a crisp crust when roasted, especially if they are shaken in the pot to roughen the surface.

Parboiling lasts longer than blanching, and the food is usually not cooled in ice water. The most common mistake is boiling too long, so the food falls apart in the final step.
steps: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.
Add the food and boil it until the outside is just tender and the center is still firm.
Drain well and let the food steam dry for a few minutes.
Finish cooking by roasting, frying, or another method.
tips: Parboil meat or poultry only if you will finish cooking it immediately, because partly cooked meat can allow bacteria to grow.
Dry the food well before roasting or frying so it browns and does not spatter.
If you must wait before finishing, cool the food quickly and refrigerate it within 2 hours.

reduce.name: Reduce
reduce.short: Simmer or boil a liquid uncovered so water evaporates, leaving a thicker, more concentrated sauce.
reduce.long:
Reducing means cooking a liquid in an open pan so that some of the water turns to steam and escapes. What remains is thicker, with more concentrated flavor, sugar, and salt. Stocks, wine, juices, and sauces are reduced to make glossy, intense sauces without adding starch.

Use a wide pan, because a larger surface lets water evaporate faster. Bring the liquid to a simmer or a gentle boil and leave it uncovered, stirring only occasionally and skimming off foam as it appears. A liquid is reduced enough when it coats the back of a spoon and a finger drawn through it leaves a clear line. Sauces thicken a little more as they cool.

The most common mistake is reducing too far or too fast over high heat, which makes the sauce sticky, bitter, or burnt.
steps: Pour the liquid into a wide pan.
Bring it to a simmer or a gentle boil over medium heat, uncovered.
Skim off any foam and stir only occasionally while the liquid level drops.
Stop when the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
tips: Add salt only after reducing, because salt becomes more concentrated as the water leaves.
Dip a wooden spoon handle in the liquid at the start to mark the level, so you can see how much has evaporated.
Stay near the pan, because a nearly reduced sauce can scorch within moments.
reduce.diagramAlt: A wide pan is shown in numbered stages: liquid poured in, the liquid heated to a simmer, the liquid level dropping as steam rises and foam is skimmed off, and a spoon coated with the thickened sauce.

deglaze.name: Deglaze
deglaze.short: Add liquid to a hot pan after searing to dissolve the browned bits stuck to the bottom and turn them into a sauce.
deglaze.long:
When meat or vegetables brown in a pan, sugars and proteins stick to the bottom as dark, flavor-rich bits. Deglazing uses a liquid such as stock, wine, vinegar, or water to dissolve those bits so they can flavor a sauce, gravy, or soup. The hot pan and the liquid together lift the bits easily as you scrape.

Remove the food from the pan and pour off the excess fat, leaving only a thin layer. Return the pan to medium-high heat, pour in the liquid, and scrape the base with a wooden spoon until the bits dissolve. Simmer briefly to reduce the liquid to a light sauce.

The most common mistake is deglazing a pan where the bits have burnt rather than browned. Black bits taste bitter, so start with a fresh pan instead. Non-stick pans form few brown bits, so use stainless steel or cast iron.
steps: Remove the cooked food from the pan and keep it warm.
Pour off all but a thin layer of fat.
Return the pan to medium-high heat and pour in the liquid.
Scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon until the browned bits dissolve, then simmer to make a sauce.
tips: Take the pan off the heat before adding wine or spirits, because the alcohol can flare up over a gas flame, and pour slowly with your face back, because the liquid steams and spits.
Scrape while the pan is still hot, since the bits release more easily than after the pan cools.
Taste the sauce before adding salt, because stock and reduced liquids are already salty.
deglaze.diagramAlt: A pan is shown in numbered stages: the seared food lifted out, excess fat poured off, liquid poured into the hot pan, and a wooden spoon scraping the browned bits into a simmering sauce.

en-papillote.name: En papillote
en-papillote.short: Bake food sealed inside a folded packet of parchment paper or foil so it cooks in its own steam.
en-papillote.long:
En papillote is a French term for cooking food inside a sealed packet, usually made of parchment paper or foil. Heat from the oven turns the moisture in the food, and any liquid added, into steam. The packet traps the steam, so the food cooks gently, stays moist, and keeps its aroma, and little or no fat is needed.

Cut a large sheet of parchment paper, fold it, and place the food next to the fold with seasoning, thinly sliced vegetables, herbs, and a splash of wine or stock. Fold the paper over and crimp the edges tightly so no steam escapes. Bake at about 200 °C (400 °F) on a tray until the packet puffs up. Fish fillets, chicken pieces, and tender vegetables suit this method well.

The most common mistake is a poor seal, which lets steam leak so the food dries out. Open the packet carefully, because hot steam escapes at once.
steps: Cut a large sheet of parchment paper and crease it down the middle.
Place the seasoned food, vegetables, and a little liquid on one side of the fold.
Fold the paper over the food and crimp the edges tightly to seal.
Bake on a tray until the packet puffs up with steam.
Open the packet carefully, keeping your face away from the steam.
tips: Slice vegetables thinly so they finish cooking at the same time as the main food.
Cook fish to 63 °C (145 °F) and chicken to 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part.
Choose parchment paper over foil for acidic ingredients such as lemon or tomato, which can react with foil.
en-papillote.diagramAlt: A sheet of parchment paper is shown in numbered stages: creased down the middle, food and liquid placed on one side, the edges crimped closed, the puffed packet baking on a tray, and the packet opened with steam rising.

pressure-cook.name: Pressure-cook
pressure-cook.short: Cook food in a sealed pot that traps steam, raising the pressure and temperature so food cooks much faster.
pressure-cook.long:
A pressure cooker is a sealed pot with a locked lid. As the liquid inside heats, the steam cannot escape, so the pressure rises. Under pressure, water boils at a higher temperature, roughly 115-120 °C (239-248 °F), so food cooks in a fraction of the usual time. It works well for beans, stocks, tough cuts of meat, and grains.

Add at least the minimum amount of liquid stated in the manual, because the steam is made from that liquid. Do not fill the pot above 2/3 of its capacity, or above 1/2 for foods that foam or expand, such as beans, grains, and pasta. Lock the lid, heat until the pot reaches pressure, then lower the heat to keep it steady and start timing. Release the pressure as the manual instructs, either by letting it fall naturally or by using the quick-release valve.

The most common mistakes are overfilling the pot and opening it too early. Do not use a pressure cooker for home canning, because its settings are not tested for jars.
steps: Add the food and at least the minimum amount of liquid given in the manual.
Check that the sealing ring is in place, then close and lock the lid.
Heat until the pot reaches pressure, then lower the heat to keep the pressure steady.
Cook for the time given in the recipe.
Release the pressure as the manual describes before opening the lid.
tips: Never force the lid; it opens easily once the pressure is gone, so if it resists, wait and follow the manual.
Release pressure only as the manual describes, keeping your hands and face away from the steam vent.
Check before every use that the vent and valve are clean and unblocked, because foaming foods can clog them.

slow-cook.name: Slow-cook
slow-cook.short: Cook food for many hours at a low, steady temperature in a covered pot, usually an electric slow cooker.
slow-cook.long:
Slow cooking uses low, steady heat over many hours, so tough cuts of meat and dense vegetables become tender while the flavors blend. An electric slow cooker has a heating element around a ceramic or metal pot, with a tight lid that holds in moisture, so very little liquid is lost. The contents come to a gentle simmer over time, and the food is held there until it is done.

Fill the pot 1/2-2/3 full, keep the lid on, and do not lift it often, because each lift loses heat and adds cooking time. The low setting takes roughly twice as long as the high setting. Add dairy, delicate vegetables, and fresh herbs near the end so they do not break down. Check with a thermometer that poultry reaches 74 °C (165 °F).

The most common mistake is adding too much liquid. Food releases juices and little evaporates, so the sauce turns thin. Use less liquid than in a stove-top recipe.
steps: Cut the food into even pieces and brown the meat first if you want deeper flavor.
Place firm vegetables on the bottom and the meat on top.
Add less liquid than a stove-top recipe would use, since little evaporates.
Cover with the lid and cook on low or high without lifting the lid.
Stir in delicate ingredients such as herbs, cream, or peas near the end.
tips: Never put frozen meat in a slow cooker; thaw it in the refrigerator first so it does not stay in the danger zone of 4-60 °C (40-140 °F) for long.
Boil dried red kidney beans hard for 10 minutes before slow cooking, because a slow cooker may not get hot enough to destroy their natural toxin.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours instead of leaving them in the pot on the warm setting.

fold.name: Fold
fold.short: Folding gently combines a light, airy mixture with a heavier mixture using a scooping and turning motion that keeps the trapped air.
fold.long:
Folding is a gentle mixing method used to combine a light, aerated mixture, such as whipped egg whites or whipped cream, with a heavier base such as a batter or a custard. The air bubbles are what make mousses, soufflés and sponge cakes light, and stirring would burst them, so folding uses slow, wide movements instead of beating.

Stir about 1/3 of the light mixture into the base to loosen it, then add the rest on top. Cut a flexible spatula down through the middle to the bottom of the bowl, sweep it along the bottom and up the side, and lay the mixture over the top. Turn the bowl a small amount and repeat.

Stop as soon as no streaks remain. The most common mistake is over-folding, which deflates the mixture, or stopping too early, which leaves pockets of unmixed egg white or dry flour.
steps: Stir about 1/3 of the light mixture into the heavier base to loosen it.
Add the remaining light mixture on top of the base.
Cut a spatula down through the middle, sweep along the bottom of the bowl, and lift the mixture up and over the top.
Turn the bowl a small amount and repeat until no streaks remain.
tips: Use a wide, flexible spatula and a wide bowl so you can lift the mixture without crushing the air out of it.
Add whipped egg whites in 2 or 3 additions instead of adding them all together.
Raw or lightly cooked egg whites carry a small risk of Salmonella, so use pasteurized eggs for children, older adults, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system.
fold.diagramAlt: A bowl and spatula shown in 4 numbered marks: a portion of light mixture is stirred into the base, the remaining light mixture is added on top, the spatula cuts down and sweeps up and over, and the bowl is turned a small amount before the next stroke.

whisk.name: Whisk
whisk.short: Whisking beats ingredients with a wire tool to blend them smoothly, add air, or form an emulsion.
whisk.long:
Whisking means moving ingredients quickly with a wire whisk in a bowl or pan. A whisk has many thin wires, so it breaks liquids into small droplets and traps air. This lets it smooth lumps out of sauces, combine oil and water-based liquids into an emulsion, and whip egg whites or cream into foam.

Hold the bowl steady and move the whisk in fast circles or back and forth, using your wrist rather than your whole arm. For foam, lift the whisk through the mixture to carry in air. For a sauce on the stove, reach the corners of the pan so nothing sticks and scorches. A balloon whisk with many wires is best for adding air, and a flatter, stiffer whisk suits thick sauces.

The most common mistakes are whipping egg whites in a bowl that has traces of fat or egg yolk, which stops them foaming, and whisking cream too long, which turns it grainy.
steps: Place the ingredients in a clean, dry bowl or pan that is large enough to allow movement.
Hold the bowl steady and move the whisk in fast circles or back and forth.
Lift the whisk through the mixture to add air when making a foam.
Stop when the mixture is smooth, thick, or holds the shape you want.
tips: Rest the bowl on a folded damp towel so that it does not slide while you whisk.
Add oil to an emulsion slowly while whisking constantly so that it does not separate.
Wipe the bowl with a little lemon juice or vinegar and dry it well before whipping egg whites.

cream.name: Cream
cream.short: Creaming beats soft butter with sugar until pale and fluffy, trapping air that makes baked goods light and tender.
cream.long:
Creaming is the method of beating soft butter with sugar until the mixture becomes lighter in color and fluffy. The sugar crystals cut tiny air pockets into the fat. During baking, these pockets expand with steam and with gas from the leavening, such as baking powder, which gives cakes and cookies a fine, tender crumb.

Use butter that is soft but still cool, about 20 °C (68 °F): a finger pressed into it should leave a dent without sinking in. Beat with an electric mixer for 3-5 minutes, or longer by hand with a wooden spoon, scraping down the sides of the bowl partway through, until the mixture is pale and has clearly increased in volume. Then add the eggs gradually, beating well after each egg.

The most common mistakes are using butter that is too cold, which cannot hold air, or too warm and almost melted, which gives dense, greasy results. Stopping too early also gives a heavy cake.
steps: Cut the butter into pieces and leave it until it is soft but still cool, about 20 °C (68 °F).
Add the sugar to the butter in a bowl.
Beat on medium speed for 3-5 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl partway through.
Stop when the mixture is pale and fluffy and has increased in volume.
Add the eggs gradually, beating well after each egg.
tips: Press a finger into the butter: it should leave a dent without feeling greasy or sliding.
If the mixture looks curdled after adding eggs, beat in a spoonful of the flour from the recipe.
Do not eat raw batter, because raw eggs and raw flour can carry harmful bacteria.

knead.name: Knead
knead.short: Kneading presses, folds and stretches dough to develop gluten, which gives bread its structure and chew.
knead.long:
Kneading is the repeated pressing, folding and stretching of dough. When wheat flour is mixed with water, 2 proteins join to form gluten, a stretchy network. Kneading lines up and strengthens this network so that the dough can hold the gas made by yeast and rise into a springy loaf.

By hand, push the dough away from you with the heel of your hand, fold it back over itself, turn it a small amount, and repeat. Most bread doughs need about 10 minutes by hand, or about 5-8 minutes in a stand mixer with a dough hook on low speed. The dough is ready when it feels smooth and elastic and springs back slowly when you press it with a finger.

The most common mistake is adding too much flour, which gives dry, dense bread. Do not knead tender doughs such as pastry or biscuit dough, which need very little handling.
steps: Turn the dough onto a lightly floured or oiled surface.
Push the dough away from you with the heel of your hand to stretch it.
