Fold the stretched dough back over itself and turn it a small amount.
Repeat for about 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth and elastic.
Press a finger into the dough: it should spring back slowly.
tips: Use as little extra flour as you can, because it makes the bread drier.
Let a very sticky dough rest for 20 minutes and then knead again, because it becomes easier to handle as the flour absorbs water.
Keep fingers, hair and loose sleeves away from a running mixer.

marinate.name: Marinate
marinate.short: Marinating soaks raw food in a seasoned liquid, often with acid and oil, to add flavor to its surface before cooking.
marinate.long:
Marinating means soaking raw food in a seasoned liquid before cooking. A marinade usually contains oil, an acid such as vinegar, citrus juice or yogurt, salt, and flavorings such as garlic or herbs. The flavor reaches only the outer layer of the food, so a marinade adds surface flavor rather than deep flavor. Acid can soften the surface, but too much time makes meat mushy and fish chalky.

Put the food and marinade in a covered container made of glass, ceramic or stainless steel, or in a sealed bag, and keep it in the refrigerator at 4 °C (40 °F) or below. Never marinate at room temperature. As a guide, fish and shellfish in an acidic marinade need no more than 30 minutes, chicken up to 12 hours, and beef, pork and lamb up to 24 hours.

A marinade that has touched raw meat, poultry or fish contains bacteria. Discard it, or boil it for at least 1 minute before using it as a sauce. Pat the food dry before cooking so that it browns.
steps: Mix the oil, acid, salt and flavorings in a non-reactive bowl or a sealable bag.
Add the food and turn it to coat all sides.
Cover and refrigerate for the recommended time.
Lift the food out and pat it dry before cooking.
Discard the used marinade, or boil it for at least 1 minute before using it as a sauce.
tips: If you want a sauce, set aside a portion of fresh marinade before adding any raw food to it.
Avoid aluminum, copper and uncoated cast-iron containers with acidic marinades, because the acid reacts with the metal and gives a metallic taste.
Sugary marinades burn quickly, so wipe off the excess before cooking over high heat.

brine.name: Brine
brine.short: Brining soaks food in salted water so that meat stays juicy and is seasoned all the way through.
brine.long:
Brining means soaking food in salt dissolved in water before cooking. Salt changes the proteins in meat so they hold more water while cooking, which keeps lean meat such as chicken, turkey and pork chops juicier. The salt also seasons the meat deeply, which salting only the surface just before cooking cannot do.

A reliable ratio is 5-6% salt by weight of the water, which is 50-60 g of salt for each 1 liter of water. Stir until the salt dissolves, and cool the brine completely before adding raw food. Keep the covered container in the refrigerator at 4 °C (40 °F) or below for the whole time. Use about 15-30 minutes for fish fillets and shrimp, 1-2 hours for chicken pieces and pork chops, and 4-8 hours for a whole chicken.

The most common mistakes are brining too long, which makes meat salty and spongy, and brining at room temperature, which lets bacteria grow. Do not brine meat sold as kosher, pre-salted or enhanced with a salt solution, and reduce the salt in the recipe afterward.
steps: Weigh 50-60 g of salt for each 1 liter of water.
Stir until the salt dissolves completely, and add sugar or herbs if wanted.
Cool the brine completely to refrigerator temperature, then submerge the raw food, weighing it down so it stays covered.
Refrigerate at 4 °C (40 °F) or below for the recommended time.
Remove the food, pat it dry, and cook it without adding much extra salt.
tips: Different salts weigh differently by volume, so measure salt by weight and not by spoon.
Never brine at room temperature, and never reuse a brine that has held raw meat, poultry or fish.
Dissolve the salt in a small amount of warm water, then add cold water or ice, to make a cold brine quickly.

dredge.name: Dredge
dredge.short: Dredging coats food lightly in flour, cornmeal or crumbs before cooking so it browns well and forms a crisp crust.
dredge.long:
Dredging is coating food in a dry ingredient such as flour, cornmeal, starch or breadcrumbs before cooking. The coating absorbs moisture from the surface and browns in hot fat, which gives a golden, crisp crust and helps thicken pan sauces. A thin dry layer also helps a wet coating, such as beaten egg, stick to the food.

Pat the food dry and season it, then press it into the dry coating and shake off the extra so that only a thin, even layer stays. Cook it right away in hot fat, because the coating turns pasty if it waits. For a thicker crust, use a 3-step breading line: flour, then beaten egg, then crumbs. Use 1 hand for the dry steps and the other for the wet step to avoid clumps on your fingers.

The most common mistakes are leaving a thick, uneven layer of flour, which turns gummy, and coating the food long before cooking.
steps: Pat the food dry and season it.
Spread the flour, cornmeal or crumbs in a shallow dish.
Press the food into the dry coating and turn it to cover all sides.
Shake off the excess so that only a thin layer remains.
Cook the food right away in hot fat.
tips: Season the flour as well as the food, because plain flour tastes bland.
Discard any leftover coating that has touched raw meat, poultry or fish.
Shake off the excess coating over the dish and not over the pan, so that loose flour does not burn in the fat.

infuse.name: Infuse
infuse.short: Infusing steeps flavorful ingredients such as herbs, tea or spices in a liquid so their flavor and aroma pass into it.
infuse.long:
Infusing means letting an ingredient steep in a liquid so that its flavor, aroma and color pass into the liquid. Flavor compounds dissolve into water, milk, cream, oil, vinegar or alcohol. Tea, vanilla milk, herb oils and flavored syrups are all infusions.

For a hot infusion, heat water, milk or cream until it steams, remove it from the heat, add the flavoring, cover the pot to keep the aroma in, and steep: about 3-5 minutes for black tea, and 15-30 minutes for herbs or vanilla in milk or cream. Then strain out the solids. Oil needs only gentle warming, never smoking heat. For a gentler flavor, steep in the refrigerator for several hours.

The most common mistakes are boiling delicate herbs, which makes them taste bitter and dull, and steeping tea or herbs too long, which draws out bitterness. Taste along the way and strain when the flavor is right.
steps: Heat water, milk or cream until it steams, warm oil gently, or keep the liquid cold for a gentle infusion.
Add the flavoring and cover the pot.
Steep for the recommended time.
Taste, and remove the flavoring when the flavor is strong enough.
Strain the liquid and use it, or cool it and refrigerate.
tips: Crush or lightly bruise herbs and spices to release more flavor.

Keep oil infused with fresh garlic, herbs or chilies in the refrigerator and use it within 3 days, even if the oil was heated, because at room temperature it can grow the bacteria that cause botulism.
Cover the pot while steeping so the aroma does not escape.

macerate.name: Macerate
macerate.short: Macerating soaks fruit in sugar, alcohol or acid so it softens and releases juice, creating a flavorful syrup.
macerate.long:
Macerating means soaking pieces of fruit in sugar, alcohol or acid so that they soften and release their juice. Sugar draws water out of the fruit cells by osmosis, and the juice then dissolves the sugar into a syrup. Alcohol such as a liqueur adds flavor, and acid such as lemon juice keeps colors bright and balances sweetness.

Slice or halve the fruit and toss it gently with sugar, about 15-30 g for each 250 g of fruit, depending on how ripe it is. Cover and leave it for 30-60 minutes, stirring now and then. The fruit and its syrup are good over cakes, yogurt, ice cream and tarts.

The most common mistakes are macerating too long, which makes the fruit mushy, and using underripe fruit, which stays hard and sour. Cut fruit must not stand at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
steps: Wash, dry, and slice or halve the fruit.
Toss the fruit gently with sugar, and with alcohol or lemon juice if using.
Cover and leave for 30-60 minutes, stirring now and then.
Spoon the fruit and its syrup over the dish.
tips: Taste the fruit before adding sugar, and add it gradually, because ripe fruit needs less.
Refrigerate the fruit if it will stand longer than 1 hour.
Keep the leftover syrup to flavor drinks or to reduce into a sauce.

zest.name: Zest
zest.short: Zesting removes the thin, colored outer peel of citrus fruit, which holds aromatic oils, and leaves the bitter white pith behind.
zest.long:
Zest is the thin, colored outer layer of the peel of citrus fruit such as lemons, limes and oranges. It holds fragrant oils that give a strong citrus flavor without the sourness of juice. The white layer beneath it, called the pith, is bitter and should be left on the fruit.

Wash the fruit with warm water and dry it well, because the peel may carry wax or residues. Hold a fine grater over a bowl and draw the fruit across it with light pressure, turning the fruit after each stroke so that you take only the colored layer. A vegetable peeler removes wide strips that can be cut into thin strips or used to flavor drinks and syrups. Zest before juicing, because a whole fruit is easier to hold.

The most common mistake is grating down into the white pith, which tastes bitter.
steps: Wash the fruit with warm water and dry it well.
Hold a fine grater or a vegetable peeler over a bowl.
Draw the fruit across the grater with light pressure, taking only the colored layer.
Turn the fruit after each stroke to avoid the white pith.
Juice the fruit afterward if the recipe needs juice.
tips: Choose unwaxed fruit when possible, and scrub it well.
Grate onto parchment paper so that you can collect all of the fine zest.
In cooked sauces and soups, add zest near the end, because long heating drives off its aroma.

sift.name: Sift
sift.short: Sifting passes dry ingredients through a fine mesh to break up lumps, add air, and mix them evenly.
sift.long:
Sifting means passing dry ingredients such as flour, cocoa, powdered sugar or baking powder through a fine mesh sieve. It breaks up lumps, adds a little air, and blends dry ingredients evenly, so that leavening agents and spices are spread through the batter and not left in clumps.

Hold the sieve over a bowl or a sheet of parchment paper and tap the side gently with your hand until the powder falls through. Press any remaining lumps through with the back of a spoon. When a recipe measures flour by volume, check whether it says to sift before or after measuring: sifted flour is lighter, so the same volume of sifted flour weighs less than unsifted flour. Weighing in grams avoids this problem.

The most common mistake is skipping this step for ingredients that clump, such as cocoa and powdered sugar, and then finding dry lumps in the finished cake.
steps: Place a fine sieve over a bowl or a sheet of parchment paper.
Add the dry ingredients to the sieve.
Tap the side of the sieve gently so the powder falls through.
Press any remaining lumps through with the back of a spoon.
Use the sifted ingredients right away.
tips: Weigh ingredients in grams instead of relying on volume measures for sifted or unsifted flour.
Sift onto parchment paper, then lift the paper to pour the ingredients into the bowl.
Whisking dry ingredients together for 30 seconds is a quick substitute when you only need to mix them evenly.

strain.name: Strain
strain.short: Straining separates liquid from solid pieces by pouring a mixture through a sieve, colander or cloth.
strain.long:
Straining is separating liquid from solid pieces by pouring a mixture through a tool with small holes. The holes let the liquid through and hold the solids back. It is used to make clear stocks and smooth sauces, to remove seeds and skins, to drain cooked pasta and vegetables, and to remove tea leaves or herbs after infusing.

Choose the tool by how fine the result should be. A colander has large holes for pasta and vegetables. A fine-mesh sieve catches small seeds. A sieve lined with a clean cloth gives the clearest liquid. Place a heatproof bowl underneath and pour slowly. Press the solids gently with a spoon to collect more liquid, but for a clear stock do not press, because pushing solids through makes it cloudy.

The most common mistakes are pressing hard on solids when a clear liquid is wanted, and straining over the sink when the liquid is the part you want to keep.
steps: Set a sieve, colander or cloth-lined sieve over a heatproof bowl or pot.
Pour the mixture in slowly.
Let the liquid drain through, pressing the solids gently only if clarity does not matter.
Discard or reuse the solids, and use or cool the liquid.
tips: Pour hot liquid slowly and away from your body, over a stable heatproof bowl.
Line the sieve with a damp, clean cloth for a clearer stock.
Cool strained stock quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate it within 2 hours.

rest.name: Rest
rest.short: Resting leaves cooked meat, or dough, undisturbed for a time so juices spread back or gluten relaxes before cutting or shaping.
rest.long:
Resting means leaving food undisturbed for a time before the next step. When meat cooks, its muscle fibers tighten and its juices become hot and thin. During the rest, the meat cools slightly, the fibers relax and the juices thicken, so less liquid runs out when you slice it. The center also keeps heating a little from stored heat. Dough and batter rest so that gluten relaxes and the flour fully absorbs the liquid.

Move cooked meat to a board and cover it loosely with foil. Do not seal it tightly, because trapped steam softens the crust. Rest steaks and chops for about 5 minutes, and large roasts or whole poultry for 15-30 minutes. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal are considered safe at 63 °C (145 °F) after at least 3 minutes of rest. Rest pastry dough in the refrigerator for 30 minutes before rolling.

The most common mistake is cutting too soon, which sends the juices onto the board.
steps: Remove the cooked food from the heat and move it to a board or plate.
Cover it loosely with foil.
Leave it undisturbed for the recommended time.
Slice or serve, and add the juices from the board to the sauce.
tips: Check with a thermometer: poultry must reach 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part, and the rest does not replace this.
Because the temperature keeps rising during the rest, remove large roasts a little before the final doneness you want, but only after they have reached the safe minimum temperature.
Do not leave cooked food standing for more than 2 hours; serve it or refrigerate it.

season.name: Season
season.short: Seasoning adds salt, pepper, herbs, spices or a little acid to food to bring out and balance its flavor.
season.long:
Seasoning means adding ingredients that improve and balance flavor, most often salt, pepper, herbs, spices and a little acid such as lemon juice or vinegar. Salt does not only make food taste salty: it reduces bitterness and makes other flavors seem stronger. Acid brightens a dish that tastes flat or heavy.

Season in layers, adding a little at several points during cooking instead of all at the end, so that the flavor goes through the whole dish. Season meat before cooking, season vegetables as they cook, and always taste near the end and adjust. Add salt in small amounts, because it is easy to add and impossible to remove. If a dish becomes too salty, add more unsalted ingredients or liquid.

The most common mistakes are salting only at the end, which leaves the surface salty and the inside bland, and over-salting a sauce that will reduce, because it gets saltier as water leaves.
steps: Add a small amount of salt at the start of cooking.
Add herbs and spices at the stage the recipe suggests, with hardy herbs early and delicate herbs at the end.
Taste with a clean spoon near the end of cooking.
Adjust with salt, pepper, acid or sweetness, a little at a time.
tips: Salt sauces lightly before reducing them, because they get saltier as they reduce.
Use a clean spoon for each taste, and never taste a mixture that contains raw meat or raw egg.
A small splash of lemon juice or vinegar at the end can lift a dish that tastes flat.

mise-en-place.name: Mise en place
mise-en-place.short: Mise en place means preparing, measuring and arranging all ingredients and tools before cooking begins.
mise-en-place.long:
Mise en place is a French phrase meaning everything in its place. It is the habit of reading the whole recipe, then washing, cutting and measuring all ingredients and setting out the pans and tools before you turn on the heat. Professional kitchens rely on it because many dishes cook in minutes, and there is no time to chop while something burns.

Gather every ingredient and tool. Wash, peel and cut. Measure into small bowls and arrange them in the order you will use them, with ingredients that go into the pan together in the same bowl. Use separate boards and knives for raw meat, poultry and fish and for vegetables and other ready-to-eat food. Keep perishable ingredients in the refrigerator until you need them, and never leave them at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

The most common mistake is starting to cook before reading the recipe, then finding a missing ingredient or step with the pan already hot.
steps: Read the whole recipe and note the times and the equipment needed.
Gather all the ingredients and tools.
Wash, peel and cut the ingredients, using separate boards for raw meat and for vegetables.
Measure the ingredients into small bowls and arrange them in the order of use.
Start preheating the oven early if the recipe needs it, but heat the pan only when everything is ready.
tips: Put ingredients that are added at the same time in the same bowl.
Keep perishable items refrigerated until the moment you need them.
Clean as you go, so the work area stays clear and safe.

puree.name: Purée
puree.short: Puréeing blends or mashes soft or cooked food until it is completely smooth, forming a thick liquid or paste.
puree.long:
To purée is to crush food into a completely smooth, thick mixture. It is done with a blender, a food processor, an immersion blender, a food mill or a sieve. Puréeing breaks down the fibers and cell walls of fruit and vegetables, so the pieces release their juices and blend into an even texture. Purées are the base of soups, sauces, dips and fillings.

Cook firm vegetables until they are very soft. Put the food in the blender with some of its cooking liquid and add more liquid a little at a time until the mixture moves freely. Start on low speed and increase gradually until smooth, then pass the purée through a fine sieve for a very smooth result.

The most common mistakes are over-blending starchy foods such as potatoes, which turns them gluey, and filling the blender too full with hot food, which can burn you.
steps: Cook firm food until very soft, or choose ripe soft fruit.
Cut the food into even pieces and add it to the blender with a little liquid.
Blend, starting on low speed and increasing gradually.
Add more liquid a little at a time until the texture is smooth.
Pass the purée through a fine sieve if you want a very smooth result.
tips: When blending hot food, fill the container no more than 1/2 full, vent the lid, and start on low speed, because steam can push the lid off and cause burns.
Use a food mill or ricer for potatoes, because a blender makes them gluey.
Cool a purée quickly and refrigerate it within 2 hours.

cut-in.name: Cut in
cut-in.short: Cutting in works cold solid fat into flour with a pastry blender, knives or fingertips until it forms small pieces coated in flour.
cut-in.long:
Cutting in is mixing cold solid fat, such as butter, lard or shortening, into flour until the fat is in small pieces. It is used for pie crust, biscuits, scones and shortcrust pastry. The pieces of fat stay separate and coated in flour. During baking the fat melts and leaves small gaps, and steam fills the gaps and lifts the dough into layers, which gives a flaky or crumbly texture.

Cut the cold fat into cubes of about 1 cm (3/8 in), add them to the flour and salt, and work with a pastry blender, 2 knives, or your fingertips until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some pieces of about 6 mm (1/4 in) for a flaky crust. Work quickly so that the fat stays cold. If it turns soft and greasy, chill the bowl for 15 minutes, then add cold liquid a little at a time.

The most common mistakes are letting the fat melt, which gives a tough, greasy crust, and mixing until no pieces remain, which loses flakiness.
steps: Chill the fat and cut it into cubes of about 1 cm (3/8 in).
Add the cubes to the flour and salt in a bowl.
Press and cut the fat into the flour with a pastry blender, 2 knives, or your fingertips.
Stop when the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some pieces of about 6 mm (1/4 in).
Chill the bowl for 15 minutes if the fat becomes soft.
tips: Use fat straight from the refrigerator, and use your fingertips only, because your palms are warm.
Add the liquid ice cold and a little at a time, just until the dough holds together.
Do not taste raw dough, because raw flour and raw egg can carry harmful bacteria.

toss.name: Toss
toss.short: Tossing lifts and turns food so that it is evenly coated with dressing, oil, seasoning or sauce.
toss.long:
Tossing is moving food by lifting and turning it, with tongs or 2 spoons or by shaking it in a bowl or pan, so that every piece is evenly coated. It is used to dress salads, coat pasta in sauce, mix vegetables with oil and seasoning before roasting, and turn food in a hot pan. The motion spreads liquid and seasoning without crushing delicate food as stirring can.

Use a bowl much larger than the food. Add the dressing a little at a time, lift the food from the bottom, and turn it over the top. Dress salads just before serving, because acid and salt make leaves wilt. For pasta, toss it in the pan with the sauce and a little of the pasta cooking water over low heat so that the sauce clings. Toss vegetables with oil in a bowl before spreading them in an even layer on a baking sheet for roasting.

The most common mistakes are adding too much dressing, which makes food soggy and heavy, and using a bowl that is too small.
steps: Place the food in a bowl or pan much larger than the amount of food.
Add the oil, dressing or sauce a little at a time.
Lift the food from the bottom with tongs or 2 spoons and turn it over.
Continue until all pieces are lightly and evenly coated.
Taste, and add more dressing only if needed.
tips: Wash salad leaves and dry them completely, because water stops dressing from sticking.
Do not use tools that touched raw meat to toss ready-to-eat food.
Start with less dressing than you think you need, because you can always add more.

emulsify.name: Emulsify
emulsify.short: Emulsify means to combine 2 liquids that normally separate, such as oil and water, into a smooth, stable mixture.
emulsify.long:
Oil and water do not mix on their own. To emulsify them, you break the oil into very small droplets and spread the droplets through the water-based liquid. An emulsifier, such as egg yolk or mustard, coats each droplet and stops the droplets from joining back together.

In practice, put the water-based liquid and the emulsifier in a bowl. Begin adding the oil very slowly, a few drops at a time, while whisking constantly. When the mixture thickens and looks smooth, add the oil in a thin, steady stream. Set the bowl on a folded damp towel so it does not slide while you whisk.

Use this method for mayonnaise, vinaigrette, hollandaise, and many pan sauces. The most common mistake is adding the oil too fast, which overloads the emulsifier and makes the sauce split into separate oily and watery layers. To repair a split sauce, whisk it a little at a time into 5 ml (1 teaspoon) of warm water in a clean bowl.
steps: Put the water-based liquid and the emulsifier in a bowl.
Add the oil a few drops at a time while whisking constantly.
Keep whisking until the oil is broken into tiny droplets and the mixture starts to thicken.
Add the remaining oil in a thin, steady stream until the sauce is thick and smooth.
tips: Start with all ingredients at room temperature, because very cold ingredients make a sauce more likely to split.
Use pasteurized eggs for any emulsion that keeps the egg raw, and keep the finished sauce refrigerated and use it within 2 days.
Slow down or stop adding oil as soon as the mixture looks oily or thin, and whisk until it is smooth again.
emulsify.diagramAlt: A left-to-right drawing in 4 numbered marks: mark 1 shows a bowl holding water and an emulsifier, mark 2 shows drops of oil falling into the bowl while a whisk moves, mark 3 shows tiny oil droplets spread through the water with each droplet surrounded by emulsifier, and mark 4 shows a thin stream of oil being poured into a thick, smooth sauce.

mount-with-butter.name: Mount with butter
mount-with-butter.short: Mounting with butter means whisking cold butter piece by piece into a warm sauce at the end of cooking to add shine, body, and richness.
mount-with-butter.long:
Mounting with butter is a finishing step. Cold butter is cut into small cubes and whisked into a hot, reduced sauce. Whisking breaks the butterfat into tiny droplets, and the milk proteins in the butter help keep them suspended in the sauce. This loose emulsion gives the sauce a glossy surface and a smoother, slightly thicker texture.

Take the pan off the heat, or keep it over very low heat. Add a few cubes of cold butter, swirl the pan or whisk until the butter melts and blends in, then add more cubes. The sauce should stay hot but never simmer, because strong heat makes the butter separate into oil.

Use it to finish pan sauces, reductions, and jus. The most common mistakes are boiling the sauce after the butter is added and adding all the butter together. Both leave a greasy layer on top. Taste and adjust the seasoning after the butter is in, because butter softens sharp flavors.
steps: Reduce the sauce until it has the flavor and thickness you want.
Lower the heat or take the pan off the heat.
Cut cold butter into cubes of about 1 cm (3/8 in).
Add a few cubes and whisk or swirl the pan until they melt completely.
Add the remaining cubes a few at a time, adjust the seasoning, and serve the sauce right away.
tips: Keep the butter cold until it goes into the sauce, because cold butter melts slowly and gives a steadier emulsion.
If the sauce looks oily, take it off the heat and whisk in 15 ml (1 tablespoon) of cold water or cream.
Serve soon after mounting, because the emulsion is delicate and does not reheat well.

roux.name: Roux
roux.short: Roux is a cooked paste of equal weights of fat and flour that thickens sauces, soups, and stews and adds color and flavor.
roux.long:
A roux is made by cooking fat, usually butter, with an equal weight of flour while stirring. Cooking removes the raw flour taste. In the finished dish, the flour starch swells in hot liquid and thickens it. The longer a roux cooks, the darker and nuttier it becomes, but the less thickening power it has.

There are 4 common color stages. White roux is cooked briefly and stays pale, for béchamel. Blond roux turns pale gold, for velouté. Brown roux turns light brown with a nutty smell, for brown sauces. Dark roux turns the color of dark chocolate, for gumbo. For a medium-thick sauce, use about 60 g of butter and 60 g of flour for every 1 liter of liquid.

Add the liquid a little at a time while whisking, and combine a hot roux with cool liquid, or a cool roux with hot liquid, to avoid lumps. The most common mistakes are scorching the roux, which makes it bitter, and not simmering the sauce long enough to cook out the raw flour taste.
steps: Melt the fat over medium heat in a heavy pan.
Add an equal weight of flour and stir to make a smooth paste.
Cook while stirring constantly until the roux reaches the color you need.
Whisk in the liquid a little at a time until the sauce is smooth.
Simmer, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and no longer tastes of raw flour.
tips: Weigh the fat and the flour instead of measuring by volume, because equal weights give the correct ratio.
Throw away a roux that has black specks or smells burnt, because it will make the whole dish bitter.
Take care with hot roux, because it is hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin.

beurre-blanc.name: Beurre blanc
beurre-blanc.short: Beurre blanc is a warm butter sauce made by reducing white wine, vinegar, and shallot, then whisking in cold butter until pale and creamy.
beurre-blanc.long:
Beurre blanc is a classic French sauce built on an emulsion of butter in a small amount of acidic reduction. White wine, vinegar, and finely chopped shallot are cooked until almost dry, leaving a few spoonfuls of concentrated liquid. Cold butter is then whisked in piece by piece. The milk proteins in the butter, together with the small amount of liquid, hold the butterfat in tiny suspended droplets.

Keep the heat low and steady. The pan should be warm enough to melt the butter slowly but never reach a simmer. The finished sauce is pale, creamy, and thick enough to coat a spoon. Strain out the shallot for a smooth sauce, and season with salt and a few drops of lemon juice.

Serve it with fish, shellfish, and vegetables. The most common mistake is overheating, which melts the butter into oil and makes the sauce split. Beurre blanc is delicate, so it is best made just before serving.
steps: Simmer the wine, vinegar, and chopped shallot until only a few spoonfuls of syrupy liquid remain.
Turn the heat down to very low.
Whisk in cold butter cubes a few at a time, adding more only after the previous cubes have melted.
Strain the sauce if you want it smooth, season it, and serve right away.
tips: Use cold butter, because it melts slowly and keeps the emulsion stable.
If the sauce starts to split, take the pan off the heat and whisk in 15 ml (1 tablespoon) of cold cream.
Keep the sauce warm, not hot, because it splits if held at 60 °C (140 °F) or above, so use it within 2 hours and then discard what is left.

hollandaise.name: Hollandaise
hollandaise.short: Hollandaise is a warm, thick sauce made by whisking melted butter into egg yolks over gentle heat and flavoring it with lemon juice.
hollandaise.long:
Hollandaise is an emulsion of melted butter in egg yolks, flavored with lemon juice, salt, and pepper. The yolks are whisked over gentle heat until they thicken into a pale, creamy foam. Warm melted butter is then whisked in slowly. The lecithin in the yolks coats the butter droplets and keeps them suspended.

Food safety matters because the yolks are only lightly cooked. Whisk them over gentle heat until they reach at least 71 °C (160 °F), or use pasteurized eggs. Heat is also the main danger for the texture of the sauce: if the yolks get much hotter than this, they scramble.

Serve it with eggs, asparagus, and fish. The most common mistakes are overheating the yolks and adding the butter too fast, which makes the sauce split. Keep the finished sauce warm at 60 °C (140 °F) or above, and discard it after 2 hours.
steps: Melt the butter and keep it warm.
Whisk the egg yolks with a little water in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, without letting the bowl touch the water.
Keep whisking until the yolks are pale and thick and have reached at least 71 °C (160 °F).
Take the bowl off the heat and whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream.
Season with lemon juice, salt, and a little ground cayenne pepper, then serve.
tips: Check the yolks with a thermometer, and if they start to set, lift the bowl off the heat and whisk hard.
Keep the sauce warm at 60 °C (140 °F) or above, and discard it after 2 hours instead of reheating it.
If the sauce splits, put 15 ml (1 tablespoon) of warm water in a clean bowl and whisk in the split sauce a little at a time.

vinaigrette.name: Vinaigrette
vinaigrette.short: Vinaigrette is a cold dressing of oil and an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice, whisked or shaken into a temporary emulsion.
vinaigrette.long:
A basic vinaigrette combines oil and acid, usually about 3 parts oil to 1 part acid by volume, plus salt and often mustard. Whisking breaks the oil into small droplets in the acid. Mustard acts as an emulsifier, so it makes the mixture thicker and slower to separate. Without mustard the emulsion is temporary, and the layers separate after a few minutes.

Dissolve the salt in the acid before adding the oil, because salt does not dissolve in oil. Add the mustard and any finely chopped shallot or herbs, then whisk in the oil in a thin stream. Taste the dressing on a salad leaf, not on a spoon, because the leaf shows how it will really taste.

Use it on salads, cooked vegetables, grains, and cold meats. The most common mistakes are adding too much acid and pouring the oil in too fast, which leaves the dressing sharp and thin. If it tastes too sharp, whisk in more oil or a little sugar.
steps: Stir the salt into the vinegar or citrus juice until it dissolves.
Add the mustard and any chopped shallot or herbs.
Whisk in the oil in a thin, steady stream until the dressing is thick and smooth.
Taste it on a salad leaf and adjust the salt, acid, and oil.
tips: For a quick version, shake all the ingredients in a closed jar.
Refrigerate any dressing made with fresh garlic, herbs, or shallot, and use it within 3 days.
Dress salad leaves just before serving, because salt and acid make them wilt.

liaison.name: Liaison
liaison.short: A liaison is a mixture, most often egg yolk and cream, that is stirred into a hot soup or sauce to thicken it and give it a smooth, rich texture.
liaison.long:
In classic French cooking, a liaison binds and enriches a soup or sauce. The most common type is a mix of egg yolk and cream. Gentle heat makes the proteins in the yolk set slightly, which thickens the liquid, while the cream adds richness and makes curdling less likely. Some cooks also use the word for other binders, such as roux.

Whisk the yolks with cream in a bowl. Stir in a ladle of the hot liquid to warm the mixture slowly, which is called tempering. Pour the mixture back into the pot and heat gently, stirring, until the sauce coats a spoon and reaches at least 71 °C (160 °F). Do not let it boil, because boiling scrambles the yolks.

Use it to finish velouté, cream soups, and stews of chicken or veal. The most common mistake is adding the cold mixture directly to hot liquid, which cooks the yolks into small lumps.
steps: Whisk the egg yolks and cream together in a bowl.
Slowly whisk a ladle of the hot liquid into the bowl to warm the mixture.
Pour the warmed mixture back into the pot, stirring constantly.
Heat gently without boiling until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and reaches at least 71 °C (160 °F).
Serve right away.
tips: Check the temperature with a thermometer, because the yolks are only lightly cooked, and use pasteurized eggs for people at higher risk.
Strain the sauce through a fine sieve if small lumps form.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

jus.name: Jus
jus.short: Jus is a thin, clear sauce made from the juices of roasted meat or a reduced stock, with a concentrated flavor and little or no added thickener.
jus.long:
Jus is the French word for juice. It is a light sauce that tastes strongly of the meat it comes from. The classic method is to roast meat or bones until deeply browned, then use the browned bits stuck to the roasting pan as the base. The pan is deglazed with wine or stock, and the liquid is reduced until the flavor is concentrated.

A jus is thinner than a gravy. Its slight body comes from the gelatin released by bones and connective tissue, not from flour. A jus lié is lightly thickened with a small amount of starch. Simmer gently, skim off fat and foam, and strain through a fine sieve for a clear result.

Serve it with roast meats. The most common mistakes are salting before the sauce is reduced, which makes it too salty, and boiling hard, which makes it cloudy and greasy.
steps: Roast the meat or bones until deeply browned, then pour off the excess fat from the pan.
Deglaze the pan with wine or stock, scraping up the browned bits.
Add stock and simmer gently until the sauce is reduced and full of flavor.
Skim off the fat, strain through a fine sieve, and season at the end.
tips: Season only at the end, because reducing concentrates the salt.
Keep the heat low and skim often, because hard boiling makes the sauce cloudy.
Cool leftover jus quickly, refrigerate it within 2 hours, and reheat it to at least 74 °C (165 °F) before serving.

coulis.name: Coulis
coulis.short: A coulis is a smooth, pourable sauce made by cooking or blending fruit or vegetables into a purée and straining out seeds and fibers.
coulis.long:
A coulis is a thin purée that is strained until completely smooth. Raspberries, strawberries, mango, and passion fruit are common sweet choices, and tomato and roasted red pepper are common savory choices. A coulis has a bright, pure flavor and a vivid color, and it is used to flavor and decorate desserts, plates, and savory dishes.

Soft ripe fresh fruit can be blended raw. Firmer fruit and vegetables should be cooked until soft before blending with a small amount of water, sugar, or stock. Blend until smooth, then press the purée through a fine sieve with the back of a spoon to remove seeds, skins, and fibers. Adjust with sugar for sweetness, lemon juice for freshness, or salt for savory types.

If the coulis is too thick, stir in a little water. If it is too thin, simmer it briefly to reduce. The most common mistakes are overcooking, which dulls the color and fresh flavor, and skipping the straining step, which leaves a gritty texture.
steps: Wash the fruit or vegetables and cook them until soft if they are firm.
Blend them until completely smooth.
Press the purée through a fine sieve to remove seeds and fibers.
Season with sugar, lemon juice, or salt to taste, and adjust the thickness with water or a short simmer.
tips: Bring frozen berries to a boil for at least 1 minute before blending, because frozen berries have been linked to outbreaks of hepatitis A and norovirus.
Wash fresh fruit well before blending, and refrigerate the coulis and use it within 3 days.
Stir in lemon juice at the end to keep the color bright.

slurry.name: Slurry
slurry.short: A slurry is a smooth mix of a starch and a cold liquid that is stirred into a hot liquid to thicken it quickly without lumps.
slurry.long:
Dry starch dropped into hot liquid forms lumps, because the outside of each clump swells and seals the dry starch inside. A slurry avoids this by spreading the starch granules in cold liquid before it meets the heat. When the slurry is stirred into a simmering liquid, the granules swell evenly and thicken it. Cornstarch, potato starch, arrowroot, and tapioca starch are common choices.

A usual ratio is 1 part starch to 2 parts cold water by volume. For a medium-thick sauce, use about 8 g (1 tablespoon) of cornstarch for every 250 ml (1 cup) of liquid. Stir the slurry again just before adding it, because the starch settles quickly. Pour it into the simmering liquid while stirring, then simmer for 1-2 minutes. Arrowroot thickens at lower heat and breaks down if boiled for long, so add it at the end.

Use it for gravies, stir-fry sauces, and fruit fillings. The most common mistakes are adding the starch dry, adding too much in a single pour, and not simmering long enough to remove the raw starch taste.
steps: Measure the starch into a small bowl.
Add cold water or cold stock and stir until completely smooth.
Bring the sauce to a simmer.
Stir the slurry again, then pour it into the simmering sauce in a thin stream while stirring.
Simmer for 1-2 minutes, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
tips: Use cold liquid, because warm liquid starts the starch swelling and causes lumps.
Add the slurry a little at a time, because the sauce keeps thickening as it cools.
Thin an over-thick sauce with a little hot stock or water.

gastrique.name: Gastrique
gastrique.short: A gastrique is a sweet and sour syrup made by cooking sugar to caramel and adding vinegar, used as a base for sauces.
gastrique.long:
A gastrique is a French sauce base made from sugar cooked to caramel and then loosened with vinegar. The sweetness of the sugar and the sharpness of the vinegar balance each other, and the cooked sugar adds a deep, slightly bitter note. Fruit, wine, or stock can be added for more flavor.

Heat the sugar in a heavy pan over medium heat, swirling the pan instead of stirring, until it melts and turns light amber. Take the pan off the heat and carefully add about the same volume of vinegar as sugar, then adjust to taste. Simmer until the sauce is syrupy.

Serve it with duck, pork, game, and roasted fruit. The most common mistakes are letting the sugar burn, which makes it bitter, and adding the vinegar too quickly, which causes spattering and makes the caramel harden into lumps. If lumps form, simmer gently until they dissolve.
steps: Heat the sugar in a heavy pan over medium heat, swirling the pan instead of stirring.
Cook until the sugar melts and turns a light amber color.
Take the pan off the heat and carefully pour in the vinegar, standing back from the steam and spatter.
Return the pan to low heat and simmer until any hard lumps dissolve and the sauce is syrupy.
Add fruit, stock, or other flavorings if you want, and simmer until the sauce coats a spoon.
tips: Molten sugar is much hotter than boiling water and causes severe burns, so never touch it and keep children away.
Take the sugar off the heat as soon as it is light amber, because it keeps darkening in the hot pan.
Pour in the vinegar slowly, and keep your face away from the steam, because vinegar steam stings the eyes.

pan-sauce.name: Pan sauce
pan-sauce.short: A pan sauce is a quick sauce made in the pan used to sear meat or fish, using the browned bits left behind and a liquid such as wine or stock.
pan-sauce.long:
After searing, browned bits called fond stick to the pan. They are full of flavor. A pan sauce dissolves them in liquid, reduces the liquid to concentrate it, and finishes with butter, cream, or herbs. It takes only a few minutes and uses the flavor that the cooking has already created.

Remove the cooked meat and let it rest. Pour off most of the fat, leaving about 15 ml (1 tablespoon). Cook chopped shallot or garlic briefly, add wine or stock to deglaze, and scrape up the fond with a wooden spoon. Simmer until the liquid is syrupy, then take the pan off the heat and whisk in cold butter. Season at the end.

Use it with chops, chicken, steak, and fish. The most common mistakes are burning the fond, which makes the sauce bitter, salting before the liquid is reduced, and boiling the sauce after the butter is added.
steps: Cook the meat or fish, then remove it from the pan and leave the browned bits in the pan.
Pour off most of the fat and cook chopped shallot or garlic for 1 minute.
Add wine or stock and scrape up the browned bits as the liquid simmers.
Simmer until the liquid is reduced and tastes concentrated.
Take the pan off the heat, whisk in cold butter, season, and serve.
tips: Make sure the sauce reaches a simmer before serving, because the pan has held raw meat juices.
Take the pan off the heat before adding alcohol, because it can flare up over a gas flame.
Season only at the end, because the sauce becomes saltier as it reduces.

proof.name: Proof
proof.short: Proofing is the final rise of shaped dough before baking, when yeast makes gas that leaves the dough light and airy.
proof.long:
Proofing is the last rise of shaped dough before it goes into the oven. Yeast keeps feeding on sugars from the flour and releases carbon dioxide gas, which is trapped by the stretchy gluten network and slowly inflates the dough. This makes the finished bread light instead of dense.

Cover the dough so its surface does not dry out, and keep it somewhere warm, ideally at 24-26 °C (75-79 °F). Judge readiness by the dough, not by the clock. It should look puffy and have grown by about 50-100%, depending on the recipe. Press a floured fingertip about 1 cm (3/8 in) into the dough: if the dent springs back slowly and only partly, the dough is ready. If it springs back immediately, wait longer. If it does not spring back at all, the dough is overproofed.

The most common mistake is overproofing, which makes the loaf collapse in the oven and taste flat. Underproofed dough bakes into a dense loaf that can burst along the side.
steps: Shape the dough and place it in a floured basket or loaf pan, or on a lined tray.
Cover it loosely so the surface stays moist.
Leave it at 24-26 °C (75-79 °F) until it looks puffy and has grown by about 50-100%.
Press a floured fingertip gently into the dough and check that the dent springs back slowly.
Bake as soon as the dough is ready.
tips: Warm rooms speed up proofing and cool rooms slow it down, so adjust the time to the temperature.
An oven that is switched off, with a tray of hot water inside, makes a warm and humid place for proofing.

autolyse.name: Autolyse
autolyse.short: Autolyse is a rest after mixing only flour and water, before adding salt and yeast or starter, so the dough becomes smoother and stretchier.
autolyse.long:
Autolyse means mixing only the flour and water of a recipe until no dry flour remains, then letting the mixture rest before adding salt, yeast, or sourdough starter. During the rest, the flour absorbs the water and natural enzymes in the flour begin to break down starch and protein. Gluten, the stretchy protein network in bread dough, starts to form by itself without any kneading.

Cover the shaggy mixture and rest it at room temperature for 20-60 minutes. After the rest, the dough feels smoother and less sticky and stretches more easily, so it needs less kneading or folding later. Bread made this way often has a more open crumb, which is the inside texture of the loaf, and a better crust color.

The most common mistakes are adding the salt too early, because salt slows the flour's water absorption, and forgetting to add the yeast or starter after the rest.
steps: Weigh the flour and water, and mix them until no dry flour remains.
Cover the bowl and rest the mixture for 20-60 minutes.
Add the salt and the yeast or starter to the rested dough.
Pinch and fold the dough until the added ingredients are evenly spread through it.
tips: Use a longer rest for whole grain flour, which absorbs water more slowly than white flour.
Keep the bowl covered so the surface does not dry into a skin.
Add the yeast or starter right after the rest, because it is easy to forget when the dough already looks finished.

stretch-and-fold.name: Stretch and fold
stretch-and-fold.short: Stretch and fold is a gentle way to strengthen wet dough by pulling an edge up and folding it over, with rests between rounds, instead of kneading.
stretch-and-fold.long:
Stretch and fold builds gluten strength in wet or sticky dough without kneading. Pulling the dough upward stretches the gluten strands, and folding it over stacks them in layers, which makes the dough tighter and more elastic. Rests between rounds let the gluten relax and keep developing by itself.

With wet hands, lift an edge of the dough, stretch it upward until you feel resistance, and fold it over the middle. Turn the bowl by 90 degrees and repeat on all 4 sides. Do this for 3-4 rounds with 30 minutes between rounds, early in bulk fermentation. The dough looks smoother and holds its shape better after each round.

This method suits dough with a hydration of 70% or more, which is messy to knead by hand. The most common mistake is tearing the dough by pulling too hard or too fast. Stretch only until you feel resistance.
steps: Wet your hands and lift an edge of the dough upward until it resists.
Fold the stretched edge over the center of the dough.
Turn the bowl by 90 degrees and repeat until all 4 sides are folded.
Cover the dough and rest it for 30 minutes before the next round.
tips: Wet hands stop the dough from sticking, so keep a small bowl of water nearby.
Stop folding when the dough feels smooth and tight, even if the recipe lists more rounds.
Keep the dough covered between rounds so the surface does not dry out.
stretch-and-fold.diagramAlt: A hand lifts and stretches an edge of the dough in a bowl (1), the stretched edge is folded over the center (2), the bowl is turned by 90 degrees to repeat on the next side (3), and the folded dough rests covered in the bowl (4).

shape-loaf.name: Shape a loaf
shape-loaf.short: Shaping a loaf means folding and rolling risen dough into a tight form that holds its shape and rises upward instead of spreading in the oven.
shape-loaf.long:
Shaping gives risen dough its final form and builds surface tension, a tight outer skin that holds gas inside and makes the loaf rise upward in the oven instead of spreading sideways. The dough is pressed gently to release the largest gas bubbles, folded to build layers, and then rolled or dragged across the work surface so the surface tightens.

Use as little flour on the work surface as possible, because flour stops the dough from gripping the surface and stops the seam from sealing. Place a round loaf in a floured basket with the seam facing up, so the smooth side faces up after turning out. For a loaf pan, place the dough with the seam facing down. The finished shape should feel firm and slightly springy, with a smooth skin and no tears.

Common mistakes are pressing out all the gas, which gives a dense loaf, and shaping too loosely, which gives a flat loaf. If the dough keeps tearing, rest it covered for 10 minutes and try again.
steps: Turn the risen dough onto a lightly floured work surface and press it gently into a rectangle.
Fold the top edge down to the center and the sides inward, then roll the dough toward you into a tight shape.
Drag the dough toward you on the work surface with cupped hands to tighten the surface.
Pinch the seam closed.
Place the dough in a floured basket with the seam up, or in a loaf pan with the seam down.
Cover the dough and proof it until it is puffy.
tips: Use a dough scraper to lift sticky dough instead of adding more flour.
Dust a basket with rice flour, which sticks less than wheat flour.
Work quickly and gently, because rough handling pushes out the gas that gives the loaf its rise.

score-loaf.name: Score a loaf
score-loaf.short: Scoring is cutting the surface of a loaf just before baking with a sharp blade, so the bread expands in a planned place instead of bursting at random.
score-loaf.long:
A score is a shallow cut made in the surface of shaped dough just before baking. In the early minutes of baking, the gas in the dough expands quickly, which is called oven spring, while the crust is still soft. Without a cut, the loaf splits wherever the crust is weakest. A score gives the gas and steam a planned path, so the loaf rises evenly and the cut opens up.

Use a razor blade on a handle (called a lame), a very sharp knife, or a small serrated knife. Cut with a quick, smooth stroke. A shallow angle of about 30 degrees lifts a raised flap called an ear, while a straight downward cut opens widely and flat. A depth of 5-10 mm (1/4-3/8 in) is typical. Cold dough from the refrigerator is firmer and cuts more cleanly.

The most common mistake is cutting slowly or hesitantly, which drags and deflates the dough. A dull blade does the same. Overproofed dough also collapses when cut.
steps: Place the proofed dough on a peel or parchment paper and dust the top lightly with flour.
Hold a sharp blade at a shallow angle of about 30 degrees to the surface.
Cut 5-10 mm (1/4-3/8 in) deep in a quick, smooth stroke.
Load the loaf into the hot oven immediately so the cut opens as the bread rises.
tips: Dip the blade in water or lightly oil it if it drags through sticky dough.
Practice on chilled dough first, because cold, firm dough is easier to score.
Hold the blade by its handle or a guard, and cut away from your fingers.
score-loaf.diagramAlt: A round loaf of dough on parchment paper is dusted with flour (1), a blade is held at a shallow angle above the top (2), the blade draws a curved cut across the surface (3), and the loaf goes into the oven where the cut opens into a raised ridge (4).

sourdough-starter.name: Sourdough starter
sourdough-starter.short: A sourdough starter is a living mixture of flour and water holding wild yeast and bacteria, used instead of commercial yeast to make bread rise.
sourdough-starter.long:
A sourdough starter is a mixture of flour and water that has fermented until wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria live in it. The yeast makes gas that raises the bread, and the bacteria make acids that give sourdough its tangy taste and help the bread stay fresh longer.

To keep it active, feed it regularly: keep a small amount, discard the rest, and add fresh flour and water. A common ratio is 1:1:1 by weight of starter, flour, and water, for example 20 g of each. At room temperature, about 24 °C (75 °F), feed it every 12 hours. In the refrigerator, feed it weekly.

A starter is ready to use when it has risen to about 2 times its starting height, has a domed top full of bubbles, and smells pleasantly sour and fruity. A sharp, solvent-like smell means it is hungry and needs feeding. The most common mistake is using it too soon or long after its peak, when it has collapsed. Liquid on top is harmless and can be stirred in.
steps: Keep 20 g of the starter in a clean jar and discard the rest.
Add 20 g of flour and 20 g of water, which makes a 1:1:1 ratio by weight.
Stir until no dry flour remains and mark the level of the mixture on the jar.
Cover loosely and leave at room temperature until the starter has risen to about 2 times its starting height and is full of bubbles.
Use the starter at this peak, or feed it again to keep it active.
tips: Discard the whole starter and do not taste it if you see fuzzy mold or pink or orange streaks.
Cover the jar loosely, because a tight lid on a glass jar can build up pressure.
Use a rubber band around the jar to mark the starting level, which makes the rise easy to see.

poolish.name: Poolish
poolish.short: A poolish is a wet pre-ferment of equal weights of flour and water with a tiny amount of yeast, fermented before being mixed into the final dough.
poolish.long:
A poolish is a pre-ferment, which is a portion of the recipe's flour and water fermented ahead of time. It is made from equal weights of flour and water, a 1:1 ratio or 100% hydration, with a very small amount of yeast. A common example is 500 g of flour, 500 g of water, and 0.5 g of instant dry yeast, which is about 0.1% of the flour weight. The result is a loose, batter-like mixture.

Cover it and leave it at about 20 °C (68 °F) for 12-16 hours. It is ready when the surface is covered in bubbles, it has risen, and the top has just begun to dip in the middle. Then mix it into the final dough with the remaining flour, water, salt, and yeast.

A poolish adds flavor and a more open crumb, and it suits baguettes, ciabatta, and pizza dough. The most common mistake is using too much yeast or leaving it too long in a warm kitchen, which leaves it exhausted and sour.
steps: Weigh equal amounts of flour and water, for example 500 g of each.
Add a very small amount of yeast, about 0.1% of the flour weight.
Stir until smooth, cover, and leave at about 20 °C (68 °F) for 12-16 hours.
Check for a bubbly surface and a slight dip in the center.
Mix the poolish into the final dough with the remaining ingredients.
tips: Count the flour and water in the poolish as part of the total recipe so the dough stays balanced.
In a warm kitchen, shorten the time or place the poolish in the refrigerator to slow it down.
Use a large container, because the poolish rises and can overflow.

blind-bake.name: Blind bake
blind-bake.short: Blind baking is baking a pastry case before the filling is added, usually with weights inside, so the base stays crisp and does not puff up.
blind-bake.long:
Blind baking means baking a tart or pie shell without its filling, so the pastry is cooked through before a wet filling goes in. Without it, liquid fillings such as custard soak into raw pastry and leave a soft, pale base. Weights hold the pastry down and against the sides, because steam trapped under the dough would otherwise puff up the base and the sides would slump.

Press the chilled pastry into the tart pan, prick the base with a fork, cover it with parchment paper, and fill it with baking weights or dried beans. Bake at 190 °C (375 °F) for 15-20 minutes, until the edges are set. Then lift out the paper and weights and bake for 5-10 minutes more, until the base looks dry and lightly golden.

Common mistakes are not chilling the pastry before baking, which makes it shrink, and not filling the weights up to the top edge, which lets the sides slump.
steps: Press the chilled pastry into the tart pan and prick the base with a fork.
Line the pastry with parchment paper and fill it with baking weights or dried beans.
Bake at 190 °C (375 °F) for 15-20 minutes, until the edges are set.
Lift out the paper and weights, then bake for 5-10 minutes more until the base is dry and lightly golden.
tips: Chill the lined pan for at least 30 minutes before baking to reduce shrinking.
The weights and paper are very hot, so lift them out by the paper edges and cool them carefully.
For a wet filling, brush the warm base with beaten egg and return it to the oven for a short time to seal it.
blind-bake.diagramAlt: A tart pan lined with pastry is pricked with a fork (1), parchment paper and weights fill the shell (2), the shell bakes in the oven until the edges are set (3), and the paper and weights are lifted out so the base can dry and turn golden (4).

par-bake.name: Par-bake
par-bake.short: Par-baking is baking bread or pastry until it is only partly cooked, then cooling and storing it so it can be finished in the oven later.
par-bake.long:
Par-baking means baking dough until it is set but not browned, usually for about 75% of the normal baking time, and then stopping. The loaf or crust has a firm structure, but the crust is still pale and the inside is only just cooked. After cooling, it can be stored and finished later, which gives a fresh crust and aroma with only a short final bake.

Cool the item completely on a wire rack, then wrap it airtight. Refrigerate it for up to 2 days or freeze it for up to 3 months. To finish, bake it straight from the refrigerator or freezer at 220 °C (425 °F) until it is golden brown and hot all the way through, usually 8-15 minutes.

Par-baking is also used for pizza bases and pie shells. The most common mistakes are baking until the crust is already brown, so it burns in the final bake, and wrapping the item while still warm, which traps steam and makes the crust soggy.
steps: Shape and proof the dough as usual.
Bake at the temperature in the recipe for about 75% of the normal time, until the crust is set but still pale.
Cool the item completely on a wire rack.
Wrap it airtight and refrigerate for up to 2 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
Bake at 220 °C (425 °F) until golden brown and hot all the way through.
tips: Stop baking while the crust is still pale, because any browning now means a dark final crust.
Label frozen items with the date so they are used in time.
Check that filled items reach 74 °C (165 °F) in the center after the final bake.

egg-wash.name: Egg wash
egg-wash.short: An egg wash is beaten egg, often thinned with water, milk, or cream, brushed onto dough before baking to add shine and golden color.
egg-wash.long:
An egg wash is a thin coating of beaten egg brushed on dough or pastry just before baking. The proteins in the egg set and brown quickly in the oven, and the fat in the yolk adds shine and richness. The coating also works as glue for seeds and sugar, and for pastry edges that must be sealed together.

The ingredients decide the result. Whole egg gives a medium golden gloss. Yolk with a little cream gives a deep, glossy brown. White alone gives a light, crisp, slightly shiny surface. Water or milk thins the egg so it spreads evenly, and milk gives a softer, more matte color. Beat well and strain if threads of egg white remain.

Brush a thin layer with a soft brush. The most common mistake is using too much, which pools in folds and runs down the sides. This glues the pastry to the tray and stops the layers from rising.
steps: Beat 1 egg with 15 ml (1 tablespoon) of water or milk until no streaks remain.
Strain the mixture if threads of egg white remain.
Brush a thin, even layer over the dough with a soft brush.
Wipe away any drips that pool in folds or run onto the tray.
Add seeds or sugar while the wash is still wet, then bake.
tips: Wash your hands, the brush, and the bowl after touching raw egg.
Throw away leftover egg wash that has stood at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
Keep the wash off cut edges of layered pastry, because it can glue the layers together.

windowpane-test.name: Windowpane test
windowpane-test.short: The windowpane test checks gluten development by stretching a small piece of dough until it is thin enough to let light through without tearing.
windowpane-test.long:
The windowpane test shows whether kneading has built enough gluten, the stretchy protein network that traps gas and gives bread its structure. A well-developed dough can be stretched into a thin, see-through film, like a window pane, without breaking. Dough with weak gluten tears quickly into ragged holes.

Pinch off a piece of dough of about 30 g. With floured or wet fingertips, stretch it slowly outward in all directions, turning it between your fingers. Hold it up to the light. If you see a thin, translucent film before it tears, the dough is ready. If it tears immediately, knead for 2-3 minutes more, rest the dough for 5 minutes, and test again.

The most common mistake is stretching too fast, which tears even well-kneaded dough. Dough made with rye or a lot of whole grain flour often tears sooner, because the bran cuts the gluten.
steps: Wet or flour your fingertips and pinch off a piece of dough of about 30 g.
Stretch the piece slowly outward in all directions.
Hold it up to a light and check whether it forms a thin, see-through film.
If it tears before turning translucent, knead for 2-3 minutes more and test again.
tips: Rest the dough for 5-10 minutes before testing, because relaxed gluten stretches further.
A smooth, round hole when the film tears means the gluten is well developed, while a ragged tear means it needs more work.
Do not expect rye or high-bran dough to pass the test as clearly as white bread dough.

bulk-fermentation.name: Bulk fermentation
bulk-fermentation.short: Bulk fermentation is the long rise of the whole batch of dough after mixing and before shaping, when gas, flavor, and structure develop.
bulk-fermentation.long:
Bulk fermentation is the period when the whole mass of dough rests after mixing and before it is divided and shaped. Yeast and bacteria feed on the sugars in the flour and make gas and acids. The gas inflates the gluten network, and the acids and other compounds create flavor. The dough also becomes stronger and easier to shape.

Time depends on temperature, the amount of yeast or starter, and the flour. At about 24 °C (75 °F), dough made with commercial yeast often needs 1-2 hours, and sourdough needs 4-8 hours. Judge by the dough rather than the clock: it should have grown by roughly 50-100%, feel airy, jiggle when the bowl is moved, and show bubbles along the edges.

Common mistakes are stopping too early, which gives a dense loaf with a tight crumb, and going too long, which gives slack, sticky dough that bakes into a flat, sour loaf.
steps: Place the mixed dough in a lightly oiled, clear container and mark the starting level.
Cover the container and keep it at about 24 °C (75 °F).
Fold the dough every 30 minutes at the start, if the recipe asks for it.
Check the growth, bubbles, and airy feel rather than relying only on time.
Turn the dough out gently for shaping when it has reached the size the recipe describes.
tips: Warm dough ferments faster, so use a cooler spot or colder water in hot weather.
A clear container with a marker line or rubber band shows the growth easily.
Do not taste raw dough, because raw flour and raw egg can carry harmful bacteria.

cold-retard.name: Cold retard
cold-retard.short: Cold retarding is leaving dough in the refrigerator for many hours to slow fermentation, which builds flavor and makes baking schedules flexible.
cold-retard.long:
Cold retarding means placing dough in the refrigerator, at about 4 °C (40 °F), so that yeast activity slows greatly while bacteria and enzymes keep working slowly. Over 8-48 hours the dough develops a deeper, more complex flavor and a darker, more blistered crust. The cold dough is also firm, which makes it easier to handle and score.

It is done after shaping, in a covered basket or loaf pan, or during bulk fermentation. Cover the dough tightly so the surface does not dry out. Bake it straight from the refrigerator in a fully preheated hot oven, because it does not need to warm up before baking.

Common mistakes are using too much yeast, which can still overproof in the refrigerator, and keeping the dough too long, until it turns slack, sour, or gray. Sourdough usually suits 8-16 hours, and yeasted dough does best with a reduced amount of yeast.
steps: Shape the dough and place it in a floured basket or loaf pan.
Cover it airtight so the surface does not dry out.
Refrigerate it at 4 °C (40 °F) for 8-16 hours.
Preheat the oven fully while the dough is still cold.
Score the cold dough and bake it right away.
tips: Keep the refrigerator at 4 °C (40 °F) or below, and keep dough containing egg or dairy cold until it is baked.
Use less yeast than in a same-day recipe, because the dough still rises slowly in the cold.
Dust the basket well, because cold dough can stick to cloth.

hydration.name: Hydration
hydration.short: Hydration is the weight of water in a dough as a percentage of the weight of flour, which describes how wet or stiff the dough is.
hydration.long:
Hydration, also called the baker's percentage of water, is the weight of water divided by the weight of flour, multiplied by 100. For example, 350 g of water and 500 g of flour gives 350 divided by 500, multiplied by 100, which is 70% hydration. In bread formulas every ingredient is given relative to the flour weight, and the flour is always 100%.

Typical ranges are 50-57% for bagels, 60-68% for sandwich bread and most pizza dough, 68-78% for baguettes and country loaves, and 78-90% for ciabatta and focaccia. A higher hydration gives a moister, more open crumb, but the dough is stickier and harder to shape. Whole grain flour absorbs more water, so the same percentage feels stiffer than it does with white flour.

The most common mistake is forgetting to count the flour and water inside a starter or poolish, which changes the true percentage.
steps: Weigh the total flour in the recipe, including the flour in any starter or poolish.
Weigh the total water in the recipe, including the water in any starter or poolish.
Divide the weight of the water by the weight of the flour.
Multiply the result by 100 to get the hydration percentage.
tips: Weigh ingredients in grams with a digital scale, because cup measures vary too much.
Raise hydration in small steps of 2-5% between bakes to learn how the dough changes.
A starter or poolish made from equal weights of flour and water has a hydration of 100%.

laminate.name: Laminate
laminate.short: Build a dough with many alternating thin layers of dough and butter by repeatedly rolling and folding, so it puffs into flaky layers when baked.
laminate.long:
Laminating means creating many thin, alternating layers of dough and butter. In the oven, the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, while the butter keeps them from fusing together, so the pastry rises into crisp, flaky layers. Croissants, puff pastry and Danish pastry are all laminated.

Wrap a flat block of cold butter inside the dough, roll the package into a long rectangle, then fold it into 3 layers like a letter. Each roll and fold is called a turn. Chill the dough for 20-30 minutes between turns so the butter stays firm but pliable.

The most common mistake is butter that is too warm or too cold. Warm butter soaks into the dough and the layers merge. Butter that is too cold cracks into pieces and tears the dough.
steps: Wrap a flat block of cold butter inside the dough.
Roll the package into a long rectangle, using firm, even pressure.
Fold the rectangle into 3 layers, like folding a letter.
Chill the dough for 20-30 minutes.
Repeat the rolling, folding and chilling for the number of turns the recipe gives.
tips: Keep the butter and the dough at the same firmness so they stretch together.
Brush off extra flour from each fold, because trapped flour makes the layers tough.
If the butter softens or starts to leak, stop and chill the dough before continuing.
laminate.diagramAlt: A dough package shown in 5 numbered stages from left to right: a block of butter wrapped in dough, the package rolled into a long rectangle, the rectangle folded into 3 layers, the folded dough resting in the refrigerator, and the sequence repeated.

temper-chocolate.name: Temper chocolate
temper-chocolate.short: Melt, cool and gently rewarm chocolate through a set temperature curve so the cocoa butter sets glossy, firm and snappy instead of dull and streaky.
temper-chocolate.long:
Tempering controls how the cocoa butter in chocolate crystallizes. Chocolate that is simply melted and cooled sets soft, dull and streaky. Chocolate taken through a precise temperature curve forms stable crystals, so it sets glossy and firm, with a clean snap.

Each type has its own curve, so use a thermometer and stir the whole time. Dark chocolate: melt to 45-50 °C (113-122 °F), cool to 27-28 °C (81-82 °F), then rewarm to 31-32 °C (88-90 °F). Milk chocolate: melt to 40-45 °C (104-113 °F), cool to 26-27 °C (79-81 °F), then rewarm to 29-30 °C (84-86 °F). White chocolate: melt to 40-45 °C (104-113 °F), cool to 25-26 °C (77-79 °F), then rewarm to 28-29 °C (82-84 °F).

Tempered chocolate is used for dipping, molding and coating. The most common mistake is overheating it while rewarming, which destroys the crystals and means starting again.
steps: Melt chopped chocolate gently to the melting temperature for its type.
Cool it to the cooling temperature while stirring constantly.
Rewarm it slightly to the working temperature.
Test a small smear on parchment paper; it should set glossy within 5 minutes.
tips: Use a digital thermometer, because judging temperature by feel is unreliable.
Keep water away from the chocolate, since even a little makes it seize into a thick paste.
Stirring in finely chopped tempered chocolate, known as seeding, helps the melted chocolate cool and form the right crystals.
temper-chocolate.diagramAlt: A temperature curve drawn from left to right with 4 numbered marks: the high melting point, the dip down to the cooling temperature, the small rise to the working temperature, and a smear of glossy chocolate on parchment paper as the final test.

meringue.name: Meringue
meringue.short: Whip egg whites with sugar into a stable, glossy foam that is used soft as a topping or baked dry and crisp.
meringue.long:
Meringue is egg whites whipped with sugar. Whisking unfolds the egg proteins so they trap air in tiny bubbles, and dissolved sugar makes the foam glossy, smooth and stable. Whisk to soft peaks, which droop at the tip, or to stiff peaks, which stand upright.

There are 3 main methods. French meringue whisks raw whites with sugar. Swiss meringue heats the whites and sugar over simmering water, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the mixture reaches 71 °C (160 °F), then whisks them. Italian meringue pours hot sugar syrup at 118-120 °C (244-248 °F) into the whites while they are whisked, which makes the most stable foam. Bake meringues at a low heat of about 100 °C (212 °F) until they are dry and crisp.

The most common mistakes are traces of fat or yolk, which stop the whites from foaming, and adding the sugar too early or too fast.
steps: Use a clean, completely dry bowl and whisk, free of any fat.
Whisk the egg whites until foamy and soft peaks form.
Add the sugar gradually, a little at a time, whisking between additions.
Whisk until the meringue is thick and glossy and holds a stiff peak.
Pipe or spoon the meringue and bake at about 100 °C (212 °F) until dry.
tips: Wait until soft peaks form before adding the sugar, and add it slowly.
Use pasteurized egg whites for any meringue that will not be baked, unless it is a Swiss meringue heated to 71 °C (160 °F), because raw or lightly heated whites can carry Salmonella.
Pour hot syrup in a thin stream down the side of the bowl, away from the whisk, to avoid splashes and burns.

ribbon-stage.name: Ribbon stage
ribbon-stage.short: Whisk egg yolks and sugar until the mixture is pale, thick and falls from the whisk in a ribbon that stays visible on the surface.
ribbon-stage.long:
Ribbon stage is the point at which egg yolks, or whole eggs, whisked with sugar become pale, thick and full of tiny air bubbles. When you lift the whisk, the mixture falls back in a thick, ribbon-like band that stays on the surface for a few seconds before it sinks.

Add the sugar to the yolks and begin whisking straight away. Whisk steadily, by hand or with a mixer, until the color lightens from deep yellow to pale and the volume increases. This usually takes about 3-5 minutes with a mixer and longer by hand. Test by lifting the whisk and watching how the mixture falls.

Use it as the base for sponge cakes, mousses and custards. The most common mistake is leaving sugar sitting on the yolks without whisking, which makes the yolks form hard, grainy lumps.
steps: Combine the egg yolks and sugar in a bowl and start whisking immediately.
Whisk steadily until the mixture turns pale and increases in volume.
Lift the whisk and let the mixture fall back onto the surface.
Check that it falls in a thick ribbon that stays visible for a few seconds before sinking.
tips: Use a bowl large enough for the mixture to grow in volume.
Fold other ingredients in gently afterward to keep the air in the mixture.
Use pasteurized yolks if the mixture will not be cooked or baked.
ribbon-stage.diagramAlt: A whisk and bowl shown in 4 numbered stages from left to right: yolks and sugar combined, whisking until pale, the whisk lifted so the mixture falls, and a thick ribbon resting on the surface.

creme-anglaise.name: Crème anglaise
creme-anglaise.short: A pouring custard of milk or cream, egg yolks and sugar, stirred over gentle heat until lightly thickened, used as a sauce or ice cream base.
creme-anglaise.long:
Crème anglaise is a thin, pourable custard. Egg yolk proteins thicken as they heat, turning milk or cream into a silky sauce without any flour or starch.

Stir the mixture constantly over low heat until it reaches 82-84 °C (180-183 °F). The visual cue is that it coats the back of a spoon: when you draw a finger across the coated spoon, the line stays clean and does not run. Do not let it go above about 85 °C (185 °F), or the eggs curdle.

Strain it and cool it quickly. Serve it with cakes, tarts and poached fruit, or churn it into ice cream. The most common mistake is overheating, which scrambles the eggs. If it starts to curdle, take it off the heat immediately, strain it and blend it until smooth.
steps: Heat the milk or cream with vanilla until steaming but not boiling.
Whisk the egg yolks and sugar until pale.
Pour the hot milk slowly into the yolks while whisking.
Return the mixture to the pan and stir over low heat until it coats the back of a spoon and reaches 82-84 °C (180-183 °F).
Strain it into a clean bowl and cool it quickly over ice.
tips: Stir in a figure-8 motion and scrape the bottom and corners of the pan so no part overheats.
Set the bowl for straining over ice to stop the cooking right away.
Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 2 days, because custard made with eggs spoils quickly.

ganache.name: Ganache
ganache.short: A smooth emulsion of melted chocolate and warm cream that sets into a soft truffle filling, a pourable glaze or a whippable frosting.
ganache.long:
Ganache is chocolate and cream blended into a smooth emulsion. The fat from the chocolate and cream is held in tiny droplets by the water in the cream, so the result is glossy and creamy rather than greasy.

Heat the cream until it is steaming but not boiling, pour it over finely chopped chocolate, wait 1-2 minutes, then stir slowly from the center outward until smooth. By weight, 1 part cream to 1 part dark chocolate gives a pourable glaze or a soft filling, and 1 part cream to 2 parts dark chocolate gives a firm truffle center.

The most common mistake is a split ganache that looks grainy or oily, caused by overheating or by too little cream for the amount of chocolate. Fix it by stirring in a little warm milk, a small amount at a time.
steps: Chop the chocolate finely and place it in a bowl.
Heat the cream until steaming, then pour it over the chocolate.
Wait 1-2 minutes so the heat melts the chocolate.
Stir slowly from the center outward until smooth and glossy.
tips: Weigh the chocolate and cream, because the ratio decides whether the ganache pours or sets firm.
Milk and white chocolate contain more milk solids and sugar, so they need a higher proportion of chocolate.
Ganache made with cream is perishable, so keep it refrigerated.

choux.name: Choux pastry
choux.short: A light dough made by cooking flour in hot water and butter, then beating in eggs, that puffs into hollow shells when baked.
choux.long:
Choux pastry is a dough cooked in 2 stages, on the stove and then in the oven. Cooking the flour in hot water and butter swells the starch, so the dough can absorb a large amount of egg. In the hot oven, the moisture turns to steam and puffs the dough into a hollow shell, with no baking powder or yeast.

Beat the eggs in a little at a time until the dough is glossy and drops slowly from the spatula in a V shape. Bake at 200 °C (400 °F) until puffed and golden, then lower to 180 °C (350 °F) to dry the shells. Do not open the oven early, as the shells can collapse.

Use choux for eclairs, cream puffs and profiteroles. The most common mistake is underbaking: pale shells deflate as they cool.
steps: Boil the water, butter and salt together until the butter melts.
Add all the flour together and stir hard over medium heat until the dough forms a ball and leaves a thin film on the bottom of the pan.
Cool the dough for a few minutes until it is warm, not hot.
Beat in the eggs a little at a time until the dough is smooth and glossy and drops slowly from the spatula in a V shape.
Pipe the dough and bake at 200 °C (400 °F) until puffed and golden, then lower to 180 °C (350 °F) to dry the shells.
Pierce each shell to let the steam out, then cool on a rack.
tips: Add the eggs gradually, because the right amount depends on how much water the dough lost while cooking.
Bake until deep golden, since pale shells collapse as they cool.
