Fill pastries with cream or custard just before serving and keep them refrigerated, as these fillings spoil quickly.

custard.name: Custard
custard.short: A mixture of milk or cream, eggs and sugar that thickens or sets as the egg proteins cook, either stirred on the stove or baked in the oven.
custard.long:
Custard relies on egg proteins, which are liquid when raw and thicken as they heat. Cooked gently, they form a delicate network that holds the milk and sets the mixture into a smooth cream or a soft gel.

Custards are either stirred on the stove, as in crème anglaise, or baked in a water bath at a gentle heat of about 150 °C (300 °F). A baked custard is ready when the edges are set and the center still wobbles slightly, because it finishes setting as it cools. For safety, make sure the center of an egg mixture reaches at least 71 °C (160 °F).

The most common mistake is too much heat, which makes the eggs curdle into a grainy, watery texture.
steps: Warm the milk or cream with the sugar until steaming.
Whisk the eggs lightly and pour in the hot milk gradually while whisking.
Strain the mixture into a baking dish or individual cups.
Place the dish in a bain-marie and bake at about 150 °C (300 °F) until the edges are set and the center wobbles slightly.
Cool, then refrigerate until cold.
tips: Pour hot liquid into the eggs slowly while whisking, so the eggs warm gradually instead of scrambling.
Strain the mixture before baking for a smooth texture.
Refrigerate cooked custard within 2 hours and keep it chilled.

bain-marie.name: Bain-marie
bain-marie.short: Gently heat food in a bowl or dish set in or over hot water, so it cannot get hotter than the water.
bain-marie.long:
A bain-marie, or water bath, heats food through hot water instead of direct heat. At sea level, water cannot get hotter than 100 °C (212 °F), so delicate foods such as custard, chocolate and cheesecake cook gently and evenly without scorching or curdling.

There are 2 common forms. In the oven, set the dish in a larger pan and pour hot water around it to about 1/2 of the height of the dish. On the stove, set a heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, with the base of the bowl kept above the water so it does not touch.

The most common mistakes are letting the water boil hard, which can overheat the food or splash into it, and letting water or steam touch chocolate, which makes it seize.
steps: Choose a larger pan and a heatproof dish or bowl that fits in or over it.
Add hot water: to about 1/2 the height of the dish for oven baking, or about 3 cm (1 in) deep for a bowl set over the pan so the bowl does not touch the water.
Heat gently, keeping the water below a hard boil.
Lift the dish or bowl out carefully with dry cloths.
tips: In the oven, put the pan in place on the oven rack before pouring in the hot water, to avoid spills and scalds.
Lift hot dishes out with dry cloths or tongs, because steam and hot water scald quickly.
Keep water and steam away from chocolate, since even a little makes it seize.
bain-marie.diagramAlt: A cross-section of a dish sitting in a larger pan of hot water, with 4 numbered marks: the larger pan and the dish, the hot water around the dish, the gentle heat below, and the dish being lifted out with dry cloths.

dock.name: Dock
dock.short: Prick small holes across rolled dough so steam can escape and the dough stays flat instead of puffing up unevenly.
dock.long:
Docking means pricking many small holes through rolled dough with a fork or a spiked roller. As the dough heats, the water in it turns to steam. The holes let the steam escape, so the base stays flat and does not form large bubbles.

Dock the dough after rolling it out and before baking, spacing the holes about 2 cm (3/4 in) apart across the area that should stay flat. It is used for tart and pie bases, crackers, flatbreads and pizza bases, and often together with pie weights when blind baking.

The most common mistake is docking a pastry shell for a liquid filling, such as custard, and then pouring the filling into the raw shell. The filling leaks through the holes. Blind bake a docked shell first so the holes seal. Chilling the dough in advance makes it easier to prick cleanly.
steps: Roll out the dough and fit it into the tart pan or onto the tray.
Chill the dough until firm.
Prick the dough all over with a fork at even intervals, leaving the raised edge alone.
Bake as directed, adding weights for blind baking if the recipe calls for them.
tips: Push the fork straight down rather than at a slant to make clean holes.
For crackers and flatbreads, dock evenly across the whole surface so they bake flat and crisp.
For puff pastry, prick only the areas that should stay flat, such as the base inside a border.

sugar-stages.name: Sugar stages
sugar-stages.short: Names for the textures that boiling sugar syrup reaches at set temperatures, from thread to caramel, which decide what sweet you can make.
sugar-stages.long:
As sugar syrup boils, water evaporates and the sugar becomes more concentrated, so the temperature climbs and the cooled syrup sets harder. Cooks name each stage by how a drop behaves in cold water. Measure with a candy thermometer.

Thread: 106-112 °C (223-234 °F), for syrups. Soft ball: 113-116 °C (235-240 °F), for fudge and fondant. Firm ball: 118-120 °C (244-248 °F), for soft caramels and Italian meringue. Hard ball: 121-130 °C (250-266 °F), for nougat and marshmallows. Soft crack: 132-143 °C (270-290 °F), for taffy and butterscotch. Hard crack: 149-154 °C (300-310 °F), for toffee, brittle and hard candy. Caramel: 160-177 °C (320-350 °F), from light amber to deep brown.

Dissolve the sugar completely before boiling, and avoid stirring after the syrup boils, as stirring can start crystals. The most common mistake is overshooting the temperature, since the syrup keeps cooking from the heat of the pan.
steps: Dissolve the sugar in water over medium heat, stirring until the liquid is clear.
Stop stirring and bring the syrup to a boil, brushing sugar crystals from the sides of the pan with a wet pastry brush.
Boil until a candy thermometer shows the target temperature or a drop in cold water forms the right texture.
Remove the pan from the heat and briefly dip its base in cold water to stop the cooking.
tips: Hot sugar sticks to skin and causes severe burns, so keep children away, keep a bowl of cold water close, and if you are splashed, run cool water over the skin right away.
Add cream or water to hot caramel slowly and stand back, as it bubbles up and spits violently.
Test your thermometer in boiling water, which should read 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level, and adjust for any difference.

whip-cream.name: Whip cream
whip-cream.short: Whisk cold cream until it holds air and thickens into soft, medium or stiff peaks for topping, filling and folding.
whip-cream.long:
Whipped cream is cream with air whisked into it. As you whisk, fat droplets stick together around the air bubbles and form a network that holds the foam. This needs cream with at least 30% fat, sold as whipping or heavy cream, and it must be cold so the fat stays firm.

Chill the cream, bowl and whisk, then whisk at medium speed. The cream passes from a thick liquid to soft peaks that droop, then medium peaks, then stiff peaks that stand upright. Add sugar and vanilla when it starts to thicken.

Stop as soon as you reach the texture you want. The most common mistake is over-whipping: the cream turns grainy and starts to separate into butter and liquid. Gently whisk in a little unwhipped cream to rescue it.
steps: Chill the bowl, whisk and cream until very cold.
Pour the cream into the bowl and whisk at medium speed until it begins to thicken.
Add sugar and vanilla, then keep whisking.
Stop as soon as the cream holds the peak you need.
tips: Use cream straight from the refrigerator and keep it chilled until serving.
Whipped cream spoils quickly, so refrigerate it and discard it if it has stayed at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
Finish the last stage by hand with a whisk to avoid over-whipping.

buttercream.name: Buttercream
buttercream.short: A fluffy frosting made by beating butter with sugar, with eggs or syrup in some versions, used to fill, cover and decorate cakes.
buttercream.long:
Buttercream is butter beaten with sugar until light and fluffy. Beating traps tiny air bubbles in the fat, making the frosting pale, soft and spreadable. The butter should be soft but still cool, about 20 °C (68 °F).

There are 4 main types. American buttercream beats butter with powdered sugar and is the simplest. Swiss and Italian meringue buttercreams beat butter into a cooked meringue made with warmed sugar and whites or with hot syrup, and they are smoother and less sweet. French buttercream beats butter into whipped yolks and hot syrup, and it is richer.

The most common mistake is butter at the wrong temperature. Too warm makes the frosting soupy, and too cold makes it curdled. If it curdles, warm the bowl gently while beating. If it is soupy, chill it briefly and beat again.
steps: Beat soft butter on medium speed until pale and creamy.
Add sifted powdered sugar gradually and beat until smooth.
Add vanilla and a small splash of milk or cream to adjust the texture.
Beat until light and fluffy, then use it immediately or keep it chilled.
tips: Sift the powdered sugar to avoid lumps.

Keep frosting that contains eggs or cream refrigerated, do not leave it out for more than 2 hours, and use pasteurized eggs for French or Italian buttercream, because the eggs are only lightly heated.
Let chilled buttercream come to room temperature and beat it again before use.

pipe.name: Pipe
pipe.short: Squeeze a soft mixture, such as cream, frosting, meringue or choux dough, through a bag fitted with a nozzle to shape it neatly.
pipe.long:
Piping shapes soft mixtures by pressing them through a bag, usually fitted with a nozzle. The shape of the nozzle sets the form and steady pressure sets the size, so you can make rosettes, lines, shells, dots and filled pastries. It works with frosting, whipped cream, meringue, choux dough and more.

Fill the bag no more than 2/3 full, twist the top closed, and squeeze from the top with your stronger hand while the other hand guides the tip. Hold the bag upright for dots and rosettes, and at an angle of about 45 degrees for lines and shells. Stop squeezing before you lift away.

The most common mistakes are overfilling the bag, squeezing from the middle of the bag, and working with a mixture that is too soft or warm, which loses its shape. Chill soft mixtures briefly beforehand.
steps: Fit the nozzle into the bag and fold the top of the bag back over your hand.
Fill the bag no more than 2/3 full and twist the top closed.
Hold the bag upright with the tip close to the surface and squeeze from the top with steady pressure.
Stop squeezing, then lift the bag away.
Repeat with even spacing on a lined tray or on the dessert.
tips: Practice on parchment paper beforehand, since you can scrape the mixture back into the bag.
Stand the bag in a tall glass to fill it without mess.
Wash reusable bags in hot soapy water after use, as they hold dairy and eggs.

glaze.name: Glaze
glaze.short: Cover pastry or cake with a thin shiny layer, such as sugar icing, chocolate or fruit jam, that sets as it cools or dries.
glaze.long:
A glaze is a thin, smooth, usually shiny coating that adds flavor and shine, and can protect against drying. It is liquid when applied and then sets into a thin film as it cools or dries.

Common types are a powdered sugar glaze, made by mixing powdered sugar with a little water, juice or milk; a chocolate glaze, such as warm ganache; and a fruit glaze, made from warmed and strained jam brushed on tarts. Add liquid a few drops at a time until the glaze coats the back of a spoon and falls in a thick but smooth stream.

The most common mistake is adding too much liquid too quickly, which makes the glaze thin and runny, or putting a sugar or chocolate glaze on a hot item, which makes it run off.
steps: Cool the item completely, unless the recipe says to glaze it warm.
Mix the glaze until smooth and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Place the item on a wire rack set over a tray to catch drips.
Pour or brush the glaze over the item in a smooth, continuous motion.
Leave the glaze to set before moving or cutting.
tips: Sift powdered sugar before mixing to avoid lumps.
Add liquid very slowly, because a small amount changes the thickness a lot.
Work quickly, because most glazes start to set within minutes.

pastry-cream.name: Pastry cream
pastry-cream.short: A thick, smooth custard of milk, egg yolks, sugar and starch that is boiled until thick, used to fill tarts, eclairs and cakes.
pastry-cream.long:
Pastry cream is a custard thickened with both egg yolks and starch, usually cornstarch. The starch lets the mixture be boiled without curdling, so it becomes thick enough to hold its shape when chilled.

After the hot milk is whisked into the yolks, the mixture goes back on the heat. Whisk constantly until it thickens and bubbles, then keep it at a gentle boil for 1-2 minutes to cook the starch fully and keep the cream from becoming runny later. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface and chill it quickly.

The most common mistakes are not whisking the bottom and corners, which causes lumps and scorching, and undercooking, which gives a thin or starchy cream. Strain the cream to remove any lumps.
steps: Heat the milk with vanilla until steaming.
Whisk the egg yolks, sugar and cornstarch until smooth and pale.
Pour the hot milk gradually into the yolks while whisking.
Return the mixture to the pan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until thick and bubbling, then keep it at a gentle boil for 1-2 minutes.
Off the heat, whisk in butter if the recipe uses it.
Spread it in a shallow dish, press plastic wrap directly onto the surface and chill quickly.
tips: Whisk into the corners of the pan, where the cream scorches fastest.
Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 2 days, because egg-based fillings spoil quickly.
Whisk the cold cream smooth before using it, since it sets firm in the refrigerator.

spherification.name: Spherification
spherification.short: A technique that sets drops of an alginate-thickened liquid in a calcium bath, forming spheres with a thin gel skin and a liquid center.
spherification.long:
Spherification shapes a liquid into soft spheres that burst in the mouth. Sodium alginate, a thickener made from brown seaweed, is mixed into the flavored liquid. When drops of this liquid fall into water that contains calcium, the calcium links the alginate together and a thin gel skin forms around each drop.

Blend about 0.5% sodium alginate by weight into the liquid, then rest it in the refrigerator for several hours, until the air bubbles have gone. Prepare a bath of about 1% calcium chloride or calcium lactate by weight in water. Drop the liquid in with a spoon or syringe, leave the spheres for 1-3 minutes, then rinse them. Serve them soon, because the gel keeps setting inward until the center is solid.

The most common mistake is using an acidic liquid: below a pH of about 3.6 the alginate does not gel properly, so raise the pH with sodium citrate. Liquids rich in calcium, such as milk, set too early and need reverse spherification instead.
steps: Mix the flavored liquid with sodium alginate.
Drop spoonfuls into a calcium bath.
Wait while a thin gel membrane forms around each drop.
Lift out the spheres and rinse them in clean water.
tips: Weigh the alginate and the calcium salt on a scale that reads to 0.1 g, because small errors change the texture.
Calcium chloride tastes bitter, so always rinse the spheres well; calcium lactate has a milder taste.
Use only food-grade additives, and keep the powders sealed, dry and out of reach of children.
spherification.diagramAlt: The drawing shows 4 numbered stages: sodium alginate being mixed into a flavored liquid, spoonfuls dropping into a calcium bath, a thin gel membrane forming around each drop, and the finished spheres being lifted out and rinsed in clean water.

reverse-spherification.name: Reverse spherification
reverse-spherification.short: A technique that drops a calcium-rich liquid into an alginate bath, forming spheres with a gel skin that stops setting once they are rinsed.
reverse-spherification.long:
Reverse spherification works the opposite way to basic spherification. The calcium goes into the flavored liquid and the sodium alginate goes into the bath. When a drop enters the bath, the calcium reacts with the alginate around it and forms a gel skin on the outside. After rinsing, no alginate is left to react, so the center stays liquid and the spheres can be made ahead.

Dissolve about 2% calcium lactate gluconate by weight in the liquid; liquids already rich in calcium, such as yogurt, may need little or none. Blend about 0.5% sodium alginate by weight into water and rest it in the refrigerator for several hours, until the air bubbles have gone. Drop the liquid into the bath with a spoon, leave the spheres for 2-3 minutes, then rinse them.

Use this method for dairy, alcohol and acidic liquids that fail with basic spherification. The most common mistake is a liquid that is too thin: it spreads out instead of sinking, so thicken it slightly with xanthan.
steps: Mix the flavored liquid with a calcium salt such as calcium lactate gluconate.
Drop spoonfuls into a sodium alginate bath.
Wait while a gel membrane forms around each drop.
Lift out the spheres, rinse them in clean water, and serve.
tips: Keep the spheres apart in the bath and stir gently, because spheres that touch stick together.
Make the alginate bath with distilled or low-calcium water, because the calcium in hard tap water can make it gel too early.
Spheres made with dairy are perishable, so keep them in the refrigerator and serve them the same day.
reverse-spherification.diagramAlt: The drawing shows 4 numbered stages: a calcium salt being mixed into the flavored liquid, spoonfuls dropping into a sodium alginate bath, a gel membrane forming around each drop, and the finished spheres being rinsed in clean water before serving.

sous-vide.name: Sous vide
sous-vide.short: A method of cooking vacuum-sealed food in a water bath held at a precise, low temperature, so it cooks evenly to an exact doneness.
sous-vide.long:
Sous vide is French for under vacuum. Food is sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath at a precise temperature, usually the temperature you want the center to reach. Because the water never gets hotter than that, meat and fish cook evenly from edge to center and stay moist.

Safety depends on both time and temperature, because bacteria die more slowly at lower temperatures. Poultry is safe as soon as its center reaches 74 °C (165 °F). At lower bath temperatures, the center must be held at that temperature for a tested time once it has heated through, and that time gets longer as the temperature drops. Follow a tested time and temperature table, and never leave food in a bath below 54.4 °C (130 °F) for more than 2 hours in total. Food that is not pasteurized is unsafe for pregnant people, young children, older adults and anyone with a weak immune system.

Use it for steaks, chicken, fish and eggs. The most common mistake is trapped air, which makes the bag float and heat unevenly.
steps: Season the food and place it in a bag.
Seal the bag, removing as much air as possible.
Cook the bag in a water bath held at the target temperature.
Remove, dry, and sear briefly to finish.
tips: Keep raw food in the refrigerator until the bath is fully heated, so it spends as little time as possible at 4-60 °C (40-140 °F), where bacteria grow fastest.
Use only bags made for cooking and rated for your bath temperature, and keep them fully under the water.
If you are not serving at once, chill the sealed bag in ice water until it is cold right through, refrigerate it at 4 °C (40 °F) or below and eat it within 3 days.
sous-vide.diagramAlt: The drawing shows 4 numbered stages: food being seasoned and placed in a bag, the bag being sealed with the air removed, the bag cooking in a water bath held at the target temperature, and the food being dried and seared briefly in a hot pan.

agar-gel.name: Agar gel
agar-gel.short: A firm gel made with agar, a gelling agent from seaweed that must be boiled to dissolve and stays solid even when served warm.
agar-gel.long:
Agar is a gelling agent made from red seaweed and a plant-based alternative to gelatin. It only dissolves in boiling liquid. As it cools below about 40 °C (104 °F) it sets into a firm gel that cuts cleanly, and it does not melt again until about 85 °C (185 °F), so agar jellies can be served warm.

Weigh the agar precisely: about 0.5% by weight of the liquid gives a tender gel and about 1% a firm gel that slices cleanly; larger amounts make it hard and brittle. Whisk the powder into the cold liquid, bring it to a boil and boil for at least 2 minutes while stirring, then pour it into molds. It sets within minutes, even at room temperature, so work quickly.

Use agar for jellies, firm layers in desserts and thin gel sheets. The most common mistake is not boiling the mixture long enough, which gives a weak or grainy gel. Very acidic liquids also weaken the gel, so stir in strong acids such as lemon juice after boiling, just before pouring.
steps: Weigh the agar and the liquid.
Whisk the agar into the cold liquid.
Bring to a boil and boil for at least 2 minutes, stirring.
Pour into molds and leave to set.
tips: Agar strength varies between products, and flakes or strands are weaker than powder and need longer boiling, so test a small batch before scaling up.
Unlike gelatin, agar is not broken down by raw pineapple, kiwi or papaya, so it can set these fruits.
Agar gels slowly release liquid as they stand, so keep them covered in the refrigerator and serve them within 2 days.

espuma.name: Espuma
espuma.short: A light foam made by charging a flavored liquid with gas in a whipping siphon, served hot or cold.
espuma.long:
Espuma is Spanish for foam. A flavored liquid is sealed in a whipping siphon and charged with nitrous oxide gas, which dissolves into the liquid under pressure. When the liquid is released through the nozzle, the gas expands and forms tiny bubbles. Fat, gelatin, starch or egg white in the base hold the bubbles in place, so the foam keeps its shape.

Make a well-seasoned base and strain it through a fine sieve so it cannot block the nozzle. Pour it in no higher than the maximum fill line, charge it with the number of gas cartridges the siphon maker recommends, shake well and dispense with the siphon held upside down. Chill cold espumas for a few hours before use; keep hot ones in a water bath at 60 °C (140 °F) or above, but never hotter than the siphon maker allows.

Use espumas for light sauces, soups and desserts. The most common mistake is a base without enough fat or stabilizer, which gives a foam that collapses within seconds.
steps: Make and season the base liquid.
Strain it through a fine sieve into the siphon, up to the maximum fill line.
Close the siphon, charge it with nitrous oxide and shake well.
Hold the siphon upside down and dispense the foam.
tips: Use only nitrous oxide cartridges made for cream siphons, never overfill the siphon, never heat it over direct heat or in a microwave, and never inhale the gas.
Always release all the gas before unscrewing the head, and check the seal and nozzle for damage before each use.
If the base contains raw egg, use pasteurized eggs, and keep dairy and egg foams in the refrigerator when they are not being served.

lecithin-foam.name: Lecithin foam
lecithin-foam.short: A very light, airy foam made by blending a thin, watery liquid with a little lecithin until bubbles collect on the surface.
lecithin-foam.long:
Lecithin is an emulsifier, usually made from soy or sunflower seeds. Dissolved in a thin, watery liquid such as fruit juice, stock or an infusion, it coats air bubbles and stops them from merging and bursting. The result is a delicate foam, often called an air, that carries flavor with almost no weight.

Whisk about 0.5-1% lecithin by weight into the liquid. Pour it into a wide container and hold an immersion blender just at the surface, tilting it so it pulls in air. Blend for a few minutes, wait about 1 minute for the foam to settle, then spoon the foam from the top.

Use lecithin foams as a light garnish. They slowly collapse, so make them just before serving; the leftover liquid can be blended again. The most common mistake is keeping the blender fully under the liquid, which mixes it but adds no air. Liquids high in fat also stop the foam from forming.
steps: Whisk the lecithin into the liquid.
Pour the liquid into a wide container.
Blend with the blender head just at the surface until foam builds up.
Let the foam settle briefly, then spoon it from the top.
tips: Thin liquids foam best, so dilute very sweet or thick liquids with water.
Blend in a wide, shallow container so the blender head can stay at the surface.
Soy lecithin can affect people with a soy allergy; sunflower lecithin is an alternative.

liquid-nitrogen.name: Liquid nitrogen
liquid-nitrogen.short: An extremely cold liquid, at -196 °C (-321 °F), used to freeze food almost instantly, for example to make very smooth ice cream.
liquid-nitrogen.long:
Liquid nitrogen boils at -196 °C (-321 °F). When it touches warmer food it boils away rapidly and freezes the food so fast that only very small ice crystals form. This gives very smooth ice cream and sorbet, lets fresh herbs or fruit be frozen and then shattered into powder, and creates frozen, crunchy shells on foams and meringues.

Pour it slowly, in small amounts, into a sturdy stainless steel bowl while stirring the food constantly. A thick fog of cold gas forms. Before serving, let every trace of liquid evaporate: the food must stop giving off fog. Swallowing liquid nitrogen, or food that still holds it, can cause severe internal injury.

Only adults trained in its handling should use it. It causes cryogenic burns, similar to frostbite, on skin and eyes, so wear loose-fitting insulated gloves and eye protection. It also expands about 700 times as it turns into gas, so never put it in a sealed container: the container can explode.
steps: Put on loose-fitting insulated gloves and eye protection, and work in a well-ventilated room.
Pour a small amount of liquid nitrogen into the food in a stainless steel bowl while stirring constantly.
Keep adding small amounts until the food is frozen to the texture you want.
Wait until no fog rises and no liquid remains before serving.
tips: Use it only in a well-ventilated room, never in a car, elevator or small closed space, because the gas pushes out oxygen and can cause suffocation.
Store and carry it only in a vented container made for cryogenic liquids, never in a sealed flask or bottle.
Keep children and pets away, and let frozen food warm briefly before eating, because very cold food can stick to and burn the lips and tongue.

transglutaminase.name: Transglutaminase
transglutaminase.short: An enzyme, often called meat glue, that bonds pieces of raw meat or fish so they hold together as a whole when cooked and sliced.
transglutaminase.long:
Transglutaminase is an enzyme that creates strong links between proteins. Spread thinly between pieces of raw meat or fish that are then pressed together, it bonds them so firmly that they cook and slice as if they had always been a whole. Cooks use it to join small pieces into an even roll, to attach skin or bacon to a fillet, or to make noodles from puréed seafood.

Pat the surfaces dry, dust them very thinly and evenly through a fine sieve, then press the pieces firmly together. Wrap them tightly in plastic wrap to remove air and refrigerate for at least 6 hours, or overnight, so the bond can form. Cooking then stops the enzyme.

The most common mistake is using too much powder, which leaves a visible, grainy line and a weaker bond. Bonding also moves surfaces that were on the outside, where bacteria may be present, into the center, so bonded meat must be cooked right through, like ground meat.
steps: Pat the surfaces of the meat or fish dry.
Dust the surfaces very thinly and evenly through a fine sieve.
Press the pieces firmly together and wrap them tightly in plastic wrap.
Refrigerate for at least 6 hours so the bond forms, then cook right through.
tips: Avoid breathing in the powder: sprinkle it gently without raising dust and wear a dust mask, because the enzyme can irritate the airways and cause allergies.
Cook bonded meat or fish to at least 71 °C (160 °F) in the center, or 74 °C (165 °F) for poultry, or use a pasteurizing sous vide time and temperature from a tested table, and never serve it rare.
Keep the powder sealed in the refrigerator or freezer, because warmth and humidity weaken it.

fluid-gel.name: Fluid gel
fluid-gel.short: A set gel blended until smooth, giving a sauce that holds its shape on a plate yet flows like thick cream when stirred.
fluid-gel.long:
A fluid gel starts as an ordinary set gel, usually made with agar. Blending breaks the gel into particles so small that they slide past each other, so the result looks and tastes like a smooth purée. It holds a clean shape when spooned or piped, flows when it is stirred, and does not leak liquid across the plate the way a thin sauce does.

Boil the flavored liquid with about 0.5-1% agar by weight, pour it into a container and let it set completely. Cut the gel into pieces and blend it at high speed until completely smooth, adding a little liquid if it is too thick. Pass it through a fine sieve, then let it rest, covered, in the refrigerator so trapped air bubbles can rise.

Use fluid gels for bright fruit or vegetable sauces and for dots and lines on a plate. The most common mistake is using too much agar, which gives a grainy, pasty texture even after long blending.
steps: Boil the flavored liquid with the agar.
Pour it into a container and let it set completely.
Cut the gel into pieces and blend at high speed until smooth.
Pass it through a fine sieve and rest it, covered, in the refrigerator.
tips: Season the liquid strongly before setting it, because gels taste milder than the liquid they are made from.
For acidic juices, boil the agar in part of the liquid, then stir in the acidic juice off the heat.
Store fluid gel covered in the refrigerator, like any fresh sauce, and use it within 3 days.

dehydrate.name: Dehydrate
dehydrate.short: To remove most of the water from food with low, dry heat and moving air, making it crisp or chewy and concentrating its flavor.
dehydrate.long:
Dehydrating removes water from food with gentle, dry heat and a steady flow of air. Without enough water, bacteria and molds cannot grow easily and flavors become stronger, which is why dried fruit, vegetable crisps and jerky keep longer than fresh food. A food dehydrator works best, but an oven at its lowest setting with the door slightly open can also work.

Cut food into even slices about 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4 in) thick and lay them in a single layer with space between them. Dry fruit and vegetables at about 60 °C (140 °F) until fruit is leathery with no moist spots and vegetables are crisp. For jerky, first heat the meat to 71 °C (160 °F), or 74 °C (165 °F) for poultry, then dry it until it bends and cracks without snapping.

The most common mistake is drying at too high a temperature: the outside hardens and traps moisture inside, which can lead to mold.
steps: Cut the food into even, thin slices.
Arrange the slices in a single layer with space between them.
Dry at a low, steady temperature until the right texture is reached.
Let the pieces cool and check that none feel moist inside.
Store them in airtight containers in a cool, dark place.
tips: Let a few pieces cool before testing them, because warm food feels softer than it really is.
Pack dried fruit loosely in a closed jar for about 1 week and shake it daily; if drops of moisture appear inside the jar, dry the fruit longer.
Dip cut apples or pears in lemon juice before drying to stop them from browning.

freeze-dry.name: Freeze-dry
freeze-dry.short: To remove water from frozen food under a vacuum, so the ice turns straight into vapor and the food stays light, crisp and full of flavor.
freeze-dry.long:
Freeze-drying, also called lyophilization, removes water without melting it. The food is frozen solid, then placed under a strong vacuum and warmed very gently, so the ice turns directly into vapor instead of liquid. Because the food never becomes wet or hot, it keeps its shape, color and flavor, and becomes light, porous and crisp. It rehydrates quickly and can be ground into intensely flavored powders.

At home it needs a freeze-dryer machine; an ordinary freezer cannot do it reliably. Cut food into small, even pieces, freeze it, then run the machine until every piece is dry right through, which often takes a day or more. Pack the food at once in airtight containers, because it quickly absorbs moisture from the air and turns soft.

The most common mistake is assuming the food is cooked or sterile. Freeze-drying does not kill bacteria, so raw meat, fish and eggs stay raw and must be cooked after rehydrating.
steps: Cut the food into small, even pieces.
Freeze the pieces solid.
Run the freeze-dryer until every piece is dry right through.
Pack the food immediately in airtight containers.
tips: Very fatty or very sugary foods do not freeze-dry well, because fat does not dry out and sugar can stay sticky.
Check a few of the thickest pieces: they should be crisp in the center, with no cold or chewy spots.
Store freeze-dried food in sealed, moisture-proof bags or jars, away from light and heat.

xanthan-thickening.name: Xanthan thickening
xanthan-thickening.short: Thickening a hot or cold liquid with a tiny amount of xanthan gum, which adds body without cooking and keeps sauces and dressings stable.
xanthan-thickening.long:
Xanthan gum is a thickener made by fermenting sugar with bacteria. Unlike flour or starch, it thickens straight away, hot or cold, without cooking, and it is not affected by acid, salt or freezing. It also keeps oil droplets and small pieces of food suspended, so dressings stay mixed and sauces do not separate.

Very small amounts are enough: about 0.1-0.2% by weight gives light body, and up to about 0.5% gives a thick sauce. That means 1 g of xanthan lightly thickens about 500 g of liquid. Sprinkle it slowly over the liquid while blending with an immersion blender, or mix it first with sugar or oil, so it does not form lumps. Let the mixture rest for a few minutes so air bubbles can escape.

Use it for dressings, cold sauces, smoothies and gluten-free baking. The most common mistake is adding too much, which gives a slimy, stringy texture.
steps: Weigh the liquid and the xanthan gum.
Sprinkle the xanthan slowly over the liquid while blending.
Blend until smooth and slightly thickened.
Let it rest for a few minutes so air bubbles can escape.
tips: Weigh xanthan on a scale that reads to 0.1 g, because measuring spoons are not precise enough for such small amounts.
Add it a little at a time and stop as soon as the texture is right, because too much cannot be taken out.
Do not add xanthan to food or drinks for babies unless a doctor advises it.

maltodextrin-powder.name: Maltodextrin powder
maltodextrin-powder.short: A powder made by mixing a fat or oil with tapioca maltodextrin, which absorbs it and melts back into liquid fat in the mouth.
maltodextrin-powder.long:
Tapioca maltodextrin is a very light, starch-based powder that can absorb a large amount of fat while staying dry. When it is mixed with a flavored oil or fat, the fat is trapped in the powder. On the tongue, the maltodextrin dissolves in saliva and the powder turns back into rich, liquid fat.

Start with roughly equal weights of fat and maltodextrin and whisk or blend them together. Keep adding maltodextrin a little at a time until the mixture becomes a dry, fluffy powder, then press it through a sieve to make it fine. Use fats that contain no water, such as oils, clarified butter or strained rendered fat.

Use it to make olive oil powder, nut butter crumbs or bacon fat powder as a garnish. The most common mistake is moisture: water in the fat, a humid room or a wet plate turns the powder into a paste.
steps: Weigh the fat and an equal weight of tapioca maltodextrin.
Whisk or blend them together.
Add more maltodextrin a little at a time until the mixture becomes a dry powder.
Press the powder through a sieve and keep it airtight until serving.
tips: Use tapioca maltodextrin sold for cooking, because ordinary maltodextrin is denser and does not absorb fat in the same way.
Make the powder close to serving time, keep it airtight and away from steam, and sprinkle it onto the plate at the last moment, away from sauces.
If you flavor the oil yourself with garlic or fresh herbs, keep that oil in the refrigerator and use it within 4 days, because garlic and herbs in oil can allow botulism to develop.

vacuum-compression.name: Vacuum compression
vacuum-compression.short: Sealing porous fruit or vegetables in a vacuum chamber so the air inside them is removed, making them denser, glossier and more intense.
vacuum-compression.long:
Many fruits and vegetables, such as watermelon, cucumber, apple and pineapple, are full of tiny air pockets. In a chamber vacuum sealer, the air is pulled out of these pockets; when normal pressure returns, the cell walls collapse, and the food becomes denser, more translucent and brighter in color, with a firmer bite. If a liquid such as juice, syrup or brine is added to the bag, it is pushed into the food at the same time and flavors it right through.

Cut the food into even pieces, place them in a single layer in a bag with any liquid, and run a full vacuum cycle. Leave the pieces in the bag for a few minutes before opening it.

This needs a chamber vacuum sealer; handheld and edge sealers do not pull a strong enough vacuum. The most common mistake is using soft, very ripe fruit, which turns mushy instead of firm.
steps: Cut the fruit or vegetables into even pieces.
Place them in a single layer in a bag, with chilled liquid if you want to flavor them.
Run a full vacuum cycle in a chamber vacuum sealer.
Leave for a few minutes, then open the bag and serve cold.
tips: Chill any liquid before adding it, because liquids boil at low pressure and warm liquid can boil over and spoil the seal.
Compression does not cook or preserve food, so keep it in the refrigerator and serve it the same day.
Wipe the open end of the bag dry before sealing, because liquid in the seal area gives a weak seal.

gelatin-bloom.name: Bloom gelatin
gelatin-bloom.short: To soak gelatin in cold water so it swells and softens, which lets it dissolve smoothly into a warm liquid without lumps.
gelatin-bloom.long:
Gelatin is a protein made from animal collagen. Its dry granules or sheets must absorb water before they can dissolve evenly, and this soaking step is called blooming. If dry gelatin goes straight into a hot liquid, the outside of each granule swells into a sticky coating that stops the inside from dissolving, which leaves lumps.

For powder, sprinkle it evenly over about 5 times its weight in cold water and leave it for 5-10 minutes, until it looks spongy. For sheets, soak them in plenty of cold water for 5-10 minutes until soft, then squeeze out the excess water. Stir the bloomed gelatin into a warm liquid until no granules remain, without boiling, because boiling weakens the gel. Most gelatin desserts need at least 4 hours in the refrigerator to set.

The most common mistake is swapping sheets and powder by count. Sheets come in different strengths, so follow the weight and type given in the recipe.
steps: Weigh the gelatin.
Sprinkle powder over cold water, or soak sheets in plenty of cold water.
Leave for 5-10 minutes until soft and swollen.
Squeeze the excess water out of sheets.
Stir into a warm liquid until fully dissolved, without boiling.
tips: Raw pineapple, kiwi, papaya, mango, fig and fresh ginger contain enzymes that stop gelatin from setting, so cook them first or use canned fruit.
Gelatin comes from animals such as pigs, cattle or fish, so use agar for vegetarian or vegan dishes.
Always bloom in cold water, because warm water starts to dissolve the gelatin before it has absorbed water evenly.

cold-smoke.name: Cold smoke
cold-smoke.short: To flavor food with smoke while keeping it cool, below 25 °C (77 °F), so it takes on a smoky taste without cooking or melting.
cold-smoke.long:
Cold smoking exposes food to smoke without heating it. The smoke comes from sawdust or wood chips smoldering in a separate box or tray, and cools on its way to the food. Because the food is not cooked, cheese stays firm, butter stays solid and cured salmon stays silky.

Keep the smoking chamber below 25 °C (77 °F); on warm days, smoke at night or put a tray of ice in the chamber. Use thin, pale smoke, and rest smoked food wrapped in the refrigerator for at least 1 day so the flavor mellows.

Cold smoking is not cooking and does not preserve food. Raw meat and fish must first be cured with a tested recipe, with the salt or curing salt weighed exactly, and other perishable foods must not spend more than 2 hours in total at 4-60 °C (40-140 °F). Foods that are safe at room temperature, such as hard cheese, nuts and salt, can be smoked for longer. The most common mistake is letting the chamber warm up, which melts cheese and makes fat seep out.
steps: Cure meat or fish first with a tested recipe, or choose a food that is safe at room temperature.
Light the smoke source in a separate box or tray, away from the food.
Smoke the food in thin smoke, keeping the chamber below 25 °C (77 °F).
Wrap the food and rest it in the refrigerator for at least 1 day.
tips: Cold-smoked fish and meat are still raw, so they are not suitable for pregnant people, young children, older adults or anyone with a weak immune system.
Freeze fish for cold smoking at -20 °C (-4 °F) or colder for 7 days before curing it, to kill parasites.
Smoke outdoors or in a well-ventilated space and burn only dry, untreated hardwood made for smoking, because smoldering wood produces carbon monoxide and treated wood gives off toxic fumes.

pickle.name: Pickle
pickle.short: Preserving food in an acidic brine, usually vinegar with salt, so that harmful bacteria cannot grow.
pickle.long:
Pickling preserves vegetables, fruit, eggs or fish by surrounding them with acid. Vinegar lowers the pH so far that spoilage bacteria and the bacteria that cause botulism cannot grow, while salt firms the texture and adds flavor. Pickles meant for storage at room temperature must also be processed in a boiling-water bath.

Use vinegar labeled at least 5% acidity and follow a tested recipe exactly: the ratio of vinegar to water and to vegetables is what makes the pickle safe. Choose firm, very fresh produce, and cut 1.5 mm (1/16 in) from the blossom end of cucumbers, because it contains enzymes that soften pickles. Heat the brine in a stainless steel or unchipped enamel pan, never in copper, brass, galvanized metal or iron, because acid reacts with these metals.

The most common mistake is improvising: adding water, reducing the vinegar or packing in extra low-acid vegetables can raise the pH to an unsafe level. Soft pickles usually come from old produce or overcooking.
steps: Wash the jars, keep them hot, and prepare new lids.
Wash and trim the produce, then cut it as the recipe directs.
Heat the vinegar, water and salt in the exact amounts given by a tested recipe until the salt dissolves.
Pack the produce into the hot jars and cover it with hot brine, leaving the headspace the recipe specifies.
Seal the jars and process them in a boiling-water bath for the stated time, adjusted for your altitude, or keep them in the refrigerator.
tips: Use pickling or canning salt, because table salt with anti-caking agents can make the brine cloudy.
Never use homemade vinegar or vinegar of unknown strength for pickles stored at room temperature, because its acidity cannot be relied on.
Discard any jar with a bulging lid, leaks, spurting liquid, mold or an off smell without tasting it, because botulism cannot be detected by smell or taste.

quick-pickle.name: Quick pickle
quick-pickle.short: Making pickles by pouring a simple vinegar brine over vegetables and keeping them in the refrigerator, ready within hours.
quick-pickle.long:
A quick pickle, also called a refrigerator pickle, flavors vegetables or fruit with vinegar, salt and often sugar, without processing the jars in a water bath. The acid seasons the food and slows spoilage, but the cold of the refrigerator does most of the work of keeping it safe, so quick pickles are never shelf-stable.

Slice the vegetables thinly so the brine penetrates quickly. A common starting brine is equal volumes of vinegar and water, with salt and sugar to taste. Pour it on hot for firm vegetables such as carrots, or cooled for delicate ones such as cucumber. Thin slices of red onion are ready in about 30 minutes; thicker pieces need a day or more.

The most common mistake is storing quick pickles in the cupboard or treating them like canned pickles. Keep them covered in the refrigerator at or below 4 °C (40 °F), always under the brine, and eat them within a few weeks.
steps: Slice the vegetables thinly and pack them into a clean jar.
Heat the vinegar, water, salt and sugar until the salt and sugar dissolve.
Pour the brine over the vegetables until they are fully covered.
Cool, cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before eating.
tips: Use a clean utensil each time you take pickles from the jar, so they keep longer.
Discard quick pickles that turn slimy, smell off or show mold.
Add whole spices, garlic or herbs to the brine for flavor, and keep the jar in the refrigerator at all times.

cure.name: Cure
cure.short: Preserving meat or fish with salt, often with sugar and nitrite curing salt, to draw out moisture and stop harmful bacteria from growing.
cure.long:
Curing preserves meat or fish with salt, often with sugar, either rubbed on dry or dissolved in water as a brine. Salt draws out water and makes the food hostile to bacteria. Bacon, ham and many sausages also use nitrite curing salt, which protects against the bacteria that cause botulism, keeps the meat pink and gives the typical cured flavor.

Weigh the meat and calculate every ingredient as a percentage of its weight, following a tested recipe. Curing salts differ in nitrite strength by country and brand, from about 0.5% to 6.25% nitrite, so the right amount depends on the exact product. Use only the product and the amount that your tested recipe names, and never apply the amount for one product to another. Nitrite is toxic when overdosed, so never use curing salt as everyday seasoning. Keep the meat at or below 4 °C (40 °F) while it cures.

The most common mistake is measuring by volume or by eye. Meat eaten without cooking, such as dry-cured ham or salami, needs controlled conditions and a tested recipe.
steps: Weigh the meat and write down its exact weight.
Calculate and weigh the salt, sugar and curing salt from a tested recipe, using a scale accurate to 0.1 g for the curing salt.
Mix the cure and rub it evenly over every surface of the meat.
Seal the meat in a bag or covered container and refrigerate it at or below 4 °C (40 °F), turning it daily, for the time the recipe gives.
Rinse off the cure if the recipe says so, pat the meat dry, then cook, smoke or dry it as directed.
tips: Store curing salt in a labeled container away from ordinary salt and out of reach of children.

For fish that will be eaten cured but not cooked, such as gravlax, first freeze it at -20 °C (-4 °F) or colder for at least 7 days to kill parasites, checking with a thermometer because many home freezers do not get this cold.
A cure does not cook meat, so bacon and most wet-cured ham must still be cooked to a safe temperature.

can.name: Can
can.short: Preserving food in sealed glass jars, heated long enough to destroy microorganisms and form a vacuum seal for storage at room temperature.
can.long:
Canning heats filled jars to destroy the microorganisms that spoil food, and a vacuum seal forms as the jars cool. The right method depends on acidity. High-acid foods with a pH of 4.6 or lower, such as most fruit, jams, pickles, and tomatoes with added lemon juice or citric acid, can be processed in a boiling-water bath at 100 °C (212 °F). Low-acid foods, such as vegetables, beans, meat, poultry and fish, must be processed in a pressure canner, which reaches about 116 °C (240 °F). Only that higher temperature destroys the heat-resistant spores of the bacteria that cause botulism.

Always follow a tested recipe from a recognized food-safety authority, with its exact jar size, headspace, processing time and altitude adjustment. Use new flat lids each time. After processing, leave the jars undisturbed for 12-24 hours, then check that every lid is sealed and curved slightly inward.

The most dangerous mistake is improvising: inventing recipes, shortening times or processing low-acid food in a water bath. Botulism toxin cannot be seen, smelled or tasted.
steps: Choose a tested recipe and the processing method it requires for that food.
Wash the jars, keep them hot, and prepare new flat lids.
Fill the hot jars, leave the stated headspace, remove air bubbles and wipe the rims clean.
Fit the lids and bands finger-tight, then process the jars for the exact time, and at the exact pressure if required, adjusted for your altitude.
Let the jars cool undisturbed for 12-24 hours, then check every seal.
Label and store sealed jars in a cool, dark place, and refrigerate any unsealed jar and eat it promptly.
tips: Discard any jar with a bulging lid, leaks, spurting liquid, mold or an off smell without tasting it, because botulism cannot be detected by smell or taste.
A standard pressure cooker or electric multi-cooker is not a pressure canner and cannot be relied on to process jars safely.
For best quality, eat home-canned food within 1 year.

confit.name: Confit
confit.short: Slowly cooking salted meat, usually duck or pork, fully submerged in fat at a low temperature, then storing it under that fat.
confit.long:
Confit is a traditional French method in which meat is first salted, then cooked very gently in fat until very tender. Salting seasons the meat and draws out some water, and the slow, low cooking melts connective tissue without drying the meat. The fat then covers the cooked meat and protects it from air.

Rub the meat with salt and aromatics and refrigerate it overnight. Rinse and dry it, cover it completely with melted fat in a heavy pot, and cook it in a low oven or over low heat with the fat barely bubbling, until the meat pulls easily from the bone. Duck legs usually take several hours. To serve, crisp the skin in a hot pan or oven.

The most common mistake is treating the fat as a substitute for refrigeration. Fat keeps out air, and the bacteria that cause botulism grow without air, so confit must be cooled quickly, kept in the refrigerator at or below 4 °C (40 °F), and eaten within a few days or frozen.
steps: Rub the meat with salt and aromatics, cover it and refrigerate it overnight.
Rinse off the salt and pat the meat dry.
Place the meat in a heavy pot and cover it completely with melted fat.
Cook gently, with only occasional small bubbles, until the meat is very tender.
Cool quickly and store the meat in the refrigerator, completely covered by fat.
tips: Eat refrigerated confit within 3-4 days, as with other cooked meat, or freeze it, because keeping it for weeks under fat is a tradition, not a tested safety method.
Garlic, herbs or vegetables kept in oil, raw or cooked, carry a botulism risk, so never leave them at room temperature: refrigerate them immediately and use them within 4 days, or freeze them.
To cool a large batch quickly, divide the meat and fat into smaller containers before refrigerating.

vacuum-seal.name: Vacuum seal
vacuum-seal.short: Removing the air from a plastic bag or container and sealing it closed to slow spoilage, oxidation and freezer burn.
vacuum-seal.long:
Vacuum sealing removes most of the air around food before the package is closed with heat or a valve. With little oxygen left, fats go rancid more slowly, colors last longer, and frozen food is protected from freezer burn. It is also the usual first step for sous vide cooking and for quick marinating.

Vacuum sealing does not kill bacteria. Some dangerous bacteria, including those that cause botulism and listeriosis, grow without oxygen, and without air the usual signs of spoilage may not appear, so food can look fine while being unsafe. Perishable food must therefore stay cold: refrigerate it at or below 4 °C (40 °F) or freeze it, and keep to the same refrigerator time limits as for unsealed food unless a tested guideline says otherwise.

The most common mistake is sealing warm food or leaving sealed packs at room temperature. Chill food before sealing, and freeze liquids or very moist food until firm so they are not drawn into the sealer.
steps: Chill the food thoroughly, and freeze liquids or very moist food until firm.
Place the food in the bag, leaving enough empty bag at the top for a clean seal.
Wipe the opening clean and dry, then vacuum and seal the bag.
Check that the seal is flat and unbroken, label the bag with the contents and date, and refrigerate or freeze it immediately.
tips: Wrap sharp bones or hard edges in paper or extra plastic so they do not pierce the bag.
Open or remove the package of vacuum-packed frozen fish before thawing it in the refrigerator, because the bacteria that cause botulism can grow in fish kept without air.
Vacuum sealing does not make perishable food shelf-stable, so never store sealed packs of it at room temperature.

jam.name: Make jam
jam.short: Cooking fruit with sugar until it thickens and sets into a spreadable preserve, held together by the fruit's natural pectin and acid.
jam.long:
Jam sets when pectin from the fruit, acid and a high concentration of sugar work together. As the mixture boils, water evaporates until the pectin strands can link into a soft gel. Sugar also preserves the jam by binding water, so reducing the sugar in a regular recipe gives a runny jam that spoils sooner. Low-sugar jams need a recipe and a pectin designed for them.

Boil hard in a wide pan, stirring often, so water evaporates quickly. The jam is set at about 105 °C (221 °F) at sea level; at high altitude, lower this by the same amount as the drop in the boiling point of water. Without a thermometer, use the wrinkle test: put a little jam on a frozen plate, wait 1 minute and push it with a finger. If the surface wrinkles, it is ready.

The most common mistakes are overcooking, which gives a dark, sticky jam with a caramel taste, and cooking very large batches, which set poorly. For storage at room temperature, process the jars in a boiling-water bath following a tested recipe.
steps: Put 2-3 small plates in the freezer and prepare clean, hot jars.
Cook the prepared fruit with the sugar, and with lemon juice or pectin if the recipe uses them, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Boil hard, stirring often, until the jam reaches its set point, about 105 °C (221 °F) at sea level, or passes the wrinkle test.
Remove the pan from the heat, skim off any foam and ladle the jam into the hot jars, leaving the headspace the recipe specifies.
Seal the jars and process them in a boiling-water bath as the recipe directs, or cool them and keep the jam in the refrigerator.
tips: Strawberries, cherries and peaches are low in pectin and usually need lemon juice or added pectin, while apples, quinces, currants and citrus fruit set easily.
Take the pan off the heat while you do the wrinkle test so the jam does not overcook.
Discard the whole jar if mold appears on jam, rather than scraping the mold off.

render.name: Render
render.short: Melting the fat out of fatty meat, skin or trimmings with gentle heat, leaving clear liquid fat and crisp solids.
render.long:
Rendering separates fat from the connective tissue and water that hold it in place. Gentle heat melts the fat and slowly drives off the water, while the remaining solids turn crisp and golden. Pork fat gives lard, beef fat gives tallow, and chicken or duck fat is often rendered with onion. The same principle applies when duck breast or bacon is started in a cold pan and cooked slowly so the fat melts out.

Chill the fat, then cut it into small pieces or grind it so it melts evenly. Start it in a heavy pot with a little water over low heat; the water stops it from scorching before the fat begins to flow. Stir occasionally. The fat is ready when the bubbling almost stops, which shows the water has gone, and the solids are golden. Strain it through a fine sieve lined with cloth into clean, dry jars.

The most common mistake is using high heat, which browns the fat and gives it a strong flavor. Any water left in the fat shortens its storage life.
steps: Chill the fat and cut it into small pieces or grind it.
Put the fat in a heavy pot with a little water to cover the bottom and set it over low heat.
Cook gently, stirring occasionally, until the bubbling almost stops and the solids are golden.
Strain the liquid fat through a fine sieve lined with cloth into clean, dry jars.
Cool, cover and store the fat in the refrigerator or freezer.
tips: Never add water to fat that is already hot, because it can spatter violently.
For the mildest lard, use the fat from around the pig's kidneys, called leaf fat.
Season the crisp solids, called cracklings, with salt and eat them as a snack.

freeze.name: Freeze
freeze.short: Storing food at -18 °C (0 °F) or below, which stops microorganisms from growing and keeps food safe for long periods.
freeze.long:
Freezing turns the water in food into ice, so bacteria, yeasts and molds cannot grow. It does not kill most of them, and they become active again when the food thaws. Food kept frozen at -18 °C (0 °F) or below stays safe indefinitely, but its quality slowly declines, so recommended freezer times are about taste and texture, not safety.

Freeze food quickly and in small portions, because slow freezing forms large ice crystals that damage texture. Cool cooked food quickly and refrigerate or freeze it within 2 hours of cooking. Blanch most vegetables before freezing to stop the enzymes that dull color and flavor. Wrap food airtight to prevent freezer burn, leave space in containers for liquids to expand, and label everything with the date.

The most common mistake is thawing food on the counter, where the surface warms into the danger zone of 4-60 °C (40-140 °F). Thaw food in the refrigerator, in cold water changed every 30 minutes, or in the microwave if you cook it immediately.
steps: Cool cooked food quickly in the refrigerator, and blanch most vegetables before freezing.
Spread small items such as berries on a tray and freeze them until firm so they do not stick together.
Pack the food in airtight freezer bags or containers, removing air and leaving space for liquids to expand.
Label each package with the contents and date.
Freeze at -18 °C (0 °F) or below, and thaw in the refrigerator.
tips: Food thawed in the refrigerator can be refrozen, although its texture may suffer, but food thawed in cold water or in the microwave should be cooked before refreezing.
Food with freezer burn, seen as dry gray-brown patches, is safe to eat, but cut those patches away for better flavor.
Add warm or large amounts of food to the freezer gradually, because overloading it slows freezing for everything inside.

salt-preserve.name: Salt-preserve
salt-preserve.short: Preserving food by burying or packing it in large amounts of salt, which draws out water and stops nearly all microorganisms from growing.
salt-preserve.long:
Salt preservation is used for fish such as cod and anchovies, and for lemons, capers, herbs and egg yolks. Salt pulls water out of the food and binds what remains, so bacteria and molds have too little free water to grow. It uses far more salt than brining or fermentation, so the food usually needs rinsing or soaking before use.

Use very fresh food and coarse salt without iodine or anti-caking agents, which can discolor food or cloud the liquid. Layer the food with salt in a glass, ceramic or food-grade plastic container so no surface is left exposed, and keep it cool. The liquid drawn out either drains away, as with salt cod, or forms a brine that must cover the food, as with preserved lemons. Follow a tested recipe for the amount of salt and the time.

The most common mistake is using too little salt or leaving parts of the food exposed, which lets spoilage start. Before cooking salt cod, soak it in cold water in the refrigerator for 1-3 days, changing the water often.
steps: Clean the food, and dry it well if the recipe asks for it.
Spread a layer of coarse salt in a glass, ceramic or food-grade plastic container.
Add the food in layers, covering every surface completely with salt.
Cover the container and keep it cool for the time the recipe gives, draining off liquid or keeping the food under its brine as directed.
Rinse or soak the food in cold water in the refrigerator to remove excess salt before using it.
tips: Discard salt-preserved food that smells rotten, turns slimy or grows fuzzy mold.
Soak thick pieces of salt fish longer than thin pieces, and keep them in the refrigerator throughout.
Throw away salt that has drawn liquid from food instead of reusing it.

sun-dry.name: Sun-dry
sun-dry.short: Drying food with the heat of the sun and moving air until it holds too little water for microorganisms to grow.
sun-dry.long:
Sun-drying removes water slowly with warm, dry, moving air. When enough water is gone, bacteria, yeasts and molds cannot grow, and flavor and sweetness become concentrated. It works best for fruit that is high in sugar and acid, such as apricots, figs, grapes, plums and tomatoes. Vegetables and meat dry too slowly and spoil too easily outdoors, so a dehydrator or oven is safer for them.

Sun-drying needs several hot, dry, breezy days in a row, with temperatures of at least 30 °C (86 °F) and low humidity. Lay evenly cut fruit, without overlapping, on food-safe screens raised off the ground, and cover them with fine netting against insects. Bring the trays inside at night, because dew adds moisture back. Fruit is dry when it is leathery and pliable, with no moisture when squeezed.

The most common mistake is drying in humid weather, which lets mold grow before the food dries. Sun-dried food should also be pasteurized to kill insect eggs before storage.
steps: Wash the fruit, cut it into even pieces, and dip light-colored fruit in lemon juice to limit browning.
Spread the pieces without overlapping on food-safe screens raised off the ground, and cover them with fine netting.
Dry them in full sun, turning the pieces daily and bringing the trays inside at night.
When the fruit is leathery with no moisture inside, pasteurize it by freezing it at -18 °C (0 °F) or below for 48 hours or heating it in an oven at 71 °C (160 °F) for 30 minutes.
Pack the dried fruit loosely in a covered jar for 7-10 days, shaking it daily, and dry it further if moisture appears.
tips: Use screens made of stainless steel or food-grade plastic, not galvanized metal, copper or aluminum, which can react with the fruit.
If rain or humid weather arrives, finish drying in an oven or dehydrator.

Store fully dried fruit in airtight containers in a cool, dark, dry place, but keep dried tomatoes or other dried food covered in oil in the refrigerator and use them within 4 days, because of the risk of botulism.

candy.name: Candy
candy.short: Preserving fruit, citrus peel or ginger by simmering and soaking it in sugar syrup until sugar replaces most of the water inside.
candy.long:
Candying replaces the water in fruit with sugar. As the fruit sits in hot syrup, water moves out and sugar moves in, until the fruit holds so much sugar that microorganisms cannot grow. The result is translucent, sweet and firm, and well-dried candied fruit keeps for months in an airtight container.

Citrus peel is first blanched in boiling water, often 2-3 times with fresh water, to soften it and remove bitterness. It is then simmered gently in syrup, often made with equal weights of sugar and water, until translucent. Whole fruit such as cherries needs a slower process: the syrup is made stronger little by little over several days so the fruit does not shrivel. Finally, the fruit is drained, dried until no longer sticky, and sometimes rolled in sugar.

The most common mistake is starting with syrup that is too strong or boiling it too hard, which shrinks and toughens the fruit or makes the syrup crystallize. A little lemon juice or glucose syrup helps prevent graininess.
steps: Cut the peel into strips, blanch it in boiling water and drain it.
Repeat the blanching 2-3 times with fresh water to remove bitterness.
Simmer the peel gently in a syrup of equal weights of sugar and water until it is translucent.
Lift the peel out and drain it on a rack until it is dry and no longer sticky.
Roll it in sugar if you like, and store it in an airtight container.
tips: To candy edible flowers, brush them with pasteurized egg white and dust them with fine sugar, because raw unpasteurized egg can carry salmonella.
Use only flowers you know are edible and that have not been sprayed with chemicals.
Keep the leftover syrup in the refrigerator and use it to sweeten drinks or desserts.

lacto-ferment.name: Lacto-ferment
lacto-ferment.short: Preserving vegetables with salt instead of vinegar, so natural lactic acid bacteria turn their sugars into acid that sours and protects them.
lacto-ferment.long:
Lacto-fermentation preserves vegetables with salt instead of vinegar. Lactic acid bacteria already live on fresh vegetables. Salt pulls water out of the vegetables and holds back spoilage microbes, while the bacteria, kept away from air under the brine, turn natural sugars into lactic acid. The acid gives the sour taste and makes the food too acidic for harmful bacteria to grow.

Weigh the vegetables plus any water you add, and use 2-3% of that total weight in salt, which is 20-30 g of salt per 1 kg. Massage shredded vegetables with the salt until they release their own liquid, or cover chopped vegetables with salted water. Hold everything under the liquid with a weight and ferment at 18-22 °C (64-72 °F). Bubbles and a cloudy brine show that fermentation is active. Most vegetables take from a few days to a few weeks; taste from day 3 and refrigerate when the sourness is right.

The most common mistake is letting pieces float above the brine, where mold can grow. A finished ferment should reach a pH below 4.6, ideally 3.5-4.0.
steps: Mix the vegetables with salt and pack them tightly into a clean jar.
Cover the vegetables with brine and hold them under it with a weight.
Leave the jar at room temperature to ferment, letting the gas escape.
Close the jar and move it to cold storage once it tastes sour enough.
tips: A flat, white, wrinkled film on the surface is usually kahm yeast, which is harmless; skim it off and make sure the vegetables stay under the brine.
If you see fuzzy mold in blue, green, black, pink or any other color, discard the whole batch; do not scrape it off, and never taste a ferment to judge whether it is safe.
Use an airlock lid, or loosen the lid briefly each day, so the gas can escape without the jar building pressure.
lacto-ferment.diagramAlt: The drawing shows 4 numbered stages from left to right: 1, vegetables mixed with salt and packed into a jar; 2, the vegetables held under brine by a weight; 3, the jar at room temperature with gas bubbles escaping; 4, the closed jar placed in cold storage.

koji.name: Koji
koji.short: Steamed rice, barley or soybeans grown with the mold Aspergillus oryzae, whose enzymes turn starch into sugar and protein into savory flavor.
koji.long:
Koji is cooked grain or beans covered in the white threads of a mold called Aspergillus oryzae. As the mold grows, it releases enzymes that break starch into sugars and protein into amino acids, which taste savory. These enzymes are the base of miso, soy sauce, sake, mirin and rice vinegar, and koji also adds sweetness and depth to marinades.

Soak the rice, steam it until each grain is cooked through but still firm, and cool it to about 35 °C (95 °F) before mixing in koji spores. Spread it in an even layer, cover it with a damp cloth, and keep it warm and humid at about 30 °C (86 °F). The mold makes its own heat, so stir the grains and spread them thinner if they rise above 40 °C (104 °F). After about 48 hours the grains should be bound by white threads and smell sweet, like chestnuts or mushrooms.

The most common mistake is letting it grow too long or too hot, so it turns green as it forms spores and tastes bitter.
steps: Soak the rice, then steam it until each grain is cooked through but still firm.
Cool the rice to about 35 °C (95 °F) and mix in the koji spores evenly.
Spread it in an even layer, cover it with a damp cloth, and keep it warm and humid.
Stir the grains when they start to warm up and clump together.
Harvest the koji when the grains are covered in white threads, before any green spores appear.
tips: Buy koji spores from a specialist supplier, because wild molds that look similar can produce toxins.
Discard any batch with black, pink, red or slimy patches, or with a smell of ammonia or rot.
Use fresh koji right away, keep it in the refrigerator for up to 1 week, or freeze it for longer storage.

brew.name: Brew
brew.short: Making beer by turning the starch in malted grain into sugar, boiling it with hops, and letting yeast ferment the sugar into alcohol.
brew.long:
Brewing makes beer in 2 main stages. First, the starch in malted grain is turned into sugar: malt contains enzymes that do this when it soaks in hot water, a step called mashing. The sweet liquid this produces, called wort, is boiled with hops for bitterness, aroma and stability. Then yeast ferments the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. In everyday cooking, brew also simply means steeping tea or coffee in hot water.

Hold the crushed malt in water at about 65 °C (149 °F) for about 60 minutes, then strain off the wort and rinse the grain. Boil the wort with hops for about 60 minutes, cool it quickly, and add yeast. Most ales ferment at 18-20 °C (64-68 °F) for 1-2 weeks. A hydrometer, a floating gauge that measures sugar, shows when fermentation has finished.

The most common mistake is poor cleaning: everything that touches the wort after the boil must be sanitized, or wild microbes will spoil the beer.
steps: Soak the crushed malt in water at about 65 °C (149 °F) for about 60 minutes.
Strain off the sweet liquid, called wort, and rinse the grain with hot water.
Boil the wort with hops for about 60 minutes.
Cool the wort quickly and pour it into a sanitized fermenter with the yeast.
Ferment until the hydrometer reading stays the same over 3 days, then bottle the beer with a measured amount of sugar.
tips: Bottle only after fermentation has finished, because leftover sugar can build enough pressure to burst glass bottles.
Keep the fermenter at a steady temperature, because large swings stress the yeast and create harsh flavors.

starter-culture.name: Starter culture
starter-culture.short: A live population of chosen bacteria, yeasts or molds added to food to start a fermentation quickly and reliably.
starter-culture.long:
A starter culture is a dose of the microbes you want, added at the beginning of a fermentation. Because the wanted microbes start in large numbers, they take over the food before spoilage organisms can grow, and they usually lower the pH faster. This makes the result more predictable and safer. Examples include yogurt from a previous batch, a sourdough starter, the rubbery disc used for kombucha, koji spores, tempeh spores, and freeze-dried powders sold for cheese, sausages or vegetables.

Commercial cultures contain known strains in exact amounts and give the same result every time. Backslopping means adding a little of a finished batch to the next batch; it is simple and free, but over many rounds the culture can weaken or pick up unwanted microbes.

The most common mistake is killing the culture with heat. Add it only after the food has cooled to the temperature the recipe gives, and mix it in evenly.
tips: Store commercial cultures as the package directs, usually in the refrigerator or freezer, and check the date before use.
For tempeh, koji, cheese and cured sausages, use a tested commercial culture rather than relying on wild microbes.
If a saved culture smells wrong, grows colored or fuzzy mold, or stops working, discard it and start again with a fresh culture.

kombucha.name: Kombucha
kombucha.short: A tart, lightly fizzy drink made by fermenting sweetened tea with a culture of yeasts and bacteria known as a SCOBY.
kombucha.long:
Kombucha is sweetened tea fermented by a SCOBY, short for symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, which forms a rubbery disc on the surface. The yeasts turn sugar into a little alcohol and carbon dioxide, and the bacteria turn that alcohol into acetic acid, the same acid found in vinegar. The acid gives the tart taste and protects the drink from spoilage.

Brew black or green tea, dissolve 50-80 g of sugar per 1 liter, and let it cool to room temperature. Pour it into a glass jar, add the SCOBY and kombucha from a previous batch equal to at least 10% of the volume, then cover with a tightly woven cloth. Ferment at 20-25 °C (68-77 °F) for 7-14 days, until it tastes pleasantly tart. For more fizz, bottle it with a little fruit or sugar for 1-3 more days, then refrigerate.

The most common mistake is leaving out the acidic starter liquid, which leaves the sweet tea unprotected while the culture gets going.
steps: Brew the tea, dissolve the sugar in it, and let it cool to room temperature.
Pour it into a glass jar and add the SCOBY with starter liquid from a previous batch.
Cover the jar with a tightly woven cloth and ferment until it tastes tart.
Lift out the SCOBY with some liquid for the next batch, then bottle and refrigerate the rest.
tips: Discard the whole batch, SCOBY included, if you see dry, fuzzy spots of mold; brown threads and a smooth new layer on top are normal.
Ferment in glass, not glazed ceramic or reactive metal such as aluminum, because the acid can draw lead or metal into the drink.
Open bottled kombucha carefully and keep it refrigerated, because pressure can build quickly and burst the bottle.

yogurt.name: Yogurt
yogurt.short: Milk thickened and soured by lactic acid bacteria held at a warm, steady temperature until it sets into a soft gel.
yogurt.long:
Yogurt is milk fermented by lactic acid bacteria. The bacteria turn lactose, the natural sugar in milk, into lactic acid, and the acid makes the milk proteins set into a soft gel with a clean, tangy taste. Heating the milk first changes the whey proteins so they join the gel, which gives a thicker, smoother yogurt, and it also kills microbes that would compete with the culture.

Use pasteurized milk and heat it to 82 °C (180 °F), stirring so it does not scorch. Cool it to 43-46 °C (109-115 °F), stir in plain yogurt with live cultures or a powdered starter, and hold it at that temperature for 4-12 hours without moving it. A longer time gives a firmer, more sour yogurt. Refrigerate it as soon as it has set.

The most common mistake is adding the starter while the milk is still too hot, which kills the bacteria and leaves the milk liquid.
steps: Heat pasteurized milk to 82 °C (180 °F), stirring often.
Cool the milk to 43-46 °C (109-115 °F).
Stir in about 30 g of plain yogurt with live cultures per 1 liter of milk, or the amount of powdered starter on the package.
Cover and hold at 43-46 °C (109-115 °F) for 4-12 hours, until set.
Refrigerate the yogurt at 4 °C (40 °F) or below.
tips: Do not use raw milk, and discard any batch that has not set after 12 hours, smells unpleasant, or shows pink or fuzzy mold.
Check the holding temperature with a thermometer, whether you use a yogurt maker, an oven with only the light on, or an insulated box.
For a thick, strained yogurt, drain the set yogurt in a cloth-lined sieve in the refrigerator for a few hours.

miso.name: Miso
miso.short: A salty, savory paste made by fermenting cooked soybeans with koji and salt for weeks to years.
miso.long:
Miso is a fermented paste of cooked soybeans, koji and salt. The enzymes in the koji break the bean protein into amino acids, which taste savory, and the starch into sugars. Salt keeps spoilage microbes out while the slow fermentation develops flavor. More koji and less salt give a sweet, pale miso in a few weeks; more salt and longer aging give a dark, strong miso after 1-2 years or more.

Soak the soybeans and cook them until they crush easily between your thumb and finger, then mash them. Mix the beans with the koji and salt; many long-aged recipes use about 12% salt by the total weight of the mixture. Press the mixture firmly into a clean container to push out air, smooth the top, cover the surface with salt and plastic film, and put a weight on it. Store it in a cool, dark place and taste it after 3 months.

The most common mistake is leaving air pockets, where mold can grow inside the paste.
steps: Soak the soybeans overnight, then cook them until very soft and mash them.
Mix the mashed beans with the koji and salt, adding a little cooking liquid if the paste is dry.
Pack the mixture tightly into a clean container, pressing out all air pockets.
Cover the surface with a layer of salt and plastic film, then add a weight.
Leave it in a cool, dark place for months, checking and tasting it from time to time.
tips: Sweet, low-salt miso ferments fast and spoils sooner, so move it to the refrigerator as soon as it tastes ready.
A thin white or pale yellow film on top is usually yeast and can be scraped off with the paste just below it; discard the batch if you see fuzzy mold in pink, black or any other color.
Add miso to soups at the end of cooking, below the boil, to keep its aroma.

tempeh.name: Tempeh
tempeh.short: A firm cake of cooked soybeans bound together by the white threads of a Rhizopus mold grown in warm conditions for 1-2 days.
tempeh.long:
Tempeh comes from Indonesia. Cooked, hulled soybeans are mixed with spores of a Rhizopus mold, which grows white threads through and around the beans and binds them into a solid cake. The mold partly breaks down the beans, which makes them easier to digest and gives a nutty, mushroom-like flavor.

Soak and split the soybeans, remove the hulls, and cook them until tender but not mushy. Drain and dry them well, stir in a little vinegar to make them slightly acidic, which holds back harmful bacteria, and cool them below 35 °C (95 °F) before mixing in the tempeh starter. Pack them 2-3 cm (about 1 in) thick in bags or boxes with small holes for air, and keep them at 30-32 °C (86-90 °F). After 24-48 hours the cake should be firm and white and smell like fresh mushrooms. Gray or black spots near the air holes are spores and are harmless.

The most common mistake is packing wet beans, which lets bacteria grow instead of the mold.
steps: Soak, split and hull the soybeans, then cook them until tender.
Drain and dry the beans well, then stir in a little vinegar.
