Cool the beans below 35 °C (95 °F) and mix in the tempeh starter evenly.
Pack them 2-3 cm (about 1 in) thick into bags or boxes with small air holes.
Keep them at 30-32 °C (86-90 °F) for 24-48 hours, lowering the outside heat once the beans start to warm up on their own.
tips: Use a tested tempeh starter from a specialist supplier and never rely on wild mold, because unwanted molds and bacteria can grow in its place.
Discard tempeh that is slimy, smells strongly of ammonia, or shows pink, yellow, green or other colored mold.
Always cook tempeh before eating it, for example by steaming, frying or baking, and refrigerate it as soon as it is finished.

kimchi.name: Kimchi
kimchi.short: A Korean fermented dish of salted vegetables, usually napa cabbage and radish, mixed with chili, garlic, ginger and often fish sauce.
kimchi.long:
Kimchi is a lacto-fermented vegetable dish from Korea. Salting the cabbage draws out water, makes the leaves flexible, and holds back spoilage microbes. Lactic acid bacteria then turn the vegetable sugars into acid, which gives kimchi its sour, fresh and gently fizzy taste. There are many styles, but napa cabbage kimchi is the most common.

Cut the cabbage, salt it, and leave it for several hours, turning it occasionally, until the thick white ribs bend without snapping. Rinse it well and drain it. Mix a paste of chili flakes, garlic, ginger, fish sauce or salted shrimp, and a little sugar or rice paste, then rub it over the leaves together with sliced radish and green onion. Pack the kimchi tightly into a jar, leave it at room temperature for 1-2 days, then refrigerate it, where it keeps ripening slowly.

The most common mistake is not tasting the cabbage after rinsing: it should taste pleasantly salty, not harsh.
steps: Cut the cabbage, salt it, and leave it until the white ribs bend without snapping.
Rinse the cabbage well and drain it.
Mix the seasoning paste and rub it over every leaf together with the radish and green onion.
Pack the kimchi tightly into a jar, pressing out air and leaving space at the top.
Ferment it at room temperature for 1-2 days, then refrigerate it.
tips: Leave 2-3 cm (about 1 in) of empty space at the top of the jar, because fermentation gas can push the liquid up and out.
Press the kimchi down under its own liquid after each use, so the top stays moist and does not grow mold.
Discard kimchi that grows fuzzy mold or smells rotten rather than sour.

vinegar-making.name: Vinegar making
vinegar-making.short: Turning wine, cider or another alcoholic liquid into vinegar by letting acetic acid bacteria convert its alcohol into acetic acid.
vinegar-making.long:
Vinegar is made in 2 stages. First, yeast turns sugar into alcohol, as in wine or cider. Then acetic acid bacteria, which need air, turn the alcohol into acetic acid. These bacteria form a smooth, jelly-like layer on the surface called the mother of vinegar.

Pour wine, cider or beer into a wide glass jar so that a large surface meets the air. Dilute strong wine with water to about 6-8% alcohol, because too much alcohol slows the bacteria. Add raw, unpasteurized vinegar, about 1 part to every 4 parts of liquid, with a piece of mother if available, so the mixture is acidic from the start. Cover the jar with a tightly woven cloth to keep out insects and leave it at 20-27 °C (68-81 °F). After 1-3 months the smell of alcohol is gone and the vinegar tastes sharp.

The most common mistake is sealing the jar, which cuts off the air the bacteria need.
steps: Pour the wine, cider or beer into a wide glass jar, diluting strong wine with water.
Add raw vinegar, and a piece of mother of vinegar if available.
Cover the jar with a tightly woven cloth and leave it in a warm place without moving it.
Taste it after 1 month and continue until no smell of alcohol remains.
Strain the vinegar into bottles, keeping some with the mother for the next batch.
tips: Do not use homemade vinegar for canning or for pickles stored at room temperature, because its acidity is unknown and safe recipes require tested vinegar of at least 5% acidity.
Discard the batch if fuzzy or colored mold grows on the surface; a smooth, pale, rubbery layer is the healthy mother.
Avoid moving the jar while the mother forms, because a disturbed mother can sink and slow the process.

debone.name: Debone
debone.short: Deboning removes the bones from meat, poultry, or fish while keeping the flesh as intact as possible.
debone.long:
Deboning means cutting the bones out of a piece of meat, a bird, or a fish while keeping the flesh as intact as possible. It works because meat is held to the bone by tendons and thin membranes, so a thin sharp blade that follows the bone can free the flesh without tearing it.

Use a short boning knife and keep the tip against the bone. Make small, controlled strokes and pull the meat away with your free hand. Cold meat is firmer and cuts more cleanly. Deboning suits stuffed or rolled roasts, quick-cooking thighs, and making stock from the bones.

The most common mistake is cutting with wide sweeping strokes, which leaves meat on the bone and tears holes in the flesh. When you finish, run your fingertips over the meat to find small bones, especially in fish and poultry.
steps: Chill the meat well and place it on a stable cutting board.
Make a shallow cut along the length of the bone to expose it.
Hold the tip of the boning knife against the bone and cut along it, pulling the meat away as you go.
Cut through joints and tendons instead of forcing the blade through bone.
Lift the bone out and check the meat for small bone fragments.
tips: Keep the knife sharp and cut away from your body and your free hand, because a dull knife slips more easily and causes more injuries.
Use a separate cutting board for raw meat and poultry, and wash the board, the knife, and your hands with hot soapy water afterward.
Refrigerate the bones and trimmings right away and use them for stock soon, or freeze them.

truss.name: Truss
truss.short: Trussing ties a bird or roast with kitchen string so it keeps a compact, even shape and cooks and browns evenly.
truss.long:
Trussing means tying a whole bird or a roast with kitchen string so that it keeps a compact, even shape. Legs and wings that stick out cook faster than the thick breast and can dry out, so pulling them close helps the whole piece cook at the same rate and brown evenly.

For a bird, tuck the wing tips, tie the legs together, and use the string to hold the wings against the body. For a boneless roast, tie loops of string at even intervals along its length. Pat the surface dry first so the string does not slip.

The most common mistake is tying too tightly, which squeezes out juices and can leave the thick thigh joints undercooked. Always check with a thermometer that the thickest part of the thigh reaches 74 °C (165 °F). Remove the string before serving.
steps: Place the bird breast side up and tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders.
Slide the center of a long piece of kitchen string under the tail end, cross it over the ankle ends of the legs, and pull the legs together.
Run both ends of the string along the sides of the breast, between the thighs and the breast, toward the neck end.
Turn the bird over, pull the string across the wings to hold them against the body, and tie a firm knot at the neck end.
tips: Use plain cotton kitchen string, because colored, synthetic, or coated string can melt or burn in the oven.
Use a separate cutting board for raw poultry, and wash your hands and every surface that touched the raw bird.
Measure the temperature in the thickest part of the thigh without touching the bone, because a bird that looks done can still be undercooked there.
truss.diagramAlt: A whole chicken seen from above with 4 numbered marks showing the wing tips tucked back, the string crossed around the legs, the string running along the sides of the breast, and the final knot at the neck end.

carve.name: Carve
carve.short: Carving cuts cooked meat or poultry into neat slices or portions, ideally across the muscle fibers so each piece is tender.
carve.long:
Carving means cutting cooked meat or poultry into slices or portions for serving. Muscle is made of long fibers, and slicing across them leaves short fibers that are easier to chew. Slicing along the fibers gives stringy, tough pieces.

Rest the meat before carving, loosely covered, for at least 10 minutes, and longer for large roasts. During resting the juices spread back through the meat, so less liquid runs out onto the board. Use a long, sharp knife with smooth strokes, and a carving fork or tongs to hold the meat steady.

The most common mistake is carving straight from the oven, which gives dry slices and a board full of juice. Also avoid pressing down on the meat, which squeezes the juices out.
steps: Rest the cooked meat on a board, loosely covered, for at least 10 minutes.
Steady the meat with a carving fork or tongs, keeping your free hand behind the blade.
Find the direction of the muscle fibers, which look like fine parallel lines.
For poultry, cut off the legs and wings at the joints before slicing the breast.
Slice across the fibers with long, smooth strokes using a sharp knife.
Arrange the slices and pour the resting juices over them.
tips: Use a board with a groove or a tray to catch the juices, and place a damp cloth under it so it does not slide.
Keep your free hand well behind the blade at all times, and carve on a stable surface.
Refrigerate leftover meat within 2 hours of cooking.

dry-age.name: Dry-age
dry-age.short: Dry-aging holds a large whole cut of beef uncovered in a cold, controlled refrigerator for weeks to improve tenderness and concentrate flavor.
dry-age.long:
Dry-aging means storing a large, whole piece of beef, uncovered, in a cold and controlled environment for several weeks. Natural enzymes slowly break down the muscle fibers, which makes the meat more tender, while evaporation concentrates the flavor. A hard, dry crust forms on the outside and must be trimmed away, so some weight is lost.

Safety comes first. Use a dedicated refrigerator that holds no other food, kept at 0-3 °C (32-37 °F), with 75-85% humidity and gentle air movement. Only large whole primal cuts (the big sections a butcher first divides a carcass into), such as a bone-in rib section, are suitable. Never dry-age small cuts, steaks, ground meat, or poultry at home.

The most common mistake is aging in an ordinary household refrigerator, where frequent opening causes temperature swings and other foods add contamination.
steps: Choose a large whole cut of fresh beef, with the bone and fat cap left on, from a trusted supplier.
Place the cut on a rack in a dedicated refrigerator held at 0-3 °C (32-37 °F), with 75-85% humidity.
Check the temperature and humidity every day with a thermometer and a humidity gauge.
Inspect the meat regularly and discard it if it feels slimy or smells sour or rotten.
When the aging time is finished, trim off all the dried crust and any discolored surface with a clean knife.
tips: Dry-age only in a dedicated refrigerator fitted with a thermometer and a humidity gauge, never in a refrigerator used for other food.
Leave space around the cut so air can move, and handle it only with clean hands and clean tools.
Never taste the meat to check whether it is safe; if the smell or surface is wrong, throw it away.

portion.name: Portion
portion.short: Portioning cuts a large piece of meat or fish into servings of even size and thickness so each cooks at the same rate.
portion.long:
Portioning means dividing a large piece of meat or fish into servings of equal weight and thickness. Pieces of the same thickness heat through at the same speed, so they finish cooking together instead of some being dry and others undercooked.

Chill the meat well first, because cold, firm flesh cuts more cleanly. Trim tough silver skin, sinew, and excess fat. Use a long, sharp knife and cut with long, smooth strokes rather than sawing, cutting steaks across the muscle fibers. Weigh the pieces on a scale if exact servings matter, and keep the trimmings for stock or grinding.

The most common mistake is cutting pieces of uneven thickness, so thin ends overcook while thick centers stay underdone. Fold thin tail ends under or trim them. After cutting, keep the portions cold until cooking.
steps: Chill the meat or fish well and place it on a stable cutting board.
Decide the portion size by weight and by the number of servings you need.
Trim silver skin, sinew, and excess fat with a sharp knife.
Cut the portions with long, smooth strokes, keeping the thickness even.
Weigh the portions if needed, then cook them or wrap and refrigerate them.
tips: Use a separate cutting board for raw meat and fish, and keep portions refrigerated at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder until cooking.
Freeze portions you will not cook soon, wrapped tightly with the air pressed out.
Rest cooked steaks for about 5 minutes before serving so the juices settle.

devein.name: Devein
devein.short: Deveining removes the dark digestive tract from the back of a shrimp (prawn) so the flesh is clean in taste and texture.
devein.long:
Deveining removes the dark digestive tract that runs along the back of a shrimp (prawn). It is harmless to eat, but it can contain grit and give a gritty texture or a slightly bitter taste, especially in large shrimp. Small shrimp have a thin vein that is often left in.

Hold the shrimp with its back curved upward. Make a shallow cut along the back from the head end to the tail end, just deep enough to expose the vein. Lift the vein out with the tip of the knife or a toothpick, and pull it free. Cut through the shell with small scissors if you want to keep the shell on during cooking.

The most common mistake is cutting too deep, which splits the flesh so the shrimp falls apart when cooked. Keep raw shrimp cold, and cook until the flesh is opaque and firm.
steps: Rinse the shrimp in cold water and peel it, leaving the tail on if you like.
Hold the shrimp with its back curved upward.
Make a shallow cut along the back from the head end to the tail end.
Lift the dark vein out with the tip of the knife and pull it free.
Rinse the shrimp and keep it refrigerated until cooking.
tips: Use a small, sharp knife and keep the blade pointing away from your fingers.
Keep raw shrimp refrigerated at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder, and thaw frozen shrimp in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.
Use a separate cutting board for raw seafood, and discard any shrimp that smell of ammonia.

scale.name: Scale a fish
scale.short: Scaling a fish removes the small, hard scales from its skin so the skin is smooth and pleasant to eat or to cook.
scale.long:
Scaling removes the small, hard, overlapping plates that cover the skin of most fish. Scales are unpleasant to eat, so remove them whenever you will cook or serve the fish with the skin on, such as when pan-frying, roasting, or grilling a whole fish.

Hold the fish firmly by the tail. Use the back of a knife blade or a scaling tool and scrape from the tail toward the head, against the direction the scales lie. Short, firm strokes work best. Work in a sink, under a light stream of cold water, or inside a large bag, because scales fly widely. Check the belly, the base of the fins, and behind the head, where scales are easily missed.

The most common mistake is using the sharp edge of the knife, which cuts the skin. Rinse the fish well afterward and run your fingers over the skin to check that it feels smooth.
steps: Hold the fish firmly by the tail on a stable board, using a towel for grip.
Hold the back of a knife blade or a scaling tool at a slight angle against the skin.
Scrape from the tail toward the head with short, firm strokes.
Turn the fish and repeat on the other side, the belly, and around the fins.
Rinse the fish and run your fingers from tail to head to check that the skin is smooth.
tips: Fin spines and gill covers are sharp, so hold the fish with a towel or wear a cut-resistant glove.
Keep the fish cold, at 4 °C (40 °F) or below, until you cook it.
Wash the board, the sink, and your hands after handling raw fish, and use a separate board for raw fish.

spatchcock.name: Spatchcock
spatchcock.short: Spatchcocking removes the backbone of a whole bird and flattens it so it cooks faster and more evenly, with crisp skin.
spatchcock.long:
Spatchcocking means removing the backbone of a whole bird and pressing it flat. A flat bird has a more even thickness, so the legs and breast cook in a shorter time and the skin browns and crisps over its whole surface.

Use strong kitchen shears to cut along both sides of the backbone, then lift it out. Turn the bird over and press hard on the breastbone until it cracks and lies flat. Season it, then roast it skin side up or cook it on a grill. Keep the backbone to make stock.

The most common mistake is judging doneness by the breast alone. Insert a thermometer into the thickest part of the thigh, not touching bone, and cook until it reaches 74 °C (165 °F). Do not wash raw poultry, because splashing spreads bacteria.
steps: Place the bird breast side down on a stable board with the legs toward you.
Cut along both sides of the backbone with strong kitchen shears and lift the backbone out.
Turn the bird over and press firmly on the breastbone until the bird lies flat.
Tuck the wing tips under, season the bird, and roast it flat with the skin side up.
tips: Cut away from your hands and keep your fingers clear of the shear blades.
Pat the skin dry before seasoning to get crisper skin.
Wash your hands, the board, and the shears with hot soapy water after handling raw poultry.

fillet.name: Fillet
fillet.short: Filleting cuts the flesh of a fish away from its bones to give boneless pieces that cook quickly and are easy to eat.
fillet.long:
Filleting means cutting the flesh of a fish away from the bones in boneless pieces. The knife follows the backbone and the rib bones, so a thin, flexible, sharp blade removes the flesh cleanly with little waste.

Start with a cold, scaled fish. Cut behind the head down to the backbone, then turn the blade toward the tail and slide it along the backbone with long, smooth strokes. Follow the curve of the rib bones. Feel along the fillet with a fingertip for pin bones, the small bones that run in a line along it, and pull them out with clean tweezers. To remove the skin, slide the knife between the flesh and the skin, keeping the blade flat.

The most common mistake is sawing with short strokes, which tears the flesh and leaves meat on the bones. Keep the frame (the bones and head) for stock.
steps: Scale the fish, rinse it, pat it dry, and place it on a stable board.
Cut behind the gill plate down to the backbone.
Turn the blade toward the tail and slide it along the backbone with long, smooth strokes, lifting the fillet away.
Follow the curve of the rib bones to free the fillet fully.
Turn the fish over and repeat on the other side.
Remove the pin bones with clean tweezers, and remove the skin if you want.
tips: Place a damp cloth under the board so it does not slide, and keep your free hand clear of the blade.
Keep the fish refrigerated at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder, and use a separate cutting board for raw fish.
Cook fish until it reaches 63 °C (145 °F) in the thickest part, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily.

shuck.name: Shuck
shuck.short: Shucking opens the hinged shell of an oyster or clam by cutting the muscle that holds it closed, so the meat can be eaten or cooked.
shuck.long:
Shucking means opening a shellfish with a hinged shell, such as an oyster or clam, by cutting the strong muscle that holds the shell closed. It is done with a short, sturdy knife with a blunt tip, because the shell is hard and the blade must not slip.

For an oyster, hold it with the rounded shell down in a folded towel, push the knife tip into the hinge, and twist until it pops. A clam is opened at the front edge instead of the hinge. Slide the blade along the inside of the top shell to cut the muscle, lift off the top shell, then cut under the meat to free it. Keep the liquid in the shell.

The most common mistake is forcing the knife while holding the shell in a bare hand, which can cause a deep cut when the blade slips. Raw shellfish can carry bacteria and viruses, so pregnant people, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity should eat them cooked.
steps: Scrub the shells under cold water and discard any shell that is cracked or open and does not close when tapped.
Wrap a folded towel around your holding hand, or wear a cut-resistant glove, and hold the oyster with the rounded shell down and the hinge toward you.
Push the tip of the oyster knife into the hinge and twist until it pops.
Slide the blade along the inside of the flat top shell to cut the muscle, then lift off the top shell.
Cut under the meat to free it from the bottom shell, keeping the liquid in the shell.
Check the meat for shell fragments and discard any oyster that smells bad.
tips: Always protect your holding hand with a cut-resistant glove or a thick folded towel, because a slipping knife is a common cause of hand injuries.
Discard any shellfish that is open and does not close when tapped, because it is dead, and after cooking discard any that stay closed.
Keep shellfish refrigerated at 4 °C (40 °F) or colder until you open them, and eat them soon after shucking.
